text:
Good morning, everyone. Before we begin, I'd like to speak on behalf of the committee in sending our thoughts to our colleague the member for Indi, Dr Helen Haines MP, her family, her team and her community as she continues to recover in hospital. The attacks against Dr Haines on Monday last week were horrific, and I know we have all come back to this place distressed and in shock at what has happened to our colleague and friend. Dr Haines is much loved as a colleague here, as a strong advocate for her community back in Indi and, indeed, around the nation as a fierce participant in our democracy. Contributions were made in the House of Representatives this week, and the committee did suspend to attend the first of these statements as a mark of respect to Dr Haines. I note that investigations are underway by Victoria Police, the AFP and ASIO, and I ask senators to please be mindful of this during these hearings. Dr Haines is known to all of us as a person of integrity and someone who conducts public debate in a robust but respectful manner. As chair, I will be especially taking this spirit on board throughout our hearings, and I'm sure my fellow senators will join me in this.

I declare open this hearing of the Senate Economics Legislation Committee into the 2026-27 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional owners of the land on which we meet today and pay my respects to their elders past and present. I extend that respect to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples here today.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise. The Senate has also resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policy or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate order specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, and I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. The committee has set Thursday 5 November as the date by which senators are to submit written questions on notice and Thursday 17 December 2026 as the date for the return of answers to questions on notice taken for today's proceedings.

The committee proceedings today begin with the Department of the Treasury, and I now welcome Senator the Hon. Katy Gallagher, Minister for Finance, representing the Treasurer. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?
No, I don't.

The committee also welcomes representatives from the Department of the Treasury Macroeconomic Group and International, Corporate and Investment Group. I welcome Ms Jenny Wilkinson, Secretary of the Treasury. Ms Wilkinson, do you wish to make an opening statement?
I do.
Please go ahead.

Can I start by joining you, Chair, in expressing my deep sympathies for Dr Haines and her family and our shock around the horrific events of last week. The global and domestic economic environment remains as challenging as it was at my last appearance in front of you, in June. Pressures are being felt across almost all economies through geopolitical disruption and uncertainty, elevated inflation, increased demand for capital and tighter financial conditions. Australia also faces these global headwinds. While domestic activity has remained resilient, supported by private demand, and the unemployment rate remains low by historical standards, inflation is above the target band. The effects of increases in interest rates are becoming evident in the economy, including in the labour and housing markets, which should assist in returning inflation to target. While higher bond yields will put upward pressure on the fiscal position, public debt and deficits are relatively low in Australia compared with other advanced economies.

Turning to international conditions, with global pressures becoming more persistent, they are also becoming more difficult to absorb. This is particularly evident in global energy markets. The unresolved conflicts in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine continue to disrupt global energy trade routes and supply chains. Drawdowns of strategic and commercial reserves have provided a partial buffer to date, but inventories can't absorb supply disruptions indefinitely. Pressure is most acute in refined fuel markets, reflecting refinery shutdowns in the Middle East and Russia alongside reduced Chinese exports of refined fuels. Singapore diesel crack spreads, which averaged a little over $10 per barrel between 2017 and 2021, have averaged about $40 per barrel so far this month. Shipping costs have also surged, with the International Energy Agency stating that the cost of transporting crude oil from the Middle East to Asia had climbed to more than five times its pre-conflict levels. This is adding to global inflation, with headline inflation across G7 economies increasing by around 1½ percentage points on average from the start of the year to September and interest rates increasing around the world.

Alongside these geopolitical pressures, the global economy is experiencing another powerful but very different force through the rapid expansion of investment in AI. While the energy shock is constraining supply and weighing on activity, the AI investment boom is supporting growth while also adding to pressure on global prices and resources. AI investment is already very strong. Capital expenditure by the five largest global hyperscalers is forecast to exceed A$1.1 trillion in 2026, which is more than four times its level in 2023. This contributes to our optimism about AI's potential longer term economic and productivity benefits. In the near term, however, the scale of investment is increasing competition for capital and key inputs, including computer chips, construction capacity and skilled labour. There are early signs of this in several economies, including the US. After decades of decline, US prices for some computer equipment have recently risen markedly. In this sense, the investment that should expand productive capacity in the future is also adding to inflationary pressures today.

These forces have contributed to a revaluation of sovereign bonds as markets anticipate tighter monetary policy and reassess neutral real interest rates. This partly reflects strong demand for capital from both the private and public sectors. In some economies, for example parts of the euro area, widening sovereign bond spreads also reflect concerns about fiscal sustainability. At the same time, the strength of the AI investment cycle has contributed to the strong performance of global equity markets this year.

These global developments are flowing through to Australia. Real GDP grew by 2.3 per cent in 2025-26, which is in line with our forecast at budget. Growth was supported by household consumption, dwelling investment and business investment. Growth in public demand has eased, while unemployment remains low by historical standards and the participation rate is close to historical highs. On the other hand, capacity constraints are contributing to persistent services and housing inflation, and this is being exacerbated by the conflict in the Middle East, with higher fuel and supply chain costs adding to those pressures. Household and business sentiment is subdued, with households and some businesses being particularly exposed to these rising costs.

The effects of tighter financial conditions and weaker sentiment are increasingly evident in the housing market in particular. Higher interest rates, heightened global uncertainty and weak consumer sentiment have contributed to a significant decline in established house prices, with the tax reforms announced in the 2026-27 budget also having some effect. The softening has been most pronounced in the wealthier suburbs of Sydney and Melbourne but is now evident across the country. Nationally, dwelling prices have declined by 5.2 per cent from their March peak but remain almost six per cent higher than their levels of a couple of years ago. The price declines have been sharper than in the early stages of most other housing slowdowns over the past 20 years, but the run-up in house prices was also more significant. Consistent with this, the major banks have revised down their dwelling price forecasts materially over recent months.

It is important to distinguish the cyclical and structural drivers of the housing market. Interest rates have a particularly strong cyclical effect because Australia's high share of variable rate mortgages means monetary policy passes relatively quickly to existing and new borrowers. The budget tax reforms are expected to have a more structural effect through their impact on the relative attractiveness of housing to investors. As outlined in the budget papers, the impacts of the tax measures on house prices and rents are expected to be modest over the medium term, while shifting the ownership of the housing stock towards owner-occupiers.

Beyond these cyclical developments, productivity remains a significant long-term challenge. There is no single reform or technology that will lift productivity growth on its own, which is why the government has a broad productivity agenda addressing issues across most sectors of the economy. Sustained improvement will require continued effort across many fronts and active engagement by businesses, workers and governments. AI is expected to make an important contribution, but its impact will depend on adoption and diffusion across the broader business sector, supported by complementary skills, organisational change, investment and policy reforms. These gains will take time to emerge and diffuse through the economy. The 2026-27 budget and the 2026 Intergenerational Report project underlying productivity growth to gradually transition to its long-term growth rate over around five years. This is a more gradual path than previously assumed.

Turning to fiscal policy, the 2026-27 budget update improved the outlook for the fiscal position. The government has taken steps to restrain spending growth, including significant reforms to the NDIS, reforms to means testing and consumer contributions in aged care, changes to the private health insurance rebate, and changes to the home batteries program and the treatment of electric vehicles under the fringe benefits tax arrangements. The temporary reduction in fuel excise announced in March provided initial support to households to help adjust to higher fuel prices, but the full rate was restored on 3 August to avoid sustained pressure on demand and limit the budget impact. The budget continues to face structural pressures, including from the increasing cost of debt, and continued fiscal consolidation will be needed to strengthen fiscal sustainability and provide the flexibility to respond to future shocks.

Treasury will update its economic and fiscal forecasts in MYEFO. Significant uncertainty will remain while the conflict in the Middle East is unresolved and as AI development continues to unfold at pace. The range of possible outcomes is unusually broad. Energy disruptions could persist, financial conditions could tighten further, and the scale and timing of AI related investment and productivity gains remain difficult to judge. Overall, we're expecting growth to slow, and there are downside risks to our budget outlook.

The Intergenerational report released in September places these developments in a longer term context. Previous reports focused on the implications of demographic change, which will continue to shape the economy for decades ahead. However, Australia's working-age population remains more resilient than that of many other OECD countries. Together with the implications of population ageing, the 2026 IGR also considers the profound implications of AI, of geopolitical fragmentation, of the energy transition and of Australia's industrial transformation.

In closing, I'd like to note several organisational changes following the recent departure of Diane Brown. Katrina Di Marco has been appointed to lead Revenue, Small Business and Law Group. Jason Allford is acting as Deputy Secretary of the International, Corporate and Investment Group. To assist the committee, Ms Di Marco will be available to answer questions in both sessions. I welcome your questions.

You talked in your opening statement about strong investment in AI domestically. I wonder if you could make some further comments around whether this is the main driver of business investment improvement. Outside of AI, what else are you seeing in business investment increasing—what sectors?

Perhaps, if I step back, I would observe that the economy has operated more strongly than expected over the period since about the middle of 2025. This has largely been on account of the AI investment boom. I think it's also the case, though, that in the second half of 2025 and the early months of 2026 we had stronger housing investment than we had expected, and the level of consumption was also probably a little stronger than we had expected. What we saw through the second half of 2025 and early 2026 was a strengthening in private sector momentum in the economy, and private demand contributed very significantly to this growth. That's broadly what we've seen. There's no question that the investment that we have seen in AI data centres and related investments was stronger than I think I had seen any of the economic forecasts project over the second half of 2025 and into early 2026. That's been a very significant element of the growth. I might just check whether Dr Grant has anything else to add in terms of investment outcomes which are different from what we expected.

We had the annual national accounts just a week ago, and that gave us a few revisions. Total business investment grew by 8.3 per cent in year average terms in 2025-26, which was quite a bit stronger than we forecast, at four per cent. In terms of the mining and non-mining business investment sectors, both were stronger than our forecasts. Non-mining business investment grew by 10.1 per cent in 2025-26. As the Secretary said, there were very strong growth rates in non-mining business investment last financial year.
What role is the energy transition playing in any of this investment? Are you seeing that as a driver as well?

The ongoing rollout of renewables and the transition of the energy sector is a structural change which has been occurring for some time. It's one of the things that we highlighted in the Intergenerational Report—the fact that this transition is one of the major forces which is impacting the evolution of the economy over the next 40 years. These investments have been occurring for some time, and they've just continued in the most recent periods. I don't think I've got anything in particular to add, but Dr Grant probably does.

Just to say that the Secretary is right; the level of renewable energy projects and investment in them remains fairly high in the economy. That means its contribution to growth has slowed down, because the level is staying up, but we continue to see strong investment in renewable energy projects across Australia.
Finally, what do intentions suggest about private capital expenditure for 2025-26 and then into 2026-27?

We're now into 2026-27. As Dr Grant has said, private business investment was certainly above previous expectations and our expectations through 2025-26. While they are now at a very high level—and sometimes when you get a very strong level of investment you expect to have some correction—I think it remains the case that we have continued to be surprised on the upside in terms of investment expectations. Dr Grant?

Yes, that's correct. In the latest capex survey, which does give us a forward estimate for what business views as the increase in capital investment in 2026-27, we received the third estimate as the last one, and that was another lift up. That suggests growth of 3.6 per cent in 2026-27. This is a slightly different translation to the national accounts, so we have to take a little bit of care, but non-mining capex is expected to grow, according to this survey, by 5.5 per cent in 2026-27, so continuing strong growth.
Senator Hume.

Secretary, last month the Reserve Bank wrote to the House economics committee. I'm assuming you've seen this letter. If you haven't, I'm quite happy to table it, but I think it's been published pretty widely. The last paragraph of this letter states:

While the composition of a specific spending proposal matters, in general lower government spending would reduce aggregate demand unless it was offset by stronger spending elsewhere. If this eased capacity pressures, it would also tend to reduce inflationary pressures.

Secretary, can I ask if you agree with the RBA that, in general, lower government spending would reduce aggregate demand and tend to reduce inflationary pressures.

What I would say is that any questions like this have to be answered in the specific, not in the general. It does matter what the spending is on, but it also matters what the aggregate fiscal position is. Generally, when economists think about the impact of government on the economy, they think about it in two ways. One of them is to look at the difference between the contribution of public and private demand in the national accounts context. The other is to look at the underlying cash balance, so the deficit—that's the net of what government is adding to or detracting from the economy—and how that changes over time. It's important to look at the change in the underlying cash balance overall, whether that's between budget updates or across time, in order to make an assessment of what the impact of government spending on aggregate activity is.

In that same letter to the House economics committee, the Reserve Bank indicated that it has already undertaken some economic modelling of how changes in government spending may impact inflation. I want to ask whether Treasury has modelled the impact of lower government spending on inflation.

In every budget update we take the projection of the underlying cash balance and the details of government spending and we incorporate those in our macroeconomic forecasts. Those are one of the important elements that we consider as we are adjusting our macroeconomic forecasts every year—not every year, I should say, but twice a year, at every update. That is part and parcel of the macroeconomic forecasting exercises that we are doing on an ongoing basis. We take into account how the government fiscal position, usually measured by the underlying cash balance—but also we can look at it more broadly—has changed in the most recent update and how that then flows through into how we are thinking about macroeconomic developments. That is just an ongoing part of the work that we do.
That's a comprehensive answer, but I'm not entirely sure it's a clear one. Have you modelled the impact of lower government spending on inflation?

As I said, I don't think that's a question that you can answer in the general. You have to look at it in the specific. What's the specific proposal? What is the specific type of expenditure which is proposed to be changed? We'd have to consider what the imported component of that expenditure is. For example, if it was a significant fall in, let's say, defence equipment, and most of that defence equipment was imported, then that wouldn't have a particularly significant impact on its own on demand in the economy. On the other hand, if the change in spending were also associated with changes in taxation, you need to take into account the net impact of all of those. That's why we look at the underlying cash balance in aggregate. That's the standard way of looking at the impact of government spending and government conditions on the macroeconomic outlook.

There is no macroeconomic model that would include specific proposals surely. Macroeconomic models, by their very nature, model macroeconomics, and they would look at government spending not as individual proposals but in general, as a whole.

As I said, when we are preparing our macroeconomic forecasts—and Dr Grant might like to add to this—the forecasting framework through which we operate is the national accounts forecasting framework, which means that we have to make assessments about what is going to happen to public demand and private demand. We have to make assessments about what the net impact of government decisions are on both public and private demand. That is the way in which that flows through into our macroeconomic forecasts. Is there anything else you'd like to add?
That's it.
Let me try another way. Is the current fiscal policy expansionary?

The way I think you need to think about this is: how have government decisions over time added to or detracted from activity in the economy? One of the things that we've observed over the last 12 months or so, since the middle of 2025, is public demand growth coming off and private demand growth lifting. Public demand has made less of a contribution to economic growth in the economy over this last period than private demand. Certainly, when I look at what the surprises have been over the past 18 months, as I mentioned earlier, the thing that we have been surprised by has been that private demand in the economy has been stronger than we expected. Business investment has been stronger than we expected. Housing investment was stronger than we expected in the second half of last year and into the first half of this year. Consumption was a bit stronger than we had expected, given the levels of sentiment. All of those things are what have surprised us on the upside. When I look at what has happened to fiscal policy over this period, the underlying cash balances in 2025-26 and 2026-27 have both fallen reasonably substantially from where they were predicted to be. When I think about what the expected level of the deficit in 2025-26 and 2026-27 was going to be—if I think back to the end of 2024, let's compare what fiscal policy has done over the period since the end of 2024 or the beginning of 2025. Over that period the underlying cash balance has come in quite substantially, by almost a per cent of GDP.
That's not due to a reduction in expenditure; that's due to an increase in revenue.

It's been a function of the broad range of decisions which have been taken by government and the changes in the underlying conditions, but it is the case—it's not unreasonable—that the underlying cash balance, as the net measure of the impact of government on the economy, has come in. That has reduced.
Spending is at its highest level in 40 years outside of the pandemic. Surely you can agree that's true?
What I'm saying is that if you're trying to think about what the net impact of government is on demand in the economy, you have to look at what the change in the underlying cash balance has done.
I have lots more questions on this.
Do you want to take another 10-minute block? Then I'll rotate the call.
Yes, absolutely. I'm very happy to do that. Is the deficit this year bigger than last year?

The deficit for 2025-26 in the final budget outcome came in at $22.3 billion, which is 0.8 per cent of GDP. That was lower than we expected at budget, that was lower than we expected at MYEFO and it was lower than we expected in the previous updates. The deficit for 2026-27 is $31.5 billion, which is about one per cent of GDP.

If we have a bigger deficit this year than last year, surely that is an indicator of an expansionary fiscal policy? If spending is higher now than it has been in 40 years, surely that is an indicator of an expansionary fiscal policy? Yes, even if public sector growth is lower than it was two or three years ago, it's not necessarily the growth that's the problem; it's the quantum, it's the amount, it's the proportion of growth in the economy that is the concern. Do we have an expansionary fiscal policy?

We're running a deficit of about one per cent of GDP. That is a much lower deficit than in many, many countries around the world. The point that I'm trying to make is that, when we're trying to understand what's contributing to the stronger growth that we've seen over this past year, where we've been surprised has not been in terms of there being a higher deficit. Where we've been surprised—I'm just telling you honestly—has been on the private sector side.
With private sector growth?
Private sector growth has been stronger than we expected; that's right.

Ms Hunter, who is the RBA Assistant Governor, said on 60 Minutes on Sunday night, in response to a question about the role of government spending in driving inflation, that government spending is definitely part of the picture. Do you agree with the RBA that government spending contributes to inflationary pressures?
No-one is denying that government spending is part of demand in the economy. No-one is denying that. That's clearly the case.

Thank you. You're a member of the Reserve Bank Board. You would be furnished with the information on which the experts at the RBA, like Ms Hunter, used to form their views. That's correct, I'm assuming? You get the benefit of Treasury information as well in your role as Treasury Secretary. Is there any conflict in the advice and the reviews that you are provided by the RBA as opposed to the Treasury?

Absolutely, I'm a member of the Reserve Bank Board. I don't think it's appropriate for me to speak to the papers that I receive in the context of the RBA Board briefings. I have to sign secrecy provisions.
I'm not asking you to reveal any details.

No. In respect of the discussions that we have around the macroeconomic outlook, to be honest, including the discussions that my officers have with RBA staff, there are times we have differences of views. I think it is healthy, frankly, that we have differences of views about the outlook, but I don't think that there is any difference of view that, if you look over the past 12 months, where we have been surprised in relation to activity—and I think the Governor has said this—is we have been surprised by the strength of private demand in the economy. To be honest, that's been a surprise not just to the government agencies; that's been something which has surprised most market economists. When I look back, frankly, when I took this role in the middle of 2025, we were in an easing phase at the Reserve Bank. The market's expectation was that there were going to be a significant number of additional easings. The outlook was for inflation to come back to target. The outlook was for growth to slow. Macroeconomic forecasting is hard, but that's just not what has turned out to have occurred. When we look at why that has not turned out to have occurred, the things that have been very different from what we had expected, as I said, have been that the private sector level of activity has been stronger than we expected. That's the predominant driver of this difference.
I'm sorry, are you telling me that is the only thing that is driving inflation?
No, I'm definitely not telling you that's the only thing that's driving inflation.
You didn't ask that question.

In fact, if I was to talk about all of the different things that are driving inflation, one of the things that I would definitely point to is, again, what was unexpected. In addition to what's happening in private demand, there is what has happened in the Middle East. The Middle East shock has been a shock that has affected inflation, as I said in my opening statement, across almost all economies around the world. The increases in fuel costs, the disruption to broader supply chains—all of that is putting an inflation pulse through the economy. That is definitely also contributing. In fact, it's making a very significant contribution to the increase in inflation that we have observed over the past six months.

A chorus of economists have now consistently highlighted the impact of government spending on inflation. Yes, there are other factors, but you can only control what you can control here. Economist Chris Richardson was recently quoted in the Australian Financial Review saying that the RBA is fighting inflation and government spending is not helping. Do you agree with Mr Richardson's assessment?

I think the point you make, which is that we can only control what we can control, is the right way of thinking about this. When I look at the net decisions—so the decisions and the changes in the budget position over these last 18 months—in aggregate, all of those have taken some pressure from the government out of the economy. There is a separate argument about whether there's additional activity that should be taken out. That's a different matter. If you're asking me whether the changes in the net fiscal position have contributed to this increase in inflation that we have observed over the past 18 months, then I think it's very hard to sustain that argument.

Sorry. You just said that we can assess the impact of government on inflation by looking at the impact of decisions over time. That's exactly what Chris Richardson has said. He has reported that the net impact of decisions is to worsen the bottom line by $110 billion; that was the number that he used. Are you suggesting that has not pushed up inflation?

We have improved the UCB at every budget and budget update, Senator Hume. If Mr Richardson wants to have an argument about what government is investing in, fair enough. I probably will disagree with him. There are so many economists and commentators on this, many with different views. I don't agree with all of them; I don't disagree with all of them. If you look in aggregate at the impact on the UCB, you will see that our decisions and the savings, including savings that you are opposing—that is, you want to spend more—are reducing pressure, because we are improving the bottom line.
You have one more minute.

In the AFR, AMP Chief Economist Shane Oliver said that the problem is that the high level of public spending is contributing to capacity constraints in the economy and lower than otherwise productivity, contributing to high inflation and rate hikes. Secretary, do you agree with Mr Oliver's assessment?

I think I've made my position clear. I think we have to be clear about this. This is always hard; with the benefit of hindsight, could there be different policies which could have been introduced? They could have been. At every budget and every MYEFO governments have to make decisions about what spending and taxation decisions they are going to make in order to set fiscal policy, frankly, in their judgement, appropriately in the context of the macroeconomic outlook which is available and in the context of their priorities. What I'm saying is that, when I think about the 2025-26 budget, the 2025-26 MYEFO and the 2026-27 budget—in all of those cases the net impact of fiscal policy on the macroeconomy in 2025-26 and 2026-27 has been reduced. You can see that if you look at what has happened to the series of estimates for the underlying cash balance in those two years. So that is—
Sorry.
I'm going to have to rotate the call.
Can I just speak? I just need to be very clear on this.
This is your last question.
Did you just say that the net decisions have reduced—

I'm not trying to be misleading. What I'm saying is when you look at the aggregate outcomes in the budget paper—so if you look at what has happened to the underlying cash balance in 2025-26 and 2026-27, the underlying cash balance for 2025-26 has come in from a deficit that was expected to be about $42 billion, or 1.5 per cent of GDP—that was at the 2025-26 budget—to $22 billion, and the deficit for 2026-27 has come in from what was expected to be about $36 billion to about $31 billion.
Sorry, are these net decisions?
I'm going to rotate the call.

I seriously need to clarify this answer, because I have a feeling it might be misleading. Ms Wilkinson, you were the one who used net decisions as the benchmark here. Are they net decisions that you're talking about?

When I say 'net', I'm saying you look at the underlying cash balance, which is the net of spending decisions, tax decisions and outcomes, which are estimates variations. I'm not trying to be misleading. I'm saying the net impact of all of the budget outcomes—
Sorry, are you talking about decisions or net impacts?

No, I'm talking about the underlying cash balance; that's what I'm talking about. I'm talking about what the change in the underlying cash balance has been, and the change in the underlying cash balance is not an unreasonable estimate of the impact of government spending on the economy.
I'm rotating the call. Senator Payman.

My questions relate to the ban on the purchase of established dwellings by foreign persons. I refer to an article published in the Australian in June titled 'Treasury warned Chalmers on housing ban', which quotes from Treasury documents released under OPD in which the department warned the Treasurer that uncertainty around the ban was reducing investor confidence and discouraging build-to-rent investments. Was this possibility considered before the policy was implemented?
I might ask Mr Tinning to take this question; he's responsible for the Foreign Investment Division.

Yes, the ban was designed to respond to the pressures on the housing market. The government announced that there would be a change to the policy which enabled investors under certain conditions, if they were foreign persons, to purchase dwellings. The government made the decision to tighten the circumstances in which foreign persons could buy established dwellings. I'm happy to go into details on the policy.

text: In February, I also asked a question about the effect the ban has had on housing supply, to which Treasury responded, 'The temporary ban on foreign purchases of established dwellings enables Australians to buy homes that would have otherwise been bought by foreign investors while retaining incentives foreign investors to contribute to new housing supply.' I feel like that was another non-answer. Does Treasury have any actual data on the effect that the ban has had on housing supply, or is the effect so small that you simply can't quantify it?

I suppose there are two points to make here. Firstly, only a very small proportion of Australian residential dwellings—and this is new and established—are purchased by foreign persons. In 2024-25, half a per cent of purchases of residential dwellings were made by foreign persons, as defined under the FATA, and the overall purchases were in excess of 540,000. Unpublished data breaks down the approvals by property type, and it indicates that there's been an approximate 77 per cent decrease in applications for established dwellings between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 years. This decrease is likely attributed to the ban commencing on 1 April 2025 and also the tripling of established dwelling application fees in April 2024. There are two factors that have contributed to that 77 per cent decrease in applications.
witness_organisation: Treasury International, Corporate and Investment Group

witness_organisation: Treasury International, Corporate and Investment Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Foreign Investment Division

witness_organisation: Treasury International, Corporate and Investment Group

text: I'm going to have to rotate the call. Senator Bragg.
I have a couple of questions on housing. How many houses will we get in Australia this year?
We have forecast dwelling investment, which is slightly different from the number of houses.

I'm asking how many houses the Treasury thinks we'll get in Australia this year. I know that housing is a key issue for the government and, Secretary, you mentioned it in your opening statement. How many houses will we get this year?
Housing Group may be better placed than I am.
You don't know? Secretary, do you know how many houses we're supposed to get in Australia this year?

I don't have that with me. As I said, from a macroeconomic perspective, we look at approvals, commencements and completions, and they have all increased reasonably significantly over the past year. Dwelling investment, as Dr Grant said—
Completions haven't increased.
All of these are measures of additions to the housing stock. From a macroeconomic perspective, we don't forecast the number of houses.
If you don't know, it's fine. We'll move on. I want to be efficient.
As we've said, the Housing Group is best placed to answer questions about conditions—
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Macroeconomic Conditions and Population Division

text: The Secretary is here. This is a key issue.
The National Housing Supply and Affordability Council publishes its report in August, and so those numbers are to be used.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Macroeconomic Conditions and Population Division

text: Coming back to you, Secretary, in terms of the other issues I want to ask about in terms of housing. The budget contains measures to restrain housing supply in terms of the taxes, but also, subsequent to the budget, there was the deal with the Greens in the Senate to cut housing supply through SMSF investment. Why is it a good idea to reduce housing supply in any event, in a housing crisis, and how many fewer houses will there be as a result of the SMSF ban?

I might come back to your question. The data I have—and I'm very happy for you to confirm this with Housing Group—is that 176,000 private dwellings were completed over 2025-26. That's how many houses were built in 2025-26. As I said, the pipeline, which we measure through things like approvals and commencements, has suggested that there is ongoing activity through into 2026-27.
The question is: why are you cutting housing supply, and how many fewer houses will there be as a result of the SMSF ban?

In the budget, the government also announced the Local Infrastructure Fund. The Local Infrastructure Fund is designed to provide the enabling infrastructure in order to support additional housing, so you need to look across all of these measures together. I don't have an estimate in front of me of the net impact of all of these figures. I don't know whether, Dr Grant does, but I'm sure that, when Housing Group appear later in the—
The Treasurer said 4,000 fewer houses will be built as a result of the SMSF ban. Did you talk to the Treasurer about this particular proposal before it passed the Senate?
I'm just saying I don't have those numbers, and I don't want to mislead the Senate. Ms Di Marco might be able to help you.

In terms of the limited recourse borrowing arrangements, I understand that's the figure that the Treasurer used. The number that we have is that overall in 2023-24 around 8,700 SMSFs entered into a new limited recourse borrowing arrangement. Again, when you look at that in terms of the scale of the overall lending or activity in the economy, that's less than half a percentage point of new residential borrowing every year. Then that's going to have both established and new. Once you start to break that down—again, these are quite small changes.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I understand that. The point here is that, why you want to restrain housing supply in a housing crisis? We just heard from the Secretary we might get 180,000 houses in this country this year. We used to get more than 200,000. Minister, you did this deal, I think, with the Greens in the Senate. There was no RIS undertaken. You say the Treasurer has said 4,000 fewer houses as a result of this ban; the industry says it is more like 16,000. Do you stand by your 4,000 figure, Minister?
I think Ms Di Marco just gave you the figure.
Do you stand by it?
The evidence that's just been given to you is evidence from Treasury, and I trust that advice. In relation to—
The reason I ask—

Can I answer? I don't know what's going on, but you are interrupting a lot, Senator Bragg. In the budget papers, overall, the budget delivers 30,000 more homes. In some of the data that we've been seeing recently, commencements were up seven per cent in the June quarter after the budget and 14.4 per cent in annual terms. When we came to office, they were going backwards 28.9 per cent in annual terms. Completions were also up 5.8 per cent in the quarter and 15.9 per cent in annual terms. When we came to office, they were going backwards seven per cent.
That's not right.

I don't think anyone could sit here and say that the government is not using every lever available to ensure we are driving supply across the housing market. You've been critical of all of the policies—
I've only had six minutes.
that we've implemented in order to do that and in fact have tried to delay it on many occasions.

I want to be efficient; I don't mean to be obtuse. I'm just trying to get a lot of information out in the short time I have. You mentioned in your opening statement the impact that the taxes—I think you called them 'tax reforms'—are having on the housing market. What is the impact they're having in terms of prices?

In the budget papers there's a box—I can't remember exactly what box it is—which outlined our analysis of the tax reforms and the budget overall. As I said in my opening statement, you do have to think differently about what the structural versus the cyclical drivers of changes in the housing market are. For the most part, the cyclical changes that we're seeing in the housing market are what you would expect from having had four increases in interest rates over the course of this year. The most significant impact—and I'm pretty sure that most private economists are also of this view—that we're seeing in the housing market is the consequence of increases in interest rates, because housing investments in Australia are typically funded through variable rates. For the most part, the housing cycle is interest rates. Is there an impact of taxes? As I said in my opening statement, yes, I think there would be some impact of that. The modelling that we did for the purpose of the budget was trying to understand what the structural impact of those changes would be, and the net impact of those changes plus the Local Infrastructure Fund was that there would be additional housing supply in the budget.

So you're saying 'some impact'; fine. In terms of the price impacts on people who have taken out 95 per cent loans—there's been 100,000 in the last year who have taken out 95 per cent loans underwritten by the government. A lot of those people would now be living in some of those suburbs, mainly in Melbourne and Sydney, that have gone down by more than five per cent. How many people do you think are in negative equity today?

I think you can talk to the RBA about this when they come in. They addressed this in the Financial Stability Review, which was recently released. What we know from the five per cent deposit scheme is that 99.7 per cent of participants in that scheme are either ahead or on schedule with their payments. Only 0.3 per cent of participant households are in more than 90 days of arrears. That's a lower proportion than in all housing loans.

Before I get the wind-up, what I wanted to ask you about is this. You talked about the recalibration of the housing market, and I've heard the Treasurer and the finance minister talk about it. I think it's code for, 'We effectively want there to be more owner-occupiers', but what we've seen since the budget is reduced lending to owner-occupiers. Who do these taxes help?

As to what we've seen since the budget—the most forward indicator of activity in the housing market is the lending data. What we see from the lending data is that within the investor community there has been a wind-back in lending for existing dwellings.
Owner-occupiers and investors?

I'm talking about investors, first of all. There has been a wind-back in lending to investors for the purchase of existing dwellings. That fell by about 13 per cent in the June quarter. On the other hand, the lending to investors for the construction of new dwellings or lending to investors for the purchase of newly erected dwellings both rose by about 6½ per cent in the June quarter and were nearly 26 per cent higher over the year. That's the June quarter indicator of what was happening in the investor market. In the owner-occupier market, there has been a fall in the value of new loan commitments to owner-occupiers. In fact, the fall has been greater for non-first home buyers than for first home buyers. For first home buyers, the value was roughly flat in the June quarter and it's still up 10 per cent over the year.
Last question.
Who does it help? It's not clear to me. If investors have been pushed out of the market—
They're not.
and therefore dwelling investment is going down, then there are fewer loans to owner-occupiers. Who are these taxes actually going to help?
That's not the evidence that you've just heard.
It is the evidence.
No. There has been a change in the investment category from owner-occupier to new construction, essentially, new builds—

We're talking about a different thing, Minister. I'm asking about loans to owner-occupiers. If the stated aim of your tax changes was to get more owner-occupiers, it has failed because every major bank is saying lending to owner is down and that is the evidence we just heard from your secretary.

I guess we're trying to distinguish between what's happening because of the cycle and what's happening in terms of the structural changes. What I'm saying is when I look at the investors and I look at the difference of their behaviour between existing dwellings and new dwellings, the investor behaviour, based on the loan commitments data that we have to date, suggests that there's been a shift, a reasonably significant shift, towards newly constructed dwellings.
Are there fewer loans to owner-occupiers or not?
Yes, and that's because—
There are. Thank you.
That's because there is a downturn in the housing market. Interest rates have gone up and therefore—
Nothing to do with the taxes?
I didn't say that. I said in my opening statement that the most significant impact is coming from four increases in interest rates this year. I think I was clear in my opening statement.
Senator McDonald.

We've spoken before at estimates about modelling, particularly Australia's net zero transformation: Treasury modelling and analysis, that was released by Treasury. We spoke, too, about the crossover on the projected decline in fossil fuel exports and the increase in green exports.
Yes, I recall that.

I want to revisit that because I specifically asked Dr Johnson from Revenue Group about the impact of that modelling. Whilst I understand we're in macro—I could see your alarm that I might be in the wrong group—I don't want to miss the relevant section. I just want to come back to this point that we have modelling from a part of Treasury that's showing that fossil fuel exports will be overtaken by green exports. From the graph it looked to be in about 2032 to me, but I just want to confirm if you have a year?
Dr Grant, can you help the senator?
I can. I think I have found the chart you are referring to, and you are correct. I don't know the exact date, but it does look like the crossover occurs around 2032.

Treasury representatives from Revenue Group directed me to the updated Intergenerational report, which hadn't been released at that time, as a guide for the impact of net zero on Australia's economy. Specifically, when I asked about the modelling behind these forecast replacements of fossil fuels by green exports, Ms Brown said that the Intergenerational report would specifically address impacts on revenue sources—because that's what I'm interested in; where's the money coming from—from climate change and also the opportunities from climate change. That was in February 2026 estimates. When I've gone back and looked at the 2026 Intergenerational report, it claims that Treasury modelling for Australia's Net Zero Plan, released in 2025, found that Australia's plan will support continued economic growth and Australia's exports were projected to grow over time with declining global demand for fossil fuels counterbalanced by the emergence of new renewable energy export markets. My question is: where is the modelling or evidence that Treasury is relying on for this claim, because the Intergenerational report is pointing back to this Treasury modelling and there is no further detail in the Intergenerational report around modelling. We're now in this circular cycle, but there's been no impact on revenue forecasts, because they're pointing to the updated Intergenerational report.

Let's see if we can help you. I've got Ms Di Marco here from Revenue Group. She's not representing Revenue Group here, so we'll see how she can go. We might need to come back to it at Revenue Group and the modelling. What specifically is your question?

My specific question is: what modelling or evidence is Treasury relying on for this claim that fossil fuel exports will have been exceeded by green exports by 2032? Then I'll follow up with the revenue side of that.

You are correct, but this is scenario modelling that was released in September of 2025 as part of the government's announcement on the Net Zero Plan. The modelling, or the lines in the chart that you're referring to, are based on three different scenarios, which I think you know so I won't labour the point. The baseline scenario accords with the government's Net Zero Plan commitments, and it's an orderly transition to net zero by 2050. Based on the model projections and all that needs to move in the economy in order to meet the net zero commitments, these are the scenarios that we've published, and they're the same as we've published in the Intergenerational Report. So they are not different to what was published in net zero.

I understand that, but we live in the world of reality of what we export and what we can bank as a nation. As to the data that underpins this—you've got these net zero targets and goals, but we have two Treasury documents here, the modelling that Treasury is using to underpin its plan for the net zero economic transition and the 2026 Intergenerational Report, both of which continue to claim that our national exports, with coal and gas making up approximately a quarter of the export value, will be overtaken sometime in the 2030s by green exports. However, there is no data that supports that, because that would highlight export earnings dropping from almost $140 billion in 2025 to around $20 billion in the 2040s. That's an annual revenue decrease of $120 billion—$1.2 trillion over a decade—of lost revenue. As an alternative, Treasury claims that these green exports will not only replace but exceed fossil fuel exports. Again, I'm trying to understand this. Apart from the climate change modelling, which is not based on tonnes of ore out of the ground or demand from overseas markets, this is purely based on an emissions target. This is really serious—$1.2 trillion over 10 years—and yet there is no data that supports this climate change projection, which I think is not flagging the revenue cliff that we're looking at. There's also no data that supports that the green export income source, particularly for revenue for Treasury, is going to in any way offset that.

There might be two different questions here. One is: what is the modelling framework, and what are the assumptions around the transitions that are likely to occur, based on assumptions about what other countries are doing and based on assumptions about technological changes going forward? There's a whole range of assumptions which feed into the modelling that Dr Grant has talked about, which is the modelling that we published last year in September. We've been pretty explicit in that report around what all of the assumptions are. As I say, there are key assumptions around other country transitions and around technology which underpin any scenario modelling of this nature. I think we've been very explicit about that. We certainly consulted extensively in the development of that modelling work. We were also open about the fact that different people can have different assumptions about some of these technological developments. That's one question, which is the modelling and whether you agree or don't agree with the modelling projection. The second question is: what flow-on effect does that then have for revenue? That's a separate question.

May I just put a pin in that, because three weeks ago, in October, ASEAN's energy ministers endorsed a new energy outlook. The report was in part funded by the Australian government, and it paints a very different picture. Under its baseline scenario, South-East Asia's coal supply more than triples by 2060. Even if member countries implement their stated energy policies and targets, coal remains a major part of their energy supply for decades. Under ASEAN's most ambitious transition scenario, the region's energy related emissions are still higher in 2060 than they are today, but yet Australia is modelling that our fossil fuel exports would have declined and declined to a point that they would be exceeded by green exports, which is a side issue. My concern is that we are modelling a transition away from a major export earner that is not supported by our nearest neighbours in their energy outlook.

I don't know what implications the report you're talking about from ASEAN countries has for the modelling. The modelling that we conducted, and we released in September of last year drew upon a very wide range of international sources and estimates. We drew heavily on the International Energy Agency, which tries to look globally at these trends. Any modelling exercise is a point-in-time exercise. In any modelling exercise there are assumptions that you have to make about a whole range of different things. No modelling exercise is a predictor of the future. It is an attempt to try to estimate, based on the available information at that time, what the likely future scenario looks like. That's what we're trying to do in that modelling exercise. I am sure that over time, as the world unfolds, as technology unfolds—and we can never predict exactly where technology is going to go—as these things change, we would come back to modelling and make an assessment as to whether there are changes in our projections. I don't know; Dr Grant might have a view as to whether there's anything significant that's changed since September of last year in relation to the key drivers and assumptions under our modelling report. Dr Grant, do you have anything?

I would simply say that all of the global assumptions are set out in the technical appendix on page 16. You are correct; there has been a range of new information, some of it global and some of it domestic. We have not updated the modelling in a holistic sense for all new information since September of 2025.

Chair, this is my last question. I'm wondering if DISR was involved with the construction of the Intergenerational Report, because DISR is certainly, I think, less fanciful than the net zero report, and the Intergenerational Report, of course, just points back to that Treasury modelling. It would seem to me that our near neighbours are saying that their demand for coal is going to triple, that it is a major income earner for Australia. Treasury is budgeting and doing modelling around expenditure on Australian government spending, but where is the really tight, disciplined work happening on where the money comes from? Unless we have a good understanding, and a realistic understanding, aren't we getting all this wrong? We're just guaranteeing growing debt for Australia. I think this is really important. Will you update your modelling to reflect this more realistic scenario of fossil fuels, coal and gas, not declining but, indeed, growing?

These sorts of long-run projections do need to be updated from time to time. Typically, the key drivers of these outcomes don't vary a lot from one month to the next. I don't have a timeframe for you about when there would be an update to that modelling exercise. That's not something which we are in the process of doing at the moment. We continue to work closely with agencies across the service, and we certainly consulted extremely widely. In fact, I think all relevant agencies were consulted deeply in the development of the modelling report that we published in September. The only thing I can say is that there is a difference between trying to think about what some of these really long-term shifts and trends are likely to be and the shorter term, such as our assessment of what's happening in the budget, what we know is happening to tax receipts and what we predict is happening to tax receipts over the forward estimates and the medium term.
Just to clarify, DISR—

I think the point you're making, which is an absolutely reasonable one, is that the net zero transition is a very significant transition for Australia and for the world. I think that's clear in the modelling report that we've done.
I'm going to have to rotate the call.
You looking at two datasets: DISR, reality; and Treasury, the agency which I always think of as being dry and reliable—
I don't think there's a difference of view between us and DISR. Dr Grant?

On page 16 and 17 of the technical appendix—it's previous DISR work, but at the time we used the DISR projections on coal, oil, critical minerals, iron ore, iron and steel—and it goes on. That is to say that they were the DISR projections at the time that we did this modelling. No doubt DISR will have updated those projections. We haven't updated the net zero modelling for any updated projections, domestic or global.
Senator McKim.

For some time, US tech companies have been charging themselves service fees, which is a way to avoid their tax liabilities in Australia and shift profit out of this country and into their tax havens in Delaware. Pleasingly, the ATO is starting to muscle up to some of these US tech companies and taxing these payments as royalties. Can I ask whether you've received any representations from the US Treasury about the ATO's actions? The tech bros are upset, so Trump is upset, so the US Administration is upset, and so the US Treasury is upset. Ms Wilkinson, have you received any correspondence from the US Treasury or any other arm of the US government or any US tech companies about the ATO's actions?

I would have to check if we've received any written correspondence since the announcement of the ATO's ruling on software royalties. We had certainly received representations from the US previously, because the ATO had been telegraphing this and there had been conversations for some time. I'm not too sure if we've seen written representations. I'm aware that at the—I'm going to get this wrong—I think it was called the institute for fiscal affairs or the Institute for Fiscal Studies conference that was in Melbourne last week, there was certainly a representative from the US Treasury there, and she certainly made remarks to that effect. I'm just not sure if we've received correspondence from them, but this is a longstanding conversation with the US. The ATO's ruling was almost the last phase of that conversation, but I would expect it to continue, given the statements that she made last week.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Ms Wilkinson, you'd expect that if a letter arrived from the US Treasury to the government or to your department that would cross your desk, wouldn't it?
I would have expected so, yes.
Can you recall whether—
I don't recall receiving any correspondence about this ruling.
Could you take on notice, please, whether you have—
I'm happy to, yes. We'll get back to you.
on that issue, including prior to the ATO's announcement and obviously post the ATO's announcement? Minister, have you received any correspondence on this matter?
Not that I am aware of, but I will check, just in case. I don't believe so.
Could you also take on notice whether you're able to provide any correspondence you've received to the committee?
If we have received any.

Are you aware that when France proposed a digital tax in the recent past Trump threatened a retaliatory increase in tariffs and France backed down from their proposal to implement their new digital tax? Minister, are you concerned that we might be facing a similar tactic from the Trump Administration, and will your government back in the ATO to the hilt in its attempt to make the tech bros pay a fair rate of tax on the profits they generate in this country?
I think the PM has always been clear in matters like this that are raised that we would always take decisions in Australia's national interest.
Does that include backing in the ATO, or are you going to collapse? You've got a Prime Minister who, astoundingly, thinks taking photos, selfies, with Donald Trump is a good idea.
We make decisions in our national interest, and we support the work of the ATO.
I beg your pardon? What was the last thing you said, sorry?
And we support the work of the Australian Taxation Office.
And you'll continue to support them if they try to make US tech companies pay a fair rate of tax on profits generated in this country?
It's a hypothetical. I've told you the government's position is that we make decisions in the national interest.

Ms Wilkinson, I presume you share the view that the economy is at or near capacity. If you do, can I just put this to you? Australia has the third-highest pipeline of data centre construction after the US and China. Globally that's the third-highest pipeline. We've got about $156 billion of investment in the pipeline for data centres. If our economy is at or near capacity and all of that construction, the materials required and the labour required gets sucked into data centres, what does that mean for, firstly, inflation, if the economy is at or near capacity; and, secondly, what does it mean for housing construction and housing inflation, given that we're already supply and labour constrained in that sector?

I think I made this clear in my opening statement. One of the things that I think we would observe is that the economy is running close to capacity. That is one of the reasons the RBA's policy board statement stated that interest rates were increased from February this year. The fact that the output gap appears to have been smaller than expected in the middle of last year is one of the things which has almost certainly led to some of the domestic inflationary pressures. As I said also in my opening statement, the very significant opportunities that present with AI also do come with very strong investment. There is a bit of a tension here, because some of this investment we would expect to improve and increase the productive capacity of the economy—in other words, to improve our long-term potential growth rate and improve the returns that can be generated for wage and salary earners.

On the other hand, you're right that, in the short term, where there's capacity constraints in the economy and where the unemployment rate remains reasonably low, it can put upward pressure onto the system. I can agree with you that there is that tension, which we've drawn out, that we're grappling with and that other countries are also grappling with in terms of the pressure on those resources. It's a little bit like the pressure on some of those construction resources that have come from some of the significant investments in public infrastructure—roads and things—over the last couple of years, which again are important for the long-term productive capacity of the economy, but they require labour and they require capital. That's right; there is a tension between them.

What's the impact? Have you done any modelling on what the impact is? Data centres are overwhelmingly private investment. The government is relying on private investment to reach its 1.2 million new homes target. What's the impact of this recent but massive investment into the pipeline for data centres and the impacts that's going to have—and you've just agreed on some of the constrained capacity, including materials and labour? What's the impact of that massive spike in investment into data centres on the government relying on private property developers to reach its 1.2 million new homes target?
I'll see whether Dr Grant has something to add here. I don't think that we have specifically modelled the impact of a particular projection for data centres in a sectoral impact—
There will be an impact though, Ms Wilkinson, will there not?

but it's captured in our macroeconomic outlook. One of the things I would say is, as I pointed out in my opening statement, that we are expecting demand growth to ease over the next year. We are expecting some of the activity in the housing sector to come off just because of the tightening in financial conditions that have taken place. In terms of some of those capacity pressures, which have been acute over this first half of the year, we're expecting some of those to ease, and we can already see that in the increase in the unemployment rate, for example, which has happened. I guess we want to be a little bit careful about an overlay of the cyclical and structural shifts which are taking place at this time.

Just before Dr Grant responds, could I ask quickly, Ms Wilkinson, you would agree there will be an impact? You've described it as a tension. Can I take from that you agree there will be an impact on housing investment as a result of a massive spike in the investment pipeline for data centres?
These are all—
I'm not asking you to quantify it; just will there be an impact?

To the extent that this is another source of demand for labour, there could be. On the other hand, if the unemployment rate is to rise because the economy is softening, then this could mitigate some of that easing that could occur.
You're at 10 minutes, Senator.
I just want to give Dr Grant hopefully quite a brief opportunity, and then I do just have one other topic, which I don't think will take long, Chair, but I'm in your hands on that. Dr Grant?

I will be very brief. On page 8 of the Intergenerational Report we do make reference to the fact that data centre construction is increasing competition for capital and resources and adding to demand for skills, increasing the importance of addressing capacity constraints across the economy. In the data we've seen for 2025-26, we saw both stronger than expected dwelling investment and stronger than expected business investment, so it didn't seem to have an impact that year, but we are monitoring this very closely as it could have an impact over the coming year. The only extra thing I will add is that the housing market is facing some capacity pressures from the cost coming from the Middle East crisis as well, so that's also playing out.
I have maybe one or two more, and that will do for me, for Ms Wilkinson.
Very quickly.

Ms Wilkinson, there's what's known as a Godzilla El Nino coming at us. The name sounds funny, but it's horrifying to look at the data around ocean temperatures. We all know that's going to have a massive impact on conditions in Australia this summer, particularly the eastern seaboard. Have you modelled the cost to the Australian economy of this El Nino?

Again, I'll ask Dr Grant to speak to this. I haven't heard it called a Godzilla El Nino. There's another term that I've heard it called. We're certainly aware that changes in weather patterns absolutely have impacts. It's always hard understanding exactly how these weather patterns might unfold. There have been earlier times where an El Nino has led to drought conditions on the east coast. I'm now reading—and I'm sure you're better informed than I am—that this El Nino, given the nature of it, might in fact lead to much wetter conditions on the east coast. It's quite hard to work out how to flow that through, but let me turn to Dr Grant.

I don't have a lot to add, except to say we are monitoring this very closely with ABARES. As the secretary said, it is impacting different regions quite differently and having different impacts on different parts of the economy. We continue to stay very close to the issue, and we'll have an assessment. The impact on the economy of weather events, droughts in particular, can be quite significant. Even though the farm sector is only two per cent of the Australian economy, they can see very significant fluctuations in output, so we will watch this closely.

I have just one last follow-on, Chair. We're heading for catastrophe. Globally, we are heading for a cataclysmic future where actuarial studies in the UK have shown up to four billion people dead this century as a result of climate change. Why don't you model the impacts of climate change on the Australian economy—not just in the context of the El Nino, the record, horrifying El Nino that's coming down the line—in the short, medium and long term? Wouldn't that focus the minds of people like the minister on the need to, for example, stop opening new coal and gas mines and stop destroying our forests and emitting all the carbon in those forests, if they could see the almost certain massive cost to our economy? Have you been asked to model the costs and the impacts of climate change on the Australian economy, and why aren't you doing that?
Again, in the Intergenerational report we went into this. Dr Grant?

We did some modelling in the Intergenerational report 2023 on heat. It was partial analysis. We tried to extend that analysis in the Intergenerational report 2026. On page 67 there is a section on physical risks. We took one of the IPCC scenarios, and what we tried to do is translate that into some of the Australian economy sectors. You could see that, in terms of higher temperatures, there are some sectors we expect will be significantly affected in the Australian economy. We do expect agricultural crop yields to be affected in the long run. We continue to do some physical climate risk modelling as part of the intergenerational reports. As part of this, one of the innovations is we are trying to do bottom-up modelling, and that is rare. Normally the international modelling is top-down; it gives much more significant impacts than the bottom-up. Part of this work is us trying to reconcile that and contribute to the analysis in this important part of the sectors and how they're affected in the economy.
Senator Hume.

I want to take you back to something that you said a little bit earlier. I was asking questions about the connection between government decisions, government spending and pressure on inflation. I'm quoting yourself back to you here. You said:

We have to make assessments about what the net impact of government decisions are on both public and private demand.

You then said:

… governments have to make decisions about what spending and taxation decisions they are going to make in order to set fiscal policy …

Then you said:

What I'm saying is that, when I think about the 2025-26 budget and the 2025-26 MYEFO and the 2026-27 budget—in all of those cases the net impact of fiscal policy on the macroeconomy in 2025-26 and 2026-27 has been reduced.

I'm looking at page 94 of BP1. I want to understand: did an additional $5.3 billion in net decisions in 2025-26 put downward pressure on inflation, because that was your testimony before?
No, that was not my testimony.
I've got a quote.

That was not my testimony, and, as I said in my testimony—and I am absolutely not trying to be misleading here—the net impact of the budget, which I think about as being the net impact of government on macroeconomic outcomes, is best represented by the change in the underlying cash balance. I think it's the most useful summary measure. It's not the only summary measure, but it's the most useful summary measure. The point that I was making was that, when you look at the net impact of the budget and you look at the change in the underlying cash balance over a series of budgets and MYEFOs, they have consistently, in this year and in last year, reduced. The deficit has been lower; that's the point that I was making. You're right; it's the net impact of decisions and estimates variations, but you have to think about those things together when you're thinking about the impact of the budget on the economy. It is those things together which are the best estimate of what the impact of the budget or fiscal policy on the economy is. That's the point that I was making, and I apologise if I was not sharp enough with my language. I didn't intend to be. What I'm trying to do is be as clear as possible about what the impact of fiscal policy on the economy is. I think the best summary measure is that measure of how the underlying cash balance has changed between budget updates, because that reflects all of the decisions that have been in front of government, including dealing with estimates variations; that's part of what government has to do. They see what's changing and they have to make decisions, and the net of those things together is the best estimate of what the fiscal impact on the macroeconomy is. That's all I was trying to say.

The decisions are the part that the government can control. Variations will be variations. Government can respond to variations, certainly, but it's decisions that government make that are the determinant of fiscal policy.

The impact of fiscal policy on the macroeconomy is the combined impact of decisions and estimates variations. Those things together you have to think about when you're trying to work out what the fiscal impact on the macroeconomy is.

Let me look at it a different way, then. Are the decisions that government is making—and, let's be honest, the decisions that government is making, according to the budget papers, are to spend more—having an inflationary impact? Is that expansionary fiscal policy? Are the decisions that government is making to spend more expansionary, and is having an expansionary fiscal policy having an impact on inflation?

Senator Hume, you have to look at decisions we take about spending, but we take decisions about savings as well. That has an overall impact, and that's why the UCB impact, as the secretary is saying, is the best measure of, essentially, the practical effect of all of those decisions on the economy.
