If we look at the year that you've talked about—I think you used the $5 billion figure—$3 billion of that was fuel cost relief. Yes, we took a decision; in the budget we've taken hundreds, if not thousands, of decisions. That's how the budget is put together. We did take a decision, which I think you supported, in order to provide some temporary relief from the uptick in fuel that people were experiencing at that time.
If you recall, Minister, the coalition in opposition wanted you to offset that spending. We called for you to offset that spending, you didn't, and that was a decision. That's a choice.

We have a range of other decisions that feed in there. Yes, I think, from memory, this is similar to some of the announcements you've made in the last few days about ending the batteries program and ending EVs, so let's not pretend that there isn't some politics at play in that. We have savings built into the budget, including ones that you are opposing, in order to offset spending. We think about spending and the investments we have to make—often investments that people are calling for us to do more on—and then we also take decisions about savings and offsetting that spending.

The government has spent $120 billion more than it has saved. That's a decision of government. That's over its entire time in office. 'Savings in the budget in order to offset spending' is what you said. Is that right? Let me be very clear.
I don't know where you get that figure.
Let me be very clear. What is the difference between a saving and a reprioritisation? Can you explain that to me, Secretary?
I can.
I asked the secretary.
A reprioritisation is where—
I don't think she needs help.

and I can give you an example—a minister comes and essentially says: 'We have this amount of money in our budget. We don't need it for that anymore, but we do need it to meet this pressing pressure.' It might not happen within the same department—more often than not it does—but it's a way of reallocating resources without providing additional resources. Without reprioritising, the spending pressures or the requests for spending would be even greater than they are now.

I need to understand this. Secretary, you said earlier—and I think the point that you make is—that we can control only what we can control, and that's the right way of thinking about this. Policy decisions, not parameter variations, are what a government can control. Since coming to office, has this government spent more than it has saved? Has it chosen to do that?

When I look at budgets that governments bring down, they represent the things that governments have control over. Governments get to choose to bring down budgets. I feel like I've made this point: the net impact of all of these is the best estimate of how fiscal policy affects the economy. Obviously, within the budget papers, the reconciliation table illustrates the difference between decisions and estimates variations, and that provides transparency about the different components that go into leading to outcomes, which, in net terms, are the outcomes that are published in the budget. All of that is what government has within its gift to respond to.
I'm going to ask the same question again, because—
You're at 10 minutes.
I'm sorry, but Senator McKim went to 15. The number that I have is $120 billion more spending than saving. Has this government, over its time in office, spent more than it has saved?

Senator Hume, I don't know the figure that you are using there. We have taken spending decisions, many of which you have endorsed, when I think about the big spending investments—probably outside of the wages investment that we've done—but when you look at the extra investment in hospitals, the Medicare bulk-billing, the urgent care clinics and the extra investments in aged care, all of those are the big decisions. In Defence, you want to spend more than we have allocated at the moment.
Right.
You've asked about spending, and I'm telling you where we have made—
I'm asking a very simple question.

decisions about additional spending. The point I'm making is that I don't recall you objecting to the big areas where we have made investments. In fact, I seem to remember, in the election campaign, you endorsing it. Those big areas like health, aged care and wages for women by all means—
Minister, I understand you want to list all the things that you have invested in—
We have invested heavily.
What I want to understand is a question for the Secretary. It's the third time I have asked it—
Last question.
and it's a very simple question.
I'm not sure. Whatever you've got—
It's a very simple question. Do the budget papers show that this government has spent more than it has saved? It's a really simple question.
Let's just go to Ms Wilkinson, and then I'm going to rotate the call.
I am allowed to answer questions here, and I hadn't finished, on the spending that we have done.
You're taking up my time with the secretary by giving me a list—
Senator Gallagher can answer and then we'll go to Ms Wilkinson.
I have sat here since 9 o'clock, with all due respect, Senator Hume. It's not unusual for a minister—
You're here until 11 tonight.
It's not for the secretary—
I would like to speak with the secretary; she's only here for a little while.
to defend decisions that we have made about spending.
You're not defending decisions. You're just explaining decisions—
That is why I have intervened. If there is further information we can provide you that says—
I don't need information. It's here. It's in your budget.

cumulatively over the budget and budget updates that we made, we will provide that to you, Senator Hume. I am merely pointing out that, yes, we have taken decisions around spending, and we have made those decisions for good reasons, including on wages for women across the economy. When I think of the biggest decision we have taken, it is probably that.
This is not—
Let's have one person talk at a time. Ms Wilkinson, would you like to add anything before I rotate the call?

I don't have an answer to the question that Senator Hume has asked. I don't have a cumulative estimate. I have the budget papers. You have the budget papers in front of you. I have the reconciliation table. That is a summary for this budget of decisions that have been taken. I thought you were talking about it over a cumulation of budgets.
I did too. I thought so too.
I don't have that information in front of me.

Can Fiscal Group do it? When we get to fiscal, can they answer this question about whether more has been spent than saved over the life of this government? I'm just giving fiscal a little heads-up here. When fiscal come on, I'm going to ask this question.
We will see how we can assist, Senator Hume.
Thank you for the heads-up. Senator Roberts, I note we have a hard stop at 11.00 am. You've got seven minutes.

I've looked over this Treasury organisational structure—a lot of boxes there—and I can't see a function on here for assessing, monitoring or costing compliance costs imposed by the government on private enterprise, having specific reference to matters administered by your department, such as taxation. Do you have that function? Who has that function of monitoring?

There are perhaps two different things. Within Revenue Group we have a team that is responsible for the oversight of the Australian Taxation Office and the administration of the Australian Taxation Office. That's a specific function which sits within Revenue Group. In International Group, the Foreign Investment Division is responsible for the administration of the foreign investment laws, and all of the ways in which that policy is implemented sits within Foreign Investment Division. More broadly, in Markets Group there is a division which is responsible for the competition and productivity agenda more broadly across government. That is the group that has been leading the work around all of the different initiatives that the government has announced to improve productivity across all sectors of the economy. There is some work that takes place within Treasury for those areas of policy we have direct responsibility for. There is other work which takes place across regulators or across other departments, but that is the part of Treasury—so in Markets Group—who would be best placed to talk about the broader productivity agenda and all of the work that's being done, including with regulators, to do things like update statements of expectations to get them to better balance the balance between regulating and imposing burdens, and to work through how to best deliver the desired regulatory outcomes while minimising growth impacts.
You're nominating four groups?

That's right, because all parts of Treasury are responsible for whole-of-economy functions. Wherever government engages across the economy, there's a regulatory footprint. That means that all parts of the department are involved in different ways in the fundamental question that I think you're getting at, which is the ways in which government can reduce regulatory burdens in order to support growth.

Yes, you mentioned four groups, and twice or three times you mentioned administration. I want to know if there's anyone dedicated to reviewing compliance costs and cutting them. We've got a headline here from the Australian, 'Tax compliance costs hit $60bn per year, up 50pc in decade'. We've got businesses drowning in red tape madness. Is there anyone overseeing compliance costs, reviewing them, monitoring them, measuring them and saying, 'For God's sake, help business out'?

Senator Roberts, across government, Finance has a role around regulatory reform, and we dealt with that last night in estimates. We had quite a discussion about regulatory reform. They lead whole-of-government efforts, but it draws on the expertise from each department in their own portfolio area.

Media reports indicate Australian businesses are being hit with $600 million per week in compliance costs, which is also called red tape. This is a $30 billion a year imposition on business. I note across business and individual taxation your department said the figure was more likely to be $40 billion. What's the correct figure, please?
I'm not quite sure what you're quoting from, and I don't have that estimate in front of me.
If you don't know, how can we have any hope of reducing red tape?

I think, again, the whole-of-government regulatory reform area sits in the Department of Finance, and we have brought two bills to this parliament which have passed in this session. We will be bringing further regulation through. I would just say this is a highly contested space. With one business's overregulation there's equally another group that will think it's underregulated. Most of it requires amendments through the parliament. I hear a lot of 'just slash red tape; just cut this, cut that'. That's not how it's done. The EPBC legislation that came through the parliament took years, essentially, to draft and get through, and that had a big focus on reducing red tape, but it was done after years of consultation. We'll continue to bring things forward to the parliament to have better regulation. Hopefully that means less, but better regulation, I think, is what everyone is after.

In addition, you mentioned the EPBC Act. That is green tape. Then there is blue UN tape—compliance with their policies. Then there is black tape, a lot to do with property rights. I just want to talk about red tape or at least learn about red tape. The compliance costs of red tape do not add to business output. It's a drain on business productivity, GDP and, ultimately, the living standards of all Australians who are here. It is, though, an issue that apparently you give no time to. Why don't you care about the compliance costs of the measures you're implementing? Government is a net burden, a drain on our economy. It's a massive imposition.
That's your assertion, but, Senator Roberts, give me an example of a piece of red tape that you would want taken away.
Everything that the climate change department does.
I thought you just said that was all green tape. Equally, there are many reasons why you do provide regulation.
Let's go on.

This is the thing: a lot of people go, 'Cut red tape, cut red tape, cut red tape', but don't provide any substantive idea of what they would like to see reduced. Often it's across government—so it's local government, it's states and it's territories—and the Commonwealth has a role to play here. We are open and engaging with business about sensible and better regulation, and my door is always open for ideas. I'm urging people to come forward and provide that to me.
I'm pleased you mentioned—
We have to break now, sorry.

I now call representatives from the Reserve Bank of Australia, appearing today via videoconference. I welcome Ms Michele Bullock, Governor of the RBA, and colleagues. Governor, would you like to make an opening statement?

Yes, I would. My colleagues and I are here to answer your questions. Our purpose at the RBA is to promote the economic prosperity and welfare of the Australian people now and into the future. One way we do this is by setting monetary policy to achieve low and stable inflation and full employment, and by supporting the stability of the financial system. We also promote the prosperity and welfare of Australians across the full range of our responsibilities, which includes supporting a reliable, efficient and competitive payments system; delivering efficient and effective banking services to Australian government agencies; and providing secure and reliable banknotes to Australians. Since the committee's previous hearing with the RBA in June, the Monetary Policy Board has increased the cash rate target by 25 basis points. It did this with the goal of returning inflation to target. This has taken the cumulative increase in the cash rate target this year to 100 basis points. I'm going to start with some background to these decisions and the outlook for the Australian economy, and then I'll provide an update on the payments system and cash distribution.

The Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy such that inflation is expected to return to the midpoint of the two to three per cent target range. There's some flexibility around the timeframe over which we meet our inflation objective to balance this with meeting our full-employment objective. It's important for the economy that inflation does not diverge from target for too long, since that risks it becoming embedded in inflation expectations, which feeds through to price- and wage-setting decisions.

Inflation fell significantly from its peak of 7.9 per cent at the end of 2022 to be within the two to three per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025. This followed a significant tightening of monetary policy over 2022 and 2023. Inflation picked up over the second half of 2025 and has remained above target since then. Recently, inflation has been around 3½ to four per cent in year ended terms. The increase in inflation reflects both persistent capacity pressures in the Australian economy and global cost pressures associated with the conflict in the Middle East. Because of both these factors, inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time.

Our most recent published forecasts, in the August Statement on Monetary Policy, suggested inflation would not return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027. At the time of the August board meeting, we assessed that the risks to that outlook were skewed to the upside. Developments since then suggest that, although growth in the Australian economy is slowing as expected, some of the international and domestic upside risks to inflation have materialised or are materialising. Inflation will therefore likely be higher than was our base case in August. The conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated, and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add materially to inflation, both directly and indirectly, as businesses facing increasing pressures from higher transport and related costs attempt to pass them on. At the same time, short-term inflation expectations are elevated.

Other global cost pressures have increased. In addition to the energy price shock, the AI boom and extreme weather events are contributing to upward pressure on a range of agricultural and technology related prices. The global AI boom is also driving stronger growth in economies that are key parts of the AI supply chain. In turn, that's driving higher global prices for some AI related technologies that are supply constrained.

Importantly, though, it's not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia. While they are certainly compounding the inflation problem, we still see inflation arising from domestic capacity pressures. Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the labour market still seems a little tighter than we previously judged. The evidence for this is elevated underlying inflationary pressures—that is, when we exclude some of the large volatile price movements, such as fuel, we see inflationary pressures in areas that reflect domestic demand for goods and services. Continued weak productivity growth means the economy cannot grow strongly without putting pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone's real spending power over the next few years.

Against this backdrop and despite growth in domestic demand slowing, a further period of subdued growth of aggregate demand is needed to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation down sustainably. We are not alone in being concerned about inflation. Central banks in many other advanced economies are responding by increasing their policy rates or signalling they will do so if needed.

Because monetary policy works with a lag, the full effects of recent rate increases are yet to be felt on domestic activity. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East on economic activity has been relatively modest so far. Household spending growth has been moderating only gradually, and business investment growth has picked up strongly, driven mostly by spending on data centres and renewable energy projects. The share of the population with a job remains high, and this is a welcome outcome for those individuals, their families and the wider Australian economy.

Conditions in the housing market have softened, reflecting the usual transmission of monetary policy but also tax policy changes and the broader economic environment. Housing prices have fallen in most capital cities, and new housing loans have declined. This follows a long period of strong growth, however, underpinned by a structural undersupply of housing, and housing prices are around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020. Financial stability risks from household borrowing remain contained. While many are facing budget pressures, only a small share of borrowers are in negative equity or facing severe repayment difficulty. I recognise how challenging it is, though, for those experiencing these issues. I want to emphasise that, while we expect housing prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary policy does not target housing prices. Rather, what matters is how changes in housing prices affect economic activity, the labour market and, ultimately, inflation.

The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week. We will discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time. We are committed to our mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.

I recognise that higher interest rates can be difficult, particularly for households with mortgages who are also facing cost-of-living pressures, but we can't allow high inflation to persist. High inflation hurts everyone. It means higher grocery costs, higher rent and higher electricity bills. It makes everyone's pay packets and savings worth less and it particularly hurts people with lower incomes and little savings. Monetary policy affects all parts of the economy, not just households with mortgages. It influences the spending, saving and borrowing decisions of all households and businesses. We're happy to expand upon this in the Q&A.

Moving on now, another key responsibility for the RBA is the regulation and oversight of the payments system. We've completed our review of surcharging and merchant payment costs. Following extensive consultation, the Payments System Board concluded that a package of reforms to remove card surcharging, reduce interchange fee caps and improve transparency of payment costs would be in the public interest. Card surcharging was removed from 1 October, and we have been monitoring the payments industry's implementation and working with industry stakeholders to support merchant awareness of the changes. So far, several large providers have reduced their card processing fees for small businesses. We're also seeing signs of increased competition, with businesses shopping around and providers responding by offering more competitive pricing. These developments are welcome.

Following amendments to the Payment Systems (Regulation) Act, which expanded our regulatory remit, we started a broader review of payment systems regulation with the publication of an issues paper in June. This review is considering how regulation should respond to rapid innovation and change in the payments landscape, including opportunities to improve competition, efficiency and safety. In the submissions, stakeholders frequently raised issues relating to mobile wallets, three-party card schemes, account-to-account payments and agentic commerce. We recently published the stakeholder submissions and a summary of them. We intend to release regulatory priorities by the end of 2026 and start further consultation on prioritised issues by mid-2027.

In May, we published the Project Acacia final report, which found that the tokenisation of assets and money, alongside upgrades to market infrastructure, has the potential to enhance the efficiency and resilience of Australia's wholesale financial markets. Coordination challenges across the financial system have meant that these innovations have yet to scale. However, momentum around tokenised finance is now building in Australia along various lines, as it is internationally, and following the post-Acacia road map we've continued to progress various initiatives to support responsible innovation. For example, we're currently consulting on how the RBA's own settlement services could support development and growth of tokenised asset markets and tokenised private money in Australia. Together with the government's financial innovation strategy, this work is drawing together the public and private sector, including the Digital Finance Cooperative Research Centre, to ensure that Australia is well placed to harness the benefits of financial innovation in a manner consistent with monetary and financial stability.

Finally, I'd like to update the committee on recent developments in the cash distribution system. Cash remains a critical part of an inclusive and resilient payments system. The RBA remains committed to supporting the government's objective that cash remains available for as long as Australians want or need to use it. The cash distribution system has faced significant challenges and needs to continue to evolve to support ongoing access to cash across Australia. Industry participants have been working on a range of initiatives to promote a more sustainable and efficient system. These will require approval by the ACCC.

As the issuer of Australian banknotes, the RBA also plays a key role in wholesale cash distribution. We provide banknotes to the major banks, which distribute these to the broader community. We're continuing to work with industry so that our distribution arrangements, programs and incentives support efficient distribution and availability of cash across the country.

The RBA welcomed the recent passage of the Cash Distribution Framework Bill 2026, which provides the RBA with crisis readiness and resolution powers to support continuity of critical cash distribution services. The ACCC, as our co-regulator, will oversee pricing, access arrangements and service-level standards. The RBA recently designated Linfox Armaguard under the new legislation. This reflects its significant role in Australia's cash distribution system and makes it subject to the framework's obligations and requirements. Designation does not mean that the RBA will exercise crisis readiness or resolution powers in relation to Linfox Armaguard. It just means that we will have the ability to act if we need to. The work to operationalise these new powers and responsibilities is being undertaken in close coordination with the ACCC. My colleagues and I look forward to answering your questions.

I want to talk about the surcharging and merchant card payment costs. You touched on it just at the end of your opening statement. You said in your opening statement that you undertook extensive consultation before coming to a decision. I was just wondering if you could talk a little bit more about what that looks like. What does 'extensive' mean? Who did you consult with and over what timeframe?

We have a longstanding process of how we manage these consultations at the Reserve Bank. We've been doing them for decades now. What it involved was, first of all, publication of an issues paper, on which we gathered feedback. I can't recall what year that was in. Brad—2023?
Late—

Anyway, I can find out the exact date. We gathered that and then we put out a consultation paper which set out our responses to the various issues that were raised. That included interchange fees and surcharging. It also included scheme fees. They were the main things that it included. We set out what our regulatory response was proposed to be. Then the industry and the public usually have at least a couple of months to respond to that, so it's a very wide consultation. We publish all of the non-confidential submissions on our website, so you can go to our website and you can see all of the responses. There are also some confidential submissions in those circumstances where we consult. That's because some organisations want to provide us with commercial-in-confidence information because they think it goes to questions we're asking. We keep those confidential, but we publish as much as we can. After that, the Payments System Board considers those submissions and finalises its reforms.

That's the process it goes through. It's a lengthy process. For example, in the current process we're going through, I don't think we are going to have any proposed solutions until probably the middle of next year. It's not a short process, but it's a very extensive process.
Sorry, you said an issues paper in 2023, and then—
We'll find out the exact—
2024. It might have the exact dates on the website.

You set out your regulatory responses, then there were a couple of months of consultation and then submissions received were published on your website. What sorts of groups did your consultation cover? Did it include large business and small business? You said members of the public could submit. What did your targeted processes look like in terms of the types of organisations you reached out to?

We reached out to anyone who wanted to give us a submission, basically. I'm just going onto the website to look, but if you look at it you will see that we got big business, small business and financial institutions and we got submissions from the public. The general public put in submissions. You may or may not recall that one of the things that was particularly prescient for the general public at the time was surcharging. There was a lot of feedback we were getting, both formally and informally, from the general public that they did not like surcharging. It was very broad. Anyone who wanted to engage, whether they be individual institutions, community organisations or business organisations—anyone was free to do so. I can't find at the moment how many submissions we got. You might be able to find it, Brad.

It's probably also worth adding, on top of the formal submissions, our teams took a large number of meetings at the bank from various associations—in fact, from a wide range of stakeholders—to hear directly extra context that perhaps they didn't want to put in a submission. There was the formal submission component and then an extensive range of meetings added to that.
Thanks for that. That's useful. Can you talk to us about who is on the Payments System Board who then ultimately made the decision post receiving all of the feedback through the consultation process?

Sure. The Payments System Board comprises me as chair and Brad as deputy chair, and then we have six non-executive members: Scott Farrell, who's a longstanding payments lawyer, a specialist in that; a guy called Ross—
Professor Buckley.

Professor Buckley, a professor in things to do with payments; a woman called Deborah Ralston, who is another academic but focuses more on innovation and so on—she's involved in a number of different financial institutions; Gina Cass-Gottlieb, of course, from the ACCC, who is there not as the head of the ACCC but as Gina Cass-Gottlieb, because she has experience in this; John Lonsdale, who is the chair of APRA; and Michelle Deaker, who is also a venture capitalist and into innovation in payment systems.

This will be my final question, and then I will need to rotate the call. In your opening statement, you talked about some of the impacts of the implementation of that decision of the Payments System Board, particularly on reducing fees for small businesses and on competition. Could you talk about what are the broader positive impacts that you think it has or will have on the economy and consumers?
How long have you got?
Only one or two minutes, please.

A few things—first of all, we think it will lower payment costs for small merchants, because we've capped interchange fees. What used to happen with interchange fees is that big merchants got low interchange fees and small merchants got high interchange fees. That is now capped, so small merchants are now paying much lower interchange fees. That's positive for them because that contributes to what they pay to accept cards. The second thing is it will increase competition, I think, because merchants used to just surcharge. Now, because they can't surcharge, they're going to look at their payment options and they're going to say, 'That's too expensive, so give me a better price or I'm not going to take that payment mechanism.' So it will increase competition there. Frankly, it's going to make it much easier for consumers, because when they go and they see that the price of a coffee is $5, that's what they pay. They don't pay $5.10 or $5.08; they will pay $5. There are a lot of advantages to consumers of just facing a single price. In the interests of time, they would be the main benefits I would highlight.
I am now going to rotate the call to Senator Hume.

We're just watching the inflation data come in, and I'm sure you're doing the same at your end, Ms Bullock. Obviously, the headline number there is 4.3 per cent, up from four per cent, and the trimmed mean or core number is 3.6 per cent, up from 3.5 per cent. Just last week the deputy governor, who I know is sitting there with you, said that the outlook is materially worse and it's turning into—and I'm quoting Mr Hauser here—'a central banker's nightmare'. Does today's data affirm that view?
Since you said that, Andrew, I'm going to pass to you.

I thought you might say that, Governor. The comment about the nightmare was specifically related to the potential for longer term inflation expectations to pick up, and we are watching that issue very closely. We don't think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk. I think that was the comment I made about the nightmare, rather than about the data. To your question about the data itself, these numbers are broadly in line—my take is—with the market expectations and, candidly, where we thought it would be as well. To your point, these are too high. We have said that repeatedly, and I'm sure that we will say that again today.
On my reckoning, both of these numbers, headline and core, mean that it's been 14 months that we have now been above the RBA's target band. Is that your count as well?
That sounds pretty close. Do we know literally how many months? It's over a year. We were last in the band in mid-2025, I think.
Yes, if I recall, the last time headline inflation was below three per cent was the month of June 2025, so I think your count is correct, Senator.

Last month, when the Reserve Bank appeared before the House economics committee, you were asked specifically about the impact of government spending on inflation and also whether the RBA had modelled the impact of that. In that committee you answered that the RBA had not modelled the impact, but subsequently a freedom-of-information request revealed that you had modelled scenarios which included the impact of government spending on inflation. The RBA secretary has provided a letter to the House economics committee correcting the record. It stated:

While the composition of a specific spending proposal matters, in general lower government spending would reduce aggregate demand unless it was offset by stronger spending elsewhere. If this eased capacity pressures, it would also tend to reduce inflationary pressure.

Governor, can I ask you then, please, to confirm that documented RBA position that, in general, lower government spending would reduce aggregate demand and tend to reduce inflation?

I confirm that's what it says, but it goes on to say:

However, the size and timing of the effect cannot be estimated from the headline figure alone. Estimating the effect of a specific proposal would require further detail about what spending would be reduced, when the reduction would occur and how other parts of the economy might respond.

We stand by that. But, back to the point, we were asked had we modelled, and would we model, a two per cent reduction in federal government spending. The answer is no, we haven't modelled that. The FOI request you are referring to, and we referred to in this letter, was asking a slightly different question. It was asking the question: what would our models tell us about changes in specific types of government spending and how that might impact the economy? That's a different question, and it's not a scenario saying what happens to inflation if we just have a blanket cut of two per cent in federal government spending.

Again, on this issue, Ms Hunter, on Sunday night, on 60 Minutes, in response to a question about the role of government spending in driving inflation, said government spending is 'definitely part of the picture'. Governor, do you agree that government spending is definitely a factor in Australia's high inflation rate?

I've said this a number of times. Part of the inflation problem is that demand is greater than the ability of the economy to supply. Demand is made up of demand from government and the private sector. I've said this a number of times: yes, to the extent that it is contributing to aggregate demand and aggregate demand is above supply, then it's contributing to that. I've said this a number of times, and I think that's exactly what Sarah said on Sunday night.

To clarify, just so everyone is clear on what my answer to the question was that was shown on Sunday evening, it was a question about whether or not government had a role to play in the economy overall. My answer to that question was that, yes, it clearly definitely does have a role to play in the economy overall. We've said that a number of times. I don't think I've said anything that's inconsistent with what we've said before.

Indeed, I think there is some consistency also from former RBA governor Phil Lowe, who said:

Government spending has been adding to demand progressively over time, and that's putting upward pressure on inflation.

Governor, do you agree with your immediate predecessor's assessment? This was only at the end of last month.

I'm only going to say what I said before, which is that government spending—federal and state, I have to say here, not just federal—all contributes to aggregate demand in some way, whether it be through infrastructure projects, services they have to provide and so on, all things which the public expect governments to provide. That contributes to aggregate demand, and, to the extent that aggregate demand is above aggregate supply, it contributes to that excess demand, yes. As I have also said repeatedly, monetary policy is independent, and fiscal policy is a matter for the parliament and the government. It is not for the central bank to tell the government what to do with their spending and particularly how to direct their spending. It's not for us to do so.

No, I understand that. You've also said that it's both domestic and international factors that are pushing inflation above the target band. Do you accept, though, that our inflation rate is above almost every other major advanced economy's, therefore domestic factors must be what is mainly at play?

You've got to be careful here because our inflation target is higher than that of other countries. The inflation targets of other countries are two per cent, mostly, and ours is 2½ per cent. If you look at how far above target we are relative to other countries, we're not much different from others. It's true that our inflation rate is higher, but our target is higher. Having said that, I don't think you can draw that conclusion at all. I think the problem for us is that we started from a position of excess demand, and other countries did not. Many other countries—I'm thinking particularly of Canada and New Zealand—started from positions of excess supply and high unemployment rates. So we had a bit of an inflation issue already, and then this has added to it. I don't think you can divide it up into specific amounts due to excess demand and supply shocks, but I think we can say that, because we started from a position of excess demand, it has made our issue more complicated.

To me, that sounds as though we weren't then prepared for the international headwinds that came our way. Our domestic situation was the problem already, and, obviously, as you have pointed out, government spending has been part of that. That was already the problem.
You might recall that we started raising interest rates before the conflict in the Middle East.
Yes.

Inflation had been rising through the back half of 2025, and we responded in February by starting to raise interest rates. We had already recognised that we had an excess demand problem, and there are two issues there. One is that demand probably didn't slow quite as much as we thought it would. In fact, it picked up a bit in the second half of that year, and that was in the private sector as well. The second point is that it seems that the supply capacity of the economy was not quite as good as we thought it was; in other words, productivity was not picking up as we thought it might.

It has got to the stage now where we hang on every word of the Statement on monetary policy. Back in 2023, that Statement on monetary policy looked at supply-and-demand drivers of inflation in Australia, and, in that analysis, you disaggregated the impact of domestic and international factors. You said in that statement:

Inflation has increased substantially over the past year. Because monetary policy primarily affects the economy by influencing demand, it's important to understand how much of the increase in inflation reflects supply-side factors versus demand-side factors, in order to determine how policy should respond.

I would like to know whether this modelling has been updated, considering that inflation has again increased substantially in the last year.

I'll pass to Sarah. I just want to make the point, yes, but it's an uncertain process. We can do our best at that, but sometimes what you think at the time is not what turns out. You think it was domestic and it turns out that it was actually international, and vice versa. So we do our best to do that. Sarah, do you want to make a few comments about this?

Yes. Let me elaborate a bit further on what the governor has just said. We do that type of analysis that you're talking about on an ongoing basis, so you'll actually find that type of discussion in every single Statement on monetary policy. You'll find our assessments of the current position, as it was at the time of publication, in the economic conditions chapter; and, in the outlook chapter, you'll find our assessment of how we think that balance of supply will evolve going forward. Within both those sections of the document, where it's appropriate, we also talk about the balance between international factors and domestic factors. To give you an example, over the last six to nine months, as you can well imagine, we spent a lot of time talking about what's happening overseas, particularly with respect to oil and refined fuel product markets, and how that's flowing into the economy here and what role that's playing in terms of inflation. That kind of analysis that you're talking about happens on an ongoing basis.
Back in 2023, you obviously quantified it, and it wasn't just a discussion. I'm wondering whether you can provide us with the same chart from that 2023 statement but updated.
That was the box in 2023.

I'm sorry. I wasn't at the bank in 2023, so I'm not aware precisely of which statement you're talking about of the four that were released that year, which also means that I don't have in front of me the box or chart that you're talking about. We can certainly take it on notice to see if we have got a more recent update. The governor is just showing it to me.
Thank you; it's box C.

Over the last couple of years, we've done various different versions of that type of analysis and published some of that through other formats, like bulletin articles and such, but we can take it on notice to see whether we have the latest version of that chart for you.

Finally, when I mentioned the updated CPI figures to you, you said that they were broadly in line with expectations. Without giving away the deliberations of the board, if these headline figures and the core inflation data are in line with expectations, can you tell me what that would say about the need for the Reserve Bank to respond with further tightening?

Perhaps it would be good if I were to clarify what my colleague said about 'in line with expectations' before the governor responds to that particular question. Broadly speaking, the data was in line with what we thought, having seen the July and August monthly CPI data. The data is stronger than we were anticipating in our August SMP. If you look at the latest forecasts that we've published—they were published in August, and you can see the charts in there—the numbers that we got today were stronger than we were anticipating around three months ago. But, given what we've seen in the data since then, we were anticipating that. I just want to clarify that so that everyone is clear on what we meant.

Senator, in answer to your question, I can't give you any guidance on what this might mean for the board. The board obviously meets next Monday and Tuesday, and we are in the process, internally here, of finalising papers for the board, which will go to these issues. I would only point you to some of the statements we made last time about the upside risks that we saw to inflation and whether or not they were materialising. This is consistent with what we thought the inflation numbers might look like, taking into account recent information. The board will obviously be considering that and the prospects for inflation to come down, and how tight they think policy is, before making a decision on Tuesday.
Senator McKim.

I just want to tease out some of the bank's expectations around medium-term and longer term inflation expectations. Obviously, when you set your horizons that far out, you do enter the territory of Mr Hauser's 'nightmare' scenario. Recently, we've seen the impacts of COVID on the supply chain, Ukraine, Trump's tariff shocks, Iran, and the bond yield leap; we've got our climate system crumbling around us; and we've got a record El Nino heading our way. Do you agree that, in the medium-term to longer term, these have a compounding impact on the bank's inflationary outlook? Also, if you do agree with that, what do you think is going to happen to interest rates as these things continue to compound; how is the bank going to respond to that; and is monetary policy equipped to respond to that?

Let me start, and then others can chip in. The first thing is that you've highlighted a number of supply shocks that have occurred, starting with COVID, and have continued. Basically, what negative supply shocks do is worsen the trade-off between inflation and unemployment. So, for any given unemployment rate or given state of the economy, inflation is higher. A traditional way of thinking about this—all central banks talk about this—is that you would try to look through the supply shock. If there's a shock, you let it flow through and then, once it has flowed through, prices and inflation will settle down again. That works, I think, if you've got a one-off shock, and you can do that if you've just had a one-off shock. But if you've got, as you point out, compounding shocks and they are continuing to raise the level of inflation, there is a concern that people start to think that inflation is just going to be higher permanently.
That's right.

If that is the case, then I think it's very difficult for central banks—again, I'm invoking some of my colleagues overseas—to look through these shocks completely, because it might become embedded in inflation expectations. There's another challenge here too, which is that something like a fuel price shock is a little bit more difficult, because it underlies costs that are embedded in businesses. If it's a very quick shock, where it goes up and it comes down again, businesses might think, 'I'll just wear it.' But the longer it goes on, the more they might think, 'Actually, do you know what? The fuel price isn't coming down, transport costs aren't coming down, and I've just got to start passing this on.'
That's right.

It does make it more challenging for central banks, but what still remains the best tool for making sure that inflation expectations remain contained and the central bank remains credible in that is using the interest rate.
Alright.

Perhaps I could comment on the market measures and what they're doing. The short-term market measures for inflation expectations for Australia picked up quite a bit through 2025, then got another kick-on earlier this year with the war in the Middle East and, I think, have since come back a bit. That's consistent with what we've seen with inflation. Actual inflation has risen, and we've got these other pressures that we've talked about. The longer term measures have been quite stable right through this period, and that's true not just for us but also for other advanced economies. One of the reasons for that is that markets anticipate central banks responding to these short-term inflationary pressures by raising interest rates. Indeed, the fact that the board has done so four times this year has probably been one of the very helpful things in containing those long-term inflation expectations.

I guess the proposition that I'd like you to respond to is this: are the first tendrils of Mr Hauser's nightmare starting to seep into the minds of the board here? Just to pick one of the things that I'd mention, the lag on climate change is massive. The very system that supports human life, all other life on the planet and, for that matter, the global economy is collapsing around us. Is it the board's view that you're just going to keep putting up interest rates and smashing people who are not responsible for creating the inflationary pressure? In your view, does monetary policy remain fit for purpose in the medium to long term?

Let me make a couple of points, and then I'll let Andrew respond, since everyone keeps talking about this comment. Let's be clear here. At the moment, yes, we've had supply shocks, but there is a demand component to this for Australia. We are not just responding to supply shocks; we are responding to a demand component. That has to be extremely clear here. The second thing is that, as I said earlier, we need to make sure that we keep demand and supply relatively well aligned, and monetary policy is fit for purpose in that. Will we have to have a better understanding of where we think supply shocks occur and we can look through them? Yes, we will, and we are working very hard on understanding that. We're working very hard on adjusting and adapting our models to try to get better at recognising supply shocks and how to respond to them. But I think the bottom line remains that there are going to be a lot of supply shocks, but there are also going to be demand consequences of interest rates, and central banks still need to be involved in setting interest rates to try to make sure that inflation remains low, stable and tight. Andrew, perhaps you would like to add something.

You've mostly covered it, Governor. Let me just say a couple of things if I can. As Chris said a moment ago, in some ways the surprising feature of the post-COVID period is how well anchored inflation expectations remain, and not just in Australia but around the world. Obviously, inflation picked up very, very sharply, and you might have expected for there to be some tendency for inflation expectations to pick up in response, and around the world it did not. That was obviously because central banks responded quite aggressively, and that obviously created pain and difficulties in their relevant economies. But, as Chris has said, that probably was what was required to keep expectations well anchored. Most of the measures of long-term expectations remain pretty well anchored.

One thing that we are looking at and, I think, has taken our interest is what companies are beginning to think about the outlook for inflation, given the cost pressures that they face. Through both our liaison with Macquarie University and a survey with that university that we've been involved in called the BOSS, there are just some signs that some companies might be thinking, 'Do you know what? Maybe prices aren't going all the way back, and, if they're not, we're going to have to take that into account in our pricing decisions.' It isn't a klaxon or my nightmare yet, but it is something we're watching quite closely. Obviously, consumer confidence measures are at historical lows, and people are very angry about the cumulative effect of inflation over the recent past. That is not unique to Australia; that is true right around the world.

I just have two more quick questions, and then I'll be done. Firstly, let's go to domestic demand. Behind the US and China, Australia is third for the pipeline of data centre projects globally, with $156 billion in the pipeline. Obviously, we're a much smaller economy than either the US or China. Ms Bullock, our economy, you'd probably agree—but, if you don't, please say so—is at or near capacity at the moment. What are the inflationary impacts of this massive looming investment into data centres? Also, would you agree that there are really only two possible outcomes: a collapse or correction in the financial markets, which basically are massively reliant on tech growth at the moment, or, if the bubble doesn't pop, obscenely high prices for AI products to justify the capital outlay? One leads to financial risk and the other to sustained inflation, which are both within your areas of responsibility. Do you share any of those concerns?

You've listed quite a lot of concerns there. In terms of demand, yes, data centre build-out in Australia is adding to demand, and investment spend is much stronger than we thought. A large chunk of that is imported, so it doesn't add to domestic capacity pressures. But it does add to some pressures, particularly in terms of construction of warehouses, for example, and skilled labour who need to do this. So it does potentially add in that way. To the extent that it's drawing resources from there, those resources have to come from somewhere, so that does add to inflationary pressure. On the financial markets side of things, this is something that we have alluded to, I think, in our Financial Stability Review, about the potential for this to unravel a bit. Very quickly, I might just ask Brad to give a couple of reflections on that.

The question here is not, 'Is this tech going to be transformative?' It's whether the financial markets have just gotten ahead of themselves in pricing in a lot of good news. That's really the issue at hand. It's not for us, I think, to suggest that there's an irrational amount of exuberance, but there's clearly been exuberance in this space, if you look at earnings expectations and the amount of debt that is now starting to be deployed to fund some of this expansion. At the moment, we're not at DEFCON 1 on AI related imbalances in the financial markets, but it's a clear watch point, because we are seeing risk appetite increasing in a pretty notable way around the world.

How worried are you about the pace of the increase in unemployment and, specifically, what rise in unemployment would give the RBA cause for a reasonable concern that we would head into recession? That's the question, but the context here is that you've said around two-thirds of rate rise impacts is through the exchange rate, and your former colleague Luci Ellis said that implies a lot of pain for little effect on inflation. Also, if the dollar is likely to rise off things like an increase in copper demand because of AI data centre investment, does this change your approach to targeting the exchange rate?

Let me be right upfront: we're not targeting the exchange rate at all. It's a freely floating exchange rate. It is determined in markets on the basis of interest differentials, commodity prices, terms of trade, and those sorts of things. We don't think it's out of line at the moment at all. Chris, would you like to comment on that?

Our best estimate is that it's in line with historical estimates and its long-run determinants, which, as the governor has said, are interest rate differentials, us versus major advanced economies, and commodity prices.

I'm sorry. Can I just ask the question again: how worried are you about the pace of the increase in the unemployment rate, and what pace of increase of unemployment would give you cause for concern that we may be heading towards a recession?

At this stage, we're not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate. We do forecast that it has to gradually move up. That is very different from saying that people have to lose their jobs. In fact, we are forecasting that employment continues to grow. It just means that the supply of labour is growing a bit more quickly than jobs can keep up with. I think you're referring to the NAIRU, and I can't be specific about what that number is, but I can say that we think it's probably above where the unemployment rate is at the moment. So, in order to ease some of these capacity pressures, the unemployment rate probably will be rising a bit further, and that's what will be in our forecasts.

I might just add to the governor's response in the context of a recession. If you're defining that through the usual technical definition, which is two-quarters of negative growth for GDP, we're obviously monitoring a very wide range of indicators across the real economy, including the labour market but also spending trends across all of the major categories, and there are various sets of lead indicators and real-time indicators that we can track to look at that. Just to reiterate what the governor says, at the moment, our assessment is that none of those indicators are suggesting that the economy is in or heading into a recession in the near term, so that's not what we're seeing or expect to see over the forecast horizon.
Senator Bragg.

In your latest Financial Stability Review, the bank has said that it's likely that more people in high-LVR situations will be in negative equity. What assessments have you done about people who might be in negative equity at the moment—you noted it briefly in your opening statement—particularly in view of the 100,000 people who have taken out 95 per cent loans under the government's scheme in the past 12 months?

I'll make a couple of comments and then pass to Brad. The first thing I would note is that, of itself, negative equity is not actually a problem, unless people, for difficult reasons, have to sell. That's the first point I'd make. The second point I would make—Brad can talk you through how we do this—is that, basically, our estimates are that people in negative equity at the moment are well under one per cent. It's a very small number. We have done some scenario analysis, which I'll let Brad talk to, about what would happen under different scenarios of home price declines.

At a system-wide level, we have run a couple of scenarios. One is where the decline in house prices matched the previous historical peak declines of around eight per cent. In that sort of a scenario, the share of borrowers in negative equity is still very small and not far above that one to two per cent range. We've also had a look at a much more severe scenario, being a 20 per cent decline, in house prices. In that context, our estimates suggest that around five per cent of borrowers would be in negative equity. That largely reflects that, in Australia, most borrowers put 20 per cent down, so there's a lot of equity cushion, if you like, in the Australian financial system for falling house prices.

For the particular scheme that you've mentioned, we can't observe directly at the moment the share of those particular borrowers, because those loans haven't entered our securitisation database yet. They will in time. It typically takes around 18 months for new loans to enter our database. At that point, we will have quite granular data on loan performance. But we have conducted liaison with the banks and with Housing Australia. Their readout is that there's nothing particularly unusual about stress in that segment of borrowers. We have also run simulations based on a lot of assumptions, because we can't directly observe what's going on with these borrowers. But under those simulations, our estimate is that it's likely that around four per cent to five per cent of the borrowers under the new deposit guarantee scheme would likely be in negative equity. Part of the reason for that number not being higher is that house price declines across Australia in suburbs where first home buyers are most active have been less pronounced than in more affluent, more expensive areas.

Effectively, you're saying that it is five per cent of the people who are in the scheme and, potentially, that's the proxy that you're comfortable with. That would be 5,000 people in the last year who joined the scheme on that basis?

Our numbers suggest that, since the October revisions, where some adjustments were made to that program, around 55,000 new entrants have come into that program. I do not have the data before that, but the scheme has been running at about 10,000 new entrants per month, so the number that you've mentioned doesn't sound wildly out of line.

So you think about 5,000 people across Australia, in a 95 per cent scheme, are in negative equity as at today? That's interesting. What about the impact of the taxes? I think a lot of people would look at it and say, 'I took out a 95 per cent loan because the government effectively proposed that I should, and the taxes and other things have pushed down the value of my house.' What impact do you think the taxes have had on the values in these suburbs where there has been a price fall of more than five per cent?
That's a very difficult one. I don't think we have any particular view on that.

In a conjunctural sense, we concentrate our analysis of the housing market and, indeed, of the whole economy at that aggregate macro level, because that's the level that's most relevant for monetary policy. Even at that aggregate macro level, we've not undertaken to decompose the individual drivers of the housing market at the moment. We can see that a number of factors are coming together. We do know that higher interest rates will slow down activity and weigh on prices in the housing market, so that's part of it. We can also see that the tax changes, broader economic conditions and people's concerns and uncertainty around the environment have played a role, and that is understandable. We think all of those factors are playing into this. But as I have said, we really concentrate at that aggregate level, when we're thinking from a monetary policy lens, and even there we haven't done that decomposition that you mentioned.
I see that you have negative dwelling investment forecasts coming through from December 2027. Is that right?

Yes. The number that you're quoting is, I think, from the August 2026 Statement on monetary policy. That says that we expect dwelling investment to be falling year on year through the December quarter 2027. That's correct.
What do you think is driving that? Is that going to be taxes and interest rates again, or other factors?

It's the play-through of all of that. Fundamentally, if you're talking about new residential construction, the driver of dwelling investment is the profitability of any given project—so demand in the market. When we get house price declines, it's not atypical—in fact, it's very typical—to see that flow through into lower levels of dwelling approvals. For developers, some projects just don't stack up because their final sale price goes down. So there are lower dwelling approvals, and then that comes through into commencements and into actual activity, which is what you're seeing here. That can also be the case when it comes to renovation activity. Some households that might have been thinking of doing a renovation, alteration or addition may not go ahead with that work because the housing market has shifted. So it's those things coming together. It just takes a little bit of time to fully get into the actual activity numbers, because, as you can imagine, particularly for medium and higher density projects, the pipeline and timelines into approvals and then into actual activity can run for months or quarters, or even into years. So it just takes time, which is why you see it from late 2027 onwards.

I take your evidence to be that the factors are the taxes, the interest rates and, I think you mentioned, profitability. These are some of the reasons, I imagine, that we have high levels of approvals but lower levels of completions on a relative basis. Politicians are loath to say this, but my sense of it is that the building and construction sector is really struggling to be profitable and, therefore, people are doing other things with their capital. I'm interested in whether you would agree with that analysis and your stats back it up or whether you think it's already profitable and we'll get the 1.2 million houses in due course.

Through our liaison program, we talk to a number of organisations right across the construction sector and across the country in different regions, and they do say to us that, through the last few years, rolling the clock all the way back through into COVID times, there were significant challenges with profitability at various points. We've had some really quite substantial and, in some cases, historically sharp movements in material costs, for example. If you're on some type of fixed-price contract for your end product and your input costs are moving sharply, that can then create some profitability challenges.

Equally, over the last year or so—this has been reported by the ABS, in the inflation data that we've had over that time—we've seen evidence that builders, in terms of new dwelling costs or prices that consumers pay, have been trying to pass through some of those cost increases that they've faced. I don't have any specific numbers or data to hand to confirm what you're saying. But certainly, as I have said, through our liaison program, we do hear of challenges around profitability. Equally, we have seen some evidence of at least some cost pass-through. I expect that it's different in different parts of the country and different in terms of the type of activity that an individual firm might be undertaking.
This is the last question from me. Surely the last thing that this sector needs is more red tape and more taxes if it's got a profitability problem?

Again, just going back to our liaison program, which is just a great source of information for us, businesses in the construction sector and many other sectors will talk to us about the challenge around costs related to the regulatory and compliance issues that you're talking about. What those regulatory settings look like is obviously a matter for government. But in the context of our liaison program and what we hear from people on the ground in that sector, this is an issue that is raised, yes.

Senator, as you well know, this is an issue that has a long history. It has been brought up for a number of years that the constraints and the regulations around new housing development are constraining the supply of new housing, and this is one of the sources of the structural undersupply of housing in the country.
Senator Payman.
I have a few premises that I'd like some confirmation around. Governor, the cash rate cannot produce more oil, resolve an overseas conflict or repair an international supply chain, correct?
Correct.
So, when inflation is caused by those factors, increasing the cash rate does not remove the source of the price increase, correct?

Yes, but I'm going to pre-empt you. The point here is that the inflation problem in Australia is not solely due to the fuel price issue and the conflict in the Middle East. It is due to the fact that the demand for goods and services in Australia is running ahead of the ability of the economy to supply those goods and services. That's why we started raising interest rates before the fuel price went up, and it still remains the problem that domestic demand is higher than domestic supply.

I understand. But what I'm hearing from constituents is that, in situations like that, the bank responds by taking spending power away from Australian households until demand elsewhere in the economy falls; is that a correct observation?

The way I described it earlier was that a supply shock like this, particularly the oil supply shock, worsens the trade-off between inflation and economic growth, in some sense. If it's a supply shock, you're quite right; the interest rate here does nothing about that particular supply shock. But it does do one important thing. If we think it's going to find its way into inflation expectations and, therefore, get ingrained in the economy, we have to respond. Earlier, Dr Kent noted that inflation expectations have remained remarkably anchored, and that's partly because markets expect that central banks around the world will respond in an appropriate way to make sure that inflation doesn't get ingrained at a high level in the economy.

My focus is on how this impacts households. How many Australian households does the RBA estimate have already exhausted their discretionary spending and have nothing meaningful left to cut? Can you provide us with a number, please?
I don't think we have that number. We do have some numbers for the people whom we think are cash flow constrained. Brad, you can talk to that.

Yes. The best visibility we've got here is over Australians who have taken out a mortgage. Here we're talking a little more than a third of the population, and our numbers suggest that only around two per cent of households are in or close to what we call a 'negative spare cash flow position', where they have less cash flow than they have essential spending obligations.

So that's the numbers we've got. The problem is we have no visibility, really, over renters, who are the people with less income—typically, they're lower income—and I don't believe that we have any visibility over renters.

When we don't have the full picture and, obviously, don't have a specific number to say how many Australian households have exhausted their discretionary spending, on what evidentiary basis does the board conclude that those households can safely withstand further rate increases?

Monetary policy is not about looking at the extent to which individual households or groups can withstand increases in interest rates. As Brad has said already, people with mortgages are obviously affected by interest rates. Renters and people on low incomes typically don't have mortgages, so they're not impacted by interest rates. They're impacted by other things and, most importantly, they are impacted by inflation; that's the thing that hurts them the most. The best thing we can do for them is to get inflation down. Inflation affects everyone, and we only have one tool in our toolbox, and that's the interest rate. We know that, over time, what higher interest rates do—and not just the cash flow channel for mortgage holders—through the economy is slow down the growth of demand in the economy and that will help to the extent that we are supply constrained.

Senator, you asked about evidence and data. As the governor and Brad have just outlined, we don't have data. But what we do, through our liaison program, is talk to community organisations and other non-profit organisations that support households, and they give us very clear and regular updates on the challenge that people are facing. We do know that some people are very challenged at the moment; that's very clear. That's also very clear in the reports that sector puts out. We are able to see it in a more qualitative way, you like, even though there aren't the precise numbers to track it, as you've just asked us about. We are aware of those groups. As I outlined earlier, and as the governor has just said, yes, we're tracking it in an aggregate sense, but we are also observing what's happening across the whole economy. While we can see, for example, that household spending growth has slowed, we can also see that it is still growing and, more broadly, at the moment, the economy doesn't look as though it's heading into a recession, and that's not our baseline forecast. Even if we don't have a precise number for some of what you're asking us about, we have ways of checking and cross-checking, if you like, what's going on.
What we do have evidence on is inflation, and the evidence there, as you will have seen from this morning, is it's far too high.

Where inflation is materially driven by factors that the cash rate cannot directly affect, has the RBA ever formally advised the government that an additional policy instrument, statutory power or institutional mechanism is required?

No, it's not our role to advise the government on these sorts of things. Our role is to set monetary policy to deal with and keep inflation in the target band and preserve full employment, to the extent that we can. It is the government's and the elected officials' role to decide what they want to do, if anything, in this space.
I understand your proposition, but obviously it would be within your remit to seek out additional tools, acknowledging the limits of interest rate policy in responding to supply shocks.

It's not within our remit. Our remit is to use the tools available to us to deal with inflation and full employment, and that is what we do. Independence goes both ways. The government and the elected officials are the people who decide what they want to do with all of these tools. A lot of these additional tools, which you haven't specifically named but people are naming, are all government tools, and they're not for us to tell the government what to do.

I have one last question. If the RBA cannot tell us how many households have nothing left to cut, you're using a tool that cannot directly address major causes of inflation and you face no comparable consequence when your judgement is wrong, on what basis should Australians have confidence that the RBA is competent and fit for purpose?

I just want to correct this notion that we have no oversight of what's happening to those who are very directly affected by an interest rate increase, and what we're talking about here, largely, is those who have a mortgage. As for those who have a mortgage, we do have quite accurate data, in a timely fashion, on things like the way in which they're servicing their loans, including most Australians paying more than the minimum requirement, and we monitor that very carefully. Those extra payments have come back a bit. But most mortgage holders are still paying those extra payments. We also look at—
That's all from me, Chair.

But I'm just saying that most are paying more than the minimum they need to to service their mortgage, and the arrears rates haven't gone up a lot. The other thing we see is the stock of savings that people have built up by paying ahead of or more than the minimum required on their mortgages. We can look at those households that are drawing down on those, and they would be the sorts of households that are under the sort of stress you're talking about. There are households who are drawing down on that stock of savings that they've put in their mortgage accounts, but that share is not rising very significantly and is in line with previous years. Just finally, on this point about our not being able to affect supply, that's absolutely correct. But inflation is caused by the difference between supply and demand, and we can influence demand. It's that difference that we do have power over.
I've got to share the call.
Senator Canavan.

I have some questions about productivity. Governor, at your press conference after the September decision, you commented that the bottom line is that productivity is doing nothing. What are the economic and other consequences for inflation of productivity doing nothing?

The bottom line on that is that, if productivity isn't growing or not growing very fast, then the economy can't grow very fast and demand can't grow very fast, because it runs into a speed limit, as I think the deputy governor has highlighted on a number of occasions.
If productivity were growing faster, would it mean that interest rates would be higher than otherwise?

It depends on what's happening to demand. But if demand is still above supply, then interest rates will need to be higher, in restrictive territory, to bring it back down so it's consistent with the slower growth in supply. The question about the level of interest rates is a slightly more complex one, because it depends on what you think is a restrictive or neutral interest rate. That's a bit more of a complicated question.
I suppose that I'm asking these questions within a frame of all other things being equal. Are there things that the RBA can do to influence productivity?

The short answer is no. But I would say that an economy with a high and variable inflation rate is not conducive to good decisions being made by businesses and households, so the best thing that we can do for productivity is to get inflation back down to target.
Are you somewhat reliant on other parts of the Australian government adopting pro-productivity policies to help you with your task of controlling inflation?
Not just the government. The businesses also have to step up here.

That is very much the case, and I'm not disputing that. This being questioning of government in Senate estimates, there's nothing we can do directly over businesses. But, of course, we can get better ourselves, so my question is trying to relate to the public sector here. Are you reliant on other public sector agencies adopting policies that are pro-productivity to make your job easier?

If productivity can be improved, then the economy can run more quickly and demand can grow more quickly, without running into inflationary pressures. We have a Productivity Commission that does work on productivity. That's what they do. They have plenty of suggestions out there for things that can be done. To the extent that some of that is in the regulatory space and the government can address those, then that's for them to do.

You mentioned the neutral cash rate earlier. I know that lots of other factors influence the neutral cash rate but, all other things being equal, does a lower productivity rate increase the neutral cash rate?
No, it's the other way around. Chris, did you want to talk about the neutral rate?

Yes. If, in the future, productivity growth is thought to be higher, that would be a signal for companies to do more investment. That's something that could be moving the neutral rate higher, which means that monetary policy for a given cash rate would be less restrictive. That's a global phenomenon that we're seeing at present.
But obviously that's not happening here. That's not the explanation with higher interest rates here, though.
No. But Australia being a small, open economy, a heavy influence on our neutral rate is what's happening offshore, because we import a lot of capital.

But then, as you said earlier, demand is higher than what we can produce. So, if our productivity were higher, we would produce goods that match that demand, which would mean that you then wouldn't have to increase interest rates as much. Am I missing something there?

If we didn't have excess demand and we had demand running more in line with supply, then we could have an interest rate which was neutral. Is that rate going to be the same as it is now because the neutral rate has risen or is it not? I don't know. Chris's point is that it does seem that, because of the global investment boom that's happening at the moment, investment globally is outstripping savings, and that's putting upward pressure on neutral interest rates. If that happens, we'll get—

I'm not really asking about the global investment framework. Obviously, you've mentioned, and your evidence is, that there's excess demand in the economy. There are two ways of fixing that. Obviously, you can cut back on demand, or you can increase supply. That would get rid of the excess demand. Wouldn't a higher productivity rate increase the supply curve side, which would take pressure off interest rates? That would be the case, wouldn't it, irrespective of what's happening in global capital markets?

This is all very uncertain, and it would really depend on how households and businesses responded.
