But the links here is that, if we had sustained stronger productivity growth over a number of years, we would expect that to manifest and come through in terms of stronger growth in incomes for both households and businesses, being revenues for businesses and wages and income flows for households, and that then might well lift their spending. So businesses would invest more, potentially, and households might consume more. That would mean that our living standards would be going up more quickly, and that would be a very good outcome for everyone, obviously. But if we saw that happening, then, yes, supply would be stronger, but it could also be the case that demand would be stronger. So that kind of dynamic is actually something that we're very conscious of in the context of the AI boom and what that might look like going forward from here over the next two, three, five and beyond years. If that dynamic comes through, then that does have implications for that neutral rate in the long run, but we don't know about the actual—
Is the AI boom influencing your cash rate decisions at the moment?

In the context of business investment, which has increased very sharply over the last 12 months, with a decent portion of that increase coming from the data centre investment that's at least partially related to the AI move, it is in—
I suppose I was more following up on your points about it potentially leading to higher revenues and income. Is that the point you just made; is that influencing it?
No, I'm not saying that. That's why I was quite careful to say 'sustained over a number of years'. We're not in that situation yet, no.

I don't want to go around in circles, because I haven't got a lot of time. But given that your job is to maintain stable inflation over the cycle, I'm obviously asking you questions more about what's influencing your cash rate decisions and not about long-run issues.

To the extent that the current investment in data centres is adding to demand and demand is already above supply, then that is part of the inflationary pressures that are in the economy at the moment.
Given the time, I'll just move on. Last year, you downgraded your productivity growth forecast from one to 0.7 per cent. What drove you to make such a downgrade?

Yes, you're right; we downgraded that technical assumption just over a year ago, in August 2025. That was really based on an observation of what we had seen happening at a macro level, looking at labour productivity outcomes over a number of years, going back five, 10 or even 20 years, and having seen a slowdown in that pace of growth. We also supplemented that sort of more macro analysis with some more bottom-up, industry-based work, where we could see that certain sectors had seen shifts in their productivity trends, mining being a particular example. Once we put those two approaches together, the overall outcome was that, yes, we downgraded our assumption from one per cent to 0.7 per cent. The final point I'd make is that, for us, our forecast horizon is two to three years, and it's what you see published in the Statement on Monetary Policy. We're really making a technical assumption that applies over that time horizon. We're not making a judgement or an assumption about five, 10, 20 or beyond years into the future.
Are those forecasts for productivity stable at the moment, or are you expecting any further downgrades?

We're always watching. As with all of our technical assumptions, they're always under constant review, if you like. We haven't downgraded or changed that assumption since August last year. But all of our technical assumptions are always under review, and that includes productivity.
Your assumptions are about half, I think, of what's in the budget. Have you discussed with Treasury why there's such a large gap between your forecasts and those of the Australian government?

We do have a number of conversations with our Treasury colleagues on an ongoing basis. Obviously, questions about their assumptions should definitely be directed to them, and I wouldn't want to speak for them. But my understanding is that their assumption that you have mentioned—I think it's the 1.2 per cent—applies to what we would call the 'long run', so well beyond the kind of forecast horizon that we focus on. Again, that's a two- to three-year horizon. I think our assumptions, or at least what both sides are projecting, if you like, for that two- to three-year horizon are much closer together, but I don't have the Treasury numbers to hand, so I can't comment further on that.
So you don't do any work on long-term estimates of productivity growth?

In the context of setting monetary policy and the time horizon that the tool works across, which is, as I have said, that two- to three-year horizon, that's really where we concentrate our efforts. So, yes, it's true that we've not focused beyond that horizon. Aspects of our work and our understanding of the economy obviously do go beyond that two- to three-year horizon. There was some earlier discussion around the impact of climate change. If we're thinking about even the data centre boom, for example, we're getting projections from the hyperscalers that go beyond that two- to three-year horizon, so we're aware of those and tracking those. But as a specific focus point, no, we don't look beyond the two- to three-year horizon, because that's the horizon for our policy instrument.
Do you see anything currently in government policy that would indicate you could lift your productivity estimates soon?

I think that question is really best directed to the government. Obviously, Treasury would have a view on that, as would other government institutions. The governor mentioned the Productivity Commission earlier on. They really are the experts in this space. We don't pretend to be experts in productivity. It's not something on which monetary policy has a significant impact, so we really do rely on and work closely with other bodies that have much more expertise than we do in this area.
Senator Sharma.
The RBA's preferred measure of inflation is trimmed mean or core inflation, as opposed to headline; is that right?

Yes, that is correct. Let me take a step back. Our target is headline, but we focus a lot on trimmed mean, this underlying measure, because we think that it abstracts from some quite volatile components of the CPI, and such components can abstract from what's going on, really, in terms of the underlying inflation rate. So it's not our target—our target is headline—but, over time, you would expect headline and underlying to move together, and it just abstracts from the volatility month to month.
When was trimmed mean inflation last within the RBA's target band?
I think we'd have to check in order to get the precise date. It has been some time; you're right. It did come back into the band in 2025, but it's been some time since it's been there sustainably.
I thought headline inflation dipped into the target band in 2025, but not underlying?
Headline certainly did. Headline went below the target band, in fact, at one point.
Trimmed mean inflation did come inside the target band in the middle of last year. It then rose back out towards the end of last year, as the governor discussed earlier.

Governor, you mentioned in your opening statement that central banks in other advanced economies are increasing their policy rates. This year, have any of the 43 advanced economies raised rates by 100 basis points or anything higher?

Of the ones we compare ourselves with, no. But as I discussed earlier, most of those economies were not coming from positions of excess demand that we were; they were coming from positions of excess supply. So they are basically in a very different situation to us.
That concludes our session with the Reserve Bank. Thank you very much for joining us. We will now suspend for lunch.

I don't want to take up any more of the committee's time, because the chair has been generous. I want to make the point to you that the Fraser government introduced FOIs so that people could see how government works. This government and maybe prior governments have used it in a way to block access to very basic information. This FOI is just an example of trying to get access to the modelling which underpinned key budget judgements. I don't think it's reasonable for the exclusions that have been used here, operational and otherwise, to be used as a justification. The reality is that most people who put in FOIs can't come into this committee and ask questions about them. I'm doing it effectively as a citizen to make the point that I don't think you're applying these exemptions properly as a department. That has been my view for a long time. It has been exposed in the past that you've incorrectly used irrelevant judgements and other things in relation to these FOIs.

Maybe this is a question for the minister. I don't want to put the officials in a difficult position. Generally speaking, the Centre for Public Integrity has found that your government is very secretive. It would aid the public debate if you would at least encourage the department to provide basic information when they are required to under the act rather than hide behind these exemptions. People ask for basic information and get pages and pages and pages of redactions that are not very useful.

If you're alleging that the FOI Act is not being applied properly, pursue that, Senator Bragg, with any evidence you have for that. The government is not involved in FOI decisions unless they relate to FOIs against ourselves. But if they are FOIs to the departments, those are handled by the department. In my experience, they are handled extremely professionally and in accordance with the law.
In general, though, what is your view about the way that the Treasury is responding to FOIs from the citizenry?
Treasury is not my portfolio area. In a general sense, the point I just made is the one that I would say is the approach Treasury takes. They need to act in accordance with the law.
Senator, the department takes its obligations under the FOI Act very seriously. I appreciate your concerns and your views that exemptions aren't applied, in your view, appropriately.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: That's right.

There are times when we have decisions that go to the Office of the Information Commissioner, for example, and the Information Commissioner comes to a different view. There are equally times when we have decisions that go to the Information Commissioner and they come to the same view as us. So we seek to do so consistently and professionally with every application we receive.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Thank you. Senator Liddle, I understand you have some questions for corporate.
Yes. Thank you. I want to ask about red tape accounting, please. Can somebody from markets group help with that?

Does anyone else have any corporate questions? No. I think we can release representatives from corporate. Thank you very much for coming. I will invite Treasury officials from markets group to join us. We will suspend for a moment until the rest of the officials join us.
I now welcome representatives from the Department of Treasury markets group. I will go straight to Senator Liddle for questions.

Thank you. I want to turn to the government's red tape cuts in financial services in reference to the May budget facts sheet, which says:

The Government will deliver reforms that reduce regulatory burden by $10.2 billion per year once fully implemented.

That includes $780 million a year in financial services. That same facts sheet outlines 14 red tape reduction measures in financial services that it says would cut that $780 million each year. As of today, how many of those 14 have actually been implemented?
I think I will turn to Mr Quinlivan to go through the 14 measures that you referred to.

Treasury is working through progressing the draft legislation for all those items. They all require legislative instruments. We're currently consulting on four of the measures. I can go through them. We've recently done consultation on the climate related financial disclosures measure.
In terms of actual implementation, nothing has actually happened yet? Is that what you are saying with the 14?
The 14 are progressing. They all require legislative instruments and agreement through those relevant processes, which may include parliament or regulation.
So for somebody out there, the impact from that announcement would be zero right now?
Of the 14, those measures are still in the process of being implemented.
So the number is zero?

I can add to that, Senator. There is the $780 million number. Taken as a whole of financial sector regulatory package, it is $960 million because it includes some regulator actions. In particular, a measure delivered by APRA, from memory, was about $180 million. That has happened, so I don't think the answer is zero. I don't think it's true to say that nothing has happened. As Mr Quinlivan has said, actually a number of these things have now gone out. The exposure drafts and the consultations are happening on these so that they can happen very soon.

Mr Kelly, the question is very specific about businesses right now having actually a reduction in red tape as a consequence of that announcement. I get that you mention that there are explanatory memorandums and ministerial consultations going on. It appears that if you ask business, they are saying red tape is getting worse. I am trying to understand whether in fact the claim that these red tape reductions are actually happening at this time is not having an effect on business because they haven't actually progressed to that point where they are being implemented.

I would be interested to know which businesses are telling you which red tape is increasing and what that relates to. I have whole-of-government regulatory reform responsibilities actually under my portfolio as Minister for Finance. A lot of people—I just said this in the previous session—raise the issue of red tape. You said red tape is increasing, I think, for business. I am asking if you could tell me what areas they are in. What areas of business are telling you that red tape is increasing in?
Minister Gallagher, I would be very happy to provide you a list of businesses I have spoken to directly. Not right now. I would certainly be very happy to provide it to you on notice.
So you can't nominate an area where it's getting worse?
These are manufacturing businesses that I have spoken to directly that are talking about red tape increasing. These are real people running businesses.
Yes. I understand that. What is the red tape that is increasing for them?
It is a compliance matter.
In relation to what—a Commonwealth area?
Manufacturing. Yes, a Commonwealth area of responsibility.
So we have increased red tape on compliance reporting in manufacturing and that is worrying them?
They are the complaints I have been getting. As I said, if you really want it, I'm happy to provide the names. I have had conversations with those people. That's fine; I can commit that outside this.
Yes.
In terms of that $780 million in claimed annual red tape cuts, how many of those are climate related financial disclosures and sustainability reporting?
Sorry, Senator, could you repeat that?
How much of the $780 million in claimed annual red tape cuts relate to relief from climate related financial disclosures and sustainability reporting?

The first measure in the package goes to increasing the threshold at which companies have to lodge audited financial statements. It will have an impact on companies that may have been brought into the climate related disclosure scheme from 1 July next year. The second measure went to improving the efficiency of the regime more generally.
Can you give us an exact number, or do you have to provide that on notice?
For the first package? For the first one?
For climate and financial disclosures related to sustainability reporting.

For the large company measure, that was $215 million, which was in the media release put out with the regulations when they were released last week. For the second measure in the package, that is about $400 million.

Treasury's August 2026 consultation paper says:

Mandatory climate-related financial disclosures commenced on 1 January 2025.

The regime was legislated by this government in the Treasury Laws Amendment (Financial Market Infrastructure and Other Measures) Act 2024 just a couple of years ago. It includes the scope 3 reporting requirement, which can require data requests to smaller businesses like farms and other suppliers to larger businesses. Is that correct?

For that list of 14, most of them belong in markets group. We can talk about the list in general. For that particular item—climate related financial disclosures—that's the responsibility of fiscal group, which is a group that will be following us. If you have detailed questions on that, I suggest you ask them.
I thought we were in markets group, Chair.
We are markets group. We deal with most of these measures. But that particular one is dealt with by fiscal group.
I will come back to them.
That is the group that follows this group.

Let me get this right. The government wrote the laws that imposed the red tape on businesses. They then considered changes that could reduce some of that burden they imposed and told Australians that means they are cutting regulatory burdens. Is that correct?

I don't know if you are specifically talking about a piece of legislation there. Is that the one that has been referred to fiscal group, or just in general? A lot of the regulatory reform isn't just legislation that we have passed. It is going back over the statute book over time. It's not clear to me when you say we did it and now we're undoing it. Like with the EPBC, for example, the legislation that we reformed was about reducing red tape. That legislation had been in place for some time.
Are things like reasonable assurance audits implemented yet or not?
Senator, I refer you to fiscal group to ask those questions.
In terms of those 14 items that make up that $780 million figure, who is actually responsible for ensuring the delivery of those 14 measures? Is it you?

I think it's correct to say that 13 of the 14 are a responsibility of markets group working through ministers to deliver them. As Mr Quinlivan said, we are progressing them all. We have been working on them. Some of them have recently gone out for exposure draft processes with a view to making them in the near future.

I will start with this. The draft regulations for raising monetary threshold are out for consultation at the moment. This was announced months ago. A lot of businesses were keen to see that happen. What took so long to get the materials drafted and out for consultation?
Treasury is working through the policy details and the legislative drafting as appropriate. These things do take time.
What happens next? Is that after the consultation is finished?

I believe the consultation period ends next week. Following that, subject to the feedback we receive on that process, the government will have the option to make the regulations. There is a disallowance period in which the parliament has the opportunity to consider those. They are due to start on 1 July next year for lodgements that would apply from that period, yes.
So what you are saying is that if the Treasurer were to approve the regulations in their current form, the timeframe would be July next year?
Yes. It won't apply to this financial year. It won't apply for the financial year just passed but prospectively.
How would those changes be communicated to stakeholders and the public?

We can take on notice exactly the process for that. I think it would follow the usual arrangements of communication to the regulated entities about what their reporting requirements are and who might meet the thresholds to continue to disclose.
Has the Treasurer set a timetable for when he would like to achieve this full regulatory saving for the financial sector?

Senator, all these measures ultimately fit within the constraints within an overall legislative program. The government needs to choose how they prioritise and take things forward. It is subject as we go to consultation and feedback with people about the details of them. So it's not a case that there is a simple doing of things by these dates. We are working with the ministers' offices and the ministers to progress them as fast as we can. It is not with a view to just doing them all in one go because that would probably delay them.

CPA Australia has been saying that there are actually billions of dollars in additional red tape that is impacting businesses. Where does this sit in the priority list of things that you have to get done given businesses are hurting now?

Senator, you have been focused in your question on this package of $780 million relating to the financial regulations. There is a broader set of work being done by our regulators coming out of the roundtable, where they committed to 52 things. More than half of them have already been done. I think 13 or a lot of the rest should be done by the end of the financial year. There is a broader package that the government announced with a view to reducing regulatory costs in the budget by a total of $10.2 billion, of which the $780 million is just a part. We can talk you through those. A lot of them have been done or are well progressed as well. If you would like, I can call the relevant officers.

I'm trying to identify where the priority is for this right now. Minister, given regulatory reform sits within your portfolio responsibilities, is there a particular timeframe you would like to see these measures implemented in?

We discussed this at length yesterday in the finance committee. All of those areas are underway. Some of them require agreement from the states and territories, so it's difficult to put a timeframe on it. This has been a core feature of our budget. The regulatory reform process is a part of our productivity agenda. It is an important part of the work that I and other ministers are doing, including the Treasurer and his team.

Senator, I can give some examples of that $10.2 billion. One of the big items related to the PBC reforms—a lot of it has already been implemented and other bits are in progress—is simplifying the tax system. That is a $415 million saving. Those measures are being implemented. There is abolishing additional nuisance tariffs. That measure has been done. If you look at that broader list, you can actually see things that have been delivered and are relevant to businesses today.
Thank you.

Thanks for being here, everyone. My questions go to consulting reform and the options paper. Since the last estimates session in May, Treasury has finally released the long-awaited options paper on reforming the accounting audit and consulting sectors. Consultation and the options paper opened on 1 July and closed on 12 August. How many submissions did the consultation receive?

Senator, we were running the consultation process for six weeks on that. In parallel, we also ran the consultation on whistleblowing reforms. That was for eight weeks. On both those processes, we received 70 submissions to both of them. We ran a series of roundtables during the consultation.
Can you break down the 70 between the whistleblowers and the accounting audit and consulting sectors?
Yes. It was 70 for each of them separately.
So 140 in total?
That's right.
Tell me about the roundtables.
We conducted a series of roundtables through both of them to try to draw out a few more.
Can you provide details on notice of those roundtables?
Of course, yes.
Who was invited? How many were there?
On whistleblowing we had five roundtables. On auditing, it was a few more than that. We can provide details on notice.
How does a citizen's voice get introduced into a roundtable on audit?

We've discussed this previously, Senator, about the challenges of making sure we try to get those groups engaged. We held parts of the consultation process with academics and groups—transparency groups. There is always a challenge in getting an individual's processes.
I look forward to getting those details. Did you publish all 140 submissions?
The submissions have not been published.
Do you intend to publish them?
It's a matter for government. The usual process would be to publish them at around the time that—
Sorry, I really can't hear you.

The usual process would be that they would get published around the time of the next part of the process. For example, we published the last round of submissions at around the time we released the options paper.
Minister, is it your intention to publish these submissions given the level of public interest in the whistleblower and auditing reform of the consulting sector?
Well, I think as the evidence was provided, it is normal practice to publish submissions. If there is any change to that, I will let you know.
The timing is important. I recollect there was a long delay with publishing the submissions. It was a very long delay, as I recollect. Is it your intention, Minister, to publish them in a timely way?

Well, it's usually done at a particular part of the process and at a particular stage. I don't think there's any reason to delay them. It would be really a matter in consultation with the relevant ministers.

The reason I ask and would like to see all the submissions is that this matter has been afoot for years now. There is a considerable public interest. It is vital that the public gets the opportunity to look at the evidence and the perspectives that have been put forward. The recommendations for the various consulting inquiries have sat now, Minister, at the feet of the government for years. When do you expect the introduction of legislation, as the minister representing the relevant minister, to finally reform audit assurance and the consulting sectors?

Well, that would be a matter for the Assistant Treasurer to determine in consultation with our own processes. I don't have a date I can give you. I do know the Assistant Treasurer is very engaged on this issue and has certainly been talking to many of his colleagues about it. If there is anything further I can provide you, I will.
Thank you. I would really appreciate that. Is it your expectation that the legislation will be introduced in the current term?

Well, the work is certainly happening now. But I can't give you an answer on that because I don't think those decisions have been taken yet. We need to get through this part of the process before decisions are taken about if and when legislation is brought into the parliament.
Sorry, if?
Well, we have to go through our processes. Ministers don't make calls on the introduction of legislation or specifics of legislation without going through our processes.
I'm concerned that you used the word 'if'. It is your expectation there will be legislation. Is that the case? I have been consulted on that basis.
Yes. What I am saying is that those decisions haven't been finalised. We have to go through our processes. I think the Assistant Treasurer is leading that work and doing the work.

I understand that. Thank you. Have you made any decisions as a government about partnership caps, about subjecting large partnerships to corporate tax and transparency and accountability requirements of the kind the corporate sector faces and in relation to managing the structural conflicts that occur in multidisciplinary firms where we see that very clear conflict of interest between audit work, consulting and tax?

These are some of the issues that have come up through the work you've done and others, including Senator O'Neill. I think you've been raising concerns about this area for quite a number of years now. The government hasn't made final decisions on this matter yet.

I'm curious. A lot of people say to me, and I know it to be true, that the big four partnerships are very powerful and large, although two of them at least have suffered very significant blows in recent years. What is the pathway of consultation and lobbying by the big four firms? Can you provide, for example, a diary record of how often the relevant minister meets with officers and staff of the big four?

Well, I can't answer on behalf of the Assistant Treasurer and who he meets with. I have something to do in this sector, particularly around government procurement. From my perspective, I have not had a meeting with the big four that I can recall on an individual matter or, indeed, any lobbying from them about the government approach to their business. I've probably had some letters from PwC and KPMG from time to time when issues have arisen. But I think any suggestion that they are taking some kind off aggressive lobbying approach is certainly not my experience.
Well, I am a bit player here and I've had them walk in my door with the expectation that they will have ready access. That is not so recently. I ask that the minister—
We can certainly take it on notice.

Take it on notice. I'm very curious. I would like to be reassured that the same principle applies to him, which is that he is not meeting with them. Could I have any evidence of any diary entries or communications with the big four firms and their personnel? Thank you.
We'll take it on notice.

Thank you. I want to go to whistleblowers. Treasury is also conducting a review into issues in relation to tax and corporate whistleblowing frameworks. I've asked you about them before. How is that review of whistleblowing reform going? When do you expect an outcome and legislation to be progressed?

Senator, we've undertaken that public consultation period, which we discussed previously. We are considering that feedback. We've provided initial advice to the minister. We are preparing the statutory review report that we're required to prepare. The government is required to table that 15 sitting days after they receive it. It's in a similar spot to the auditing work and requires consideration by government as to final decisions and how to take them forward.
Do you plan to publish all the non-confidential submissions?

As part of that 70, there were a range of confidential submissions and anonymous submissions, as you would appreciate from your engagements with that group of people. Similarly, the usual practice would be to publish the non-confidential submissions.

On 9 July, the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services, chaired by my colleague to my left, wrote a joint public letter to the Prime Minister. This is a question for you, Minister. It was signed by all eight members, from across all the parties, on the JPC. It's a very explicit letter, pointing to longstanding recommendations going back to 2017 and using language that is unusually firm, about the need for urgent reform. We talk about the 'urgent enhancement' that is needed, how there is 'an overwhelming case' and how it should be done 'with haste' and 'as soon as practicable'. I don't know how many adjectives we need to use to impress on the government how critical this is and how long we have been waiting. There are many repetitive examples of the risks to our financial system created by the absence of a decent whistleblower regime. I would like to know where the response to that letter is at, please.
That was a letter to the Prime Minister?
Yes.

Well, that would really be a matter that PM&C estimates would have to deal with, not this one. I will see if there is anything I can provide that Treasury might be involved in in formulating that. There is certainly a lot of work underway. As you would know, Senator Pocock, the recent KPMG review by Dr Watt also traversed some of these issues.
Well, we're all in furious agreement about it. The letter was provided to relevant ministers. It didn't just go to the Prime Minister; it went to—
I'll see if there's any update I can provide to you.
Thank you.
Senator Smith.

Good afternoon to you. I want to very briefly continue a line of questioning that Senator Liddle was pursuing. In regard to the $780 million red-tape reduction in financial services, how in that figure and how in the reporting does an increase in the red tape, an initiative of government to increase regulation, get recorded or accounted for if that same regulation is part of the regulations that are subsequently reduced or removed?
Are you asking about the specific ones in the budget where we are saying that it's—
I'm asking about the $780 million—
Right—so a subset of the regulatory reform agenda?
Yes—the $780 million red-tape reductions in financial services.

In some ways, we do the count based on decisions taken by government and our estimate of the regulatory impact of them. For the purpose of that $780 million package or the broader $10.2 billion package, it was a set of decisions being taken to reduce regulatory burden. Any decision to reduce regulatory burden that unwinds an existing piece of legislation or a previous decision is always, in some ways, going back and unwinding something that government has imposed. They all kind of share that similar issue. There's no way of reducing regulatory burden that doesn't involve unwinding something the government has imposed in the past.

What we haven't tried to include in those packages—they are packages which are all about reducing regulation. We haven't tried to capture everything government does, because, as I think has been said many times, it's not a deregulation agenda; it's a 'better regulation' agenda. There are legitimate areas where government will sometimes need to regulate or change regulations. Senator Pocock's questions go to one of those areas that is a matter of public debate today.
I'm trying to understand whether it is a gross or net reduction in red tape.
As we discussed at the last estimates, it is both the gross and the net reduction of red tape from those measures because they're all measures that reduce regulatory burden.

So a regulatory burden or regulatory compliance of this value is introduced, then a regulatory compliance arrangement of this value is removed. It still leaves that value, so it hasn't actually been a—
We're not claiming to have removed all regulation from the system, no.
But are you moving like for like? Are you moving regulatory burdens that are of similar value?

I think we're like for like in the sense that we're counting the saving from a decision of government in the same way we would count—and OAA, I think, currently produces an annual stocktake of them—the net. So OAA produces a number that says, 'Here's the total net regulatory burden of all the decisions taken by government,' whether that ends up being positive or negative. It publishes that. I think it gives a bit of a breakdown of the major aspects of that. In the system, that's that measure that lags a bit. This is a package that was about, 'Let's explicitly look at things to reduce regulatory burden in the financial sector regulatory space.' We came up with a package of $960 million. Of that, $760 million related to things the government then had to implement. It is going from a certain level of stock and reducing it down. Clearly, one of those measures is the Financial Accountability Regime. Regulators have already taken steps to make that simpler. We are consulting on one thing to make that simpler. There are some other commitments. There will still be a financial accountability regime sitting there at the end of the day which has a regulatory burden, which is something we've always got to be conscious of when we think about its ongoing value to the system versus the costs it imposes.
If the government added $1 billion in new climate reporting red tape and then removed $400 million of that, does the document or report show that as a cut or a net increase?
As I said, that's fiscal group's responsibility. The way I think about it is that parliament has passed legislation to give effect to that regulatory burden.
Not unanimously.
But the parliament has passed it.
Not necessarily.

The government is making a decision to reduce that burden. For any burden that it reduces, our parliament must have previously passed it or some regulator must have previously imposed it. We can't remove a burden that hasn't been imposed in the past.
But the point here is that the minister is trying to claim credit for $780 million worth of—
I don't know if it's credit. That's what it has been costed at if those reforms are implemented.
Sorry, Minister?
I've made my point. I was being concise, unlike you.
We're not talking about lightening the regulatory burden just of regulatory imposts of this government?
Well, these arrangements that we are looking to reform—I would have to go through them one by one—have been around for a while. Some of them have been around longer than others.
So new regulatory imposts aren't being removed?
I don't know what—

Senator, in that list of 14 climate related financial disclosures you would say has been a measure introduced by the current government. The financial accountability regime is an initiative originally in a different form under former treasurer Morrison.

Thank you very much for that. I will move to a different matter. When did markets group first know of the ban on card surcharges? When did markets group first know the ban on card surcharges would mean additional costs for the Commonwealth? Was it something that government was contemplating when the RBA began its review process in October 2024?

I might go to Ms McKay to answer. I want to make sure I understand the question. The government knew at a certain point. That was just before it was publicly announced by the RBA. The RBA was going to move to effectively end the practice of surcharging. The government knew it would have consequences for government to work through. What those consequences weren't known at some immediate point in time. They had to be worked through.

I understand your point that when the RBA's decision was known, government would have a clear authoritative basis on which to understand the implications. Were the costs to Commonwealth entities consciously contemplated as the RBA was going through its review process?

Senator, there is one thing I should check with you and the other senators before we go further. There are obviously questions in this space relating to the ATO. They will be matters revenue group can answer. I have a question before we answer more questions here. We can speak to payments policy in general. We can speak to the RBA review. We can actually speak to some of these broader issues that you have already started asking about. If you would find it more convenient to ask all questions related to this matter in one place, Ms McKay and I can stay back for the revenue group session. I want to check how you want to do this. Are you happy for us to move things to revenue group when they relate to the ATO?
No. Let's do as much as we can here.
I will have to rotate shortly.
Will your group have contemplated the implications of the payments policy?

I guess within our branch we did give consideration or similar to how business would respond when the card payment reforms came into place. Similarly, government agencies would need to respond in ways where they would employ strategies to respond to the surcharging changes as well.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: So when did you start the work on giving consideration to the implications of changes in policy or a decision by the RBA of this kind?
I think with that it is important to say that it was a decision taken by the Payments System Board.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: Correct, yes.
That decision was not known until it was taken by the Payments System Board.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: On 31 March 2026.

Obviously, the decision was taken by the Payments System Board at the board meeting. It was communicated publicly on 31 March for agencies to consider how they respond to the changes that come into effect. They know the best way for them to respond because they will consider the use cases they have and how they will be able to do it. That being said, some initial consideration was done to give a sense of some of the strategies that would need to be employed by some agencies. That was commenced early, but it was not done in a widespread way.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: So it was considered early but not—

It wasn't done widespread. We just did an initial focus on some agencies that were thought of who may have some of the largest payment costs. It wasn't until after the decision was taken and that it was actually known what the changes would be that a more widespread approach was taken. The Assistant Treasurer mentioned that he contacted his portfolio ministers to do a more coordinated approach with entities. As part of that, that's when we started engaging with other entities.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: Thank you very much, Ms McKay. When you say 'we', do you mean markets group?
After this, I will have to rotate the call.
Yes. That was done within markets group.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: When you say some agencies, can you list those agencies?
As part of the process in terms of when we went out, we contacted portfolio CFOs. It was then the role of portfolio CFOs to engage further within their portfolios.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: You just said that's the process we're in now. I'm interested in which agencies you contemplated prior to the 31 March 2026 decision. You said 'we'. You have said you were giving consideration to it. There was early consideration. The markets group was thinking about it in the context of some agencies. The Assistant Treasurer then goes out more broadly based on this early consideration. Which agencies were part of that early consideration?
I apologise. I would have to take the specifics of the agencies on notice. I actually don't have the list. It was a small number. I don't want to get them wrong.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: I'm rotating the call now. We can come back to you, Senator Smith.
A long list or a short list?
No. It was a short list.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: It was a short list. Mr Kelly might recall how short the list was and who was on the list.

Senator, no, I don't recall the agencies on the short list. I will put it in context. This is before the Payments System Board had made its decision we were contemplating what that would mean for the Commonwealth. It is also fair to say that the Payments System Board was well aware that the decisions it made would affect what is in some ways their receiving payment on taxes or regulated prices. You can actually see that in the consultation report. That is the kind of group of entities we are thinking about.
Was the ATO on that list?
I am rotating the call. We can come back to you, Senator Smith, because this could go on.
Sorry, they are looking at you.
You keep interrupting me when I try to wind you up. They have taken elements of it on notice. You can come and have another go if you need to.
Thanks, Chair. I have some questions in particular about the CGT changes and their effect on junior explorers.
Senator, you'll have to ask revenue group those questions. They appear after fiscal group. That is two sessions from here.
I am interested in Senator Smith's last question. Was the ATO on the list?
I believe it was the ATO. I believe it would be Home Affairs and, I suspect, Services Australia.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Payments, Scams and Innovation Branch

text: When did you know that there would be charges facing different agencies in this so-called surcharge ban?

That decision was announced on 31 March, as Ms McKay said. The PSB made the decision shortly before that. We had some notice that was going to be the outcome that got announced, but it was very short notice. I think it's fair to say that in that final PSB meeting where they decided it, multiple options were in the room. It was quite open.

It is a well-oiled machine down there. I have dug into the annals here. I have gone back to dig up what we talked about on 6 November 2024 here in this committee. Helpfully, minister you were here. We had an exchange. I said to you:

Is there a risk that small business will absorb some of this cost?

You said

They're some of the issues that we need to work through.

Do you remember saying that? I then said:

But you've already announced it. The Prime Minister of the country announced this.

You said:

Yes, and in the announcement, I think it makes it clear, we want to ease costs for consumers without added costs for small business or unintended consequences for the broader economy.

So did you do that work that you said you would do? You said that you would make sure there wouldn't be added costs for small business and there wouldn't be unintended consequences.

I would have to review that Hansard. I don't recall that exchange, Senator Bragg. We've had hundreds of them over many estimates hearings, so I don't think that's particularly surprising. Yes, the work was done, Senator Bragg.
What do you say to the small businesses that have to absorb the cost?

I think it is a pretty tough message for small business.
I would also say—

You say it's a tough message for small business. I accept that based on the figures I've seen. I think from what I saw, it was 16 per cent of small businesses that have surcharging on credit cards. One more. I will then rotate to Senator Sharma.

until 1 December. So how have you already decided it's made things worse?

It is currently undertaking round 3. It is over-subscribed; that is the amount of demand there is for different types of housing in the social and affordable space. You guys in the opposition say, 'Just get rid of it.' Do what you did last time when you were in government and completely remove yourself from the housing policy space. We have a different view on that.
Is it right to say that there's a $2 billion underspend at Housing Australia?
Housing Australia will appear later. I think that is a question to put to them.
You don't know that. Okay, fine.
I don't have that information in front of me.
How much of the spending is subject to a cost-benefit analysis?
Through the ERC process, there is a rigorous assessment of the new policy proposals or any new requests for spending.
So let's go tax to GDP. In 2025-26, it will hit 24.1 per cent of the economy. When was the last time we had a tax to GDP this high?
Senator, that would be in 2005-06.
Was the budget in deficit or surplus then?
The historical table shows—

The glory years before the NDIS, before the pressures on the aged care system and before the pressures on defence. This is the reality. The budget is different to the budget that existed in 2005. Any comparison to say that it's very similar or the Commonwealth has the same responsibilities that were undertaken in 2005 to 2026 is simply incorrect.

I will take you to a couple of comments made by some recently highly employed public officials. Phil Lowe said:

Now we find ourselves running sizable budget deficits at a time where we re at full employment and commodity prices are very high. We should be running sizable surpluses.

Do you agree with his assessment?
Is that question at me?
Yes.

Well, what I would say to Phil is that we have taken difficult decisions on the big driving programs where we've seen considerable growth, such as in aged care and in the NDIS. We have halved the deficits from what were forecast. I think the budget bottom line has improved in every single budget or budget update that we have handed down. We've delivered two surpluses. We've lowered the debt from what was forecast and lowered interest on that debt. We take the job of managing the budget responsibly very seriously. We also acknowledge that the government has to fund investments into programs that the community cares about. That is hospitals and that is Medicare and that is bulk-billing. That is mental health care and it is aged care. It is defence and national security. It is making sure that pensions and payments are provided on time. The demands on the federal budget are increasing, not decreasing, in all of those areas. That is something that we have to manage.

I'm trying to apply some scrutiny here to these claims you are making about expense management. I think the final budget outcome says that the government has limited real growth in payments to an average of two per cent per year over the last four years, which is well below the 30-year average of 3.4 per cent. Is that right?
Yes.
It is right, is it?
Yes.
What is the rate of real growth in payments in 2023-24?
I'm not sure I have 2023-24.
Can the officials provide that? You have an army of people here.
They are all outlined in table B1 in the Final Budget Outcome, Senator. It is 2.9 per cent.
What about 2024-25?
It is the same table, Senator. It is 5.5 per cent.
And then in 2025-26?
It is 4.3 per cent.
Why does it say an average of two per cent, because that is not an average of two per cent? You have 2.9 per cent—
The number is over four years, Senator. It includes the year before you started, the minus 4.9 per cent in 2022-23.
What is the reason for the minus 4.9 per cent?
I think that would have been our first budget, where we removed and took savings from a number of decisions that had been made by the previous government.
Okay. But it is heading in a trajectory of growth, isn't it, at 2.9 per cent; 5.5 per cent; and 4.3 per cent?

Well, that goes to the pressures that I have been talking about—how we are dealing with those pressures that are real and growing on the budget. I should say that you are promising to spend more. If this were you now, these numbers would be worse.

It's not a credible claim to say two per cent when you are going to be growing at almost three per cent, 5½ per cent and 4.3 per cent over the next three years, is it? It's not credible marketing, is it?
What are you saying?
You are saying that spending growth is going to be two per cent.
No. Don't verbal us.
And your own numbers say 2.9 per cent, 5.5 per cent and 4.3 per cent.
We have said it's two per cent over four years, which is what it is.
I will have to rotate because we have to stop at 3.45 pm, and I think Senator Hume has some questions.
I don't want to interrupt the flow.
We have seven minutes until afternoon tea, so I'll leave it to you guys.

I want to follow up on a question that I asked the secretary this morning. I am very much hoping that everybody was listening when I asked that question. It is about the cumulative decisions taken by the government over all of their budget updates. What is that dollar value?
Senator, yes, I was listening this morning.
Terrific.

I will clarify the question. In each budget update, we put a reconciliation table that shows why the underlying cash balance changes, including estimates variations and measures. It has it for a four- or five-year period. Was your question—
The decisions as opposed to the variations.
The decisions, yes. Was your question about adding up those through the eight or nine updates since the election in 2022? Is that the question you were asking?
Yes.

That's good, because I couldn't work out where the $120 billion number came from. We'll give you some numbers, but we'll give you a bit of context as well. As my secretary said this morning, we consider the important budget aggregates when you look at the macroeconomic impact of the budget and fiscal sustainability to be things such as the underlying cash balance especially but also things like gross debt. As is set out in the Final Budget Outcome, since the government was elected in 2022, the underlying cash balance has improved by $230 billion over the years.
I don't think that's the question that I asked, though.
A good part of that was tax receipts upgrades.
Yes. Again—

They've banked 77 per cent. So governments have a choice about what they do with those unexpected tax things. They've done that. We've just talked about real growth being two per cent. Budgets have five-year periods that they add up. MYEFOs have four-year periods. We drop out the first year because it's an actual and it's no longer in the estimates. Each budget we add a new year at the end to move the forward estimates along. When we look at these things, it's not the same period we're talking about all the time. It's a four- or five-year period but it keeps moving out. The other thing which I've had a discussion at estimates on, I think this time last year, is that those are the estimates at the time. They are not an outcome of measures. If measures change from what we estimated, they are not what it is. We don't update the measures for those numbers. As I discussed at estimates a year ago, for those reasons, we don't normally add up those things like that because they are not really comparing apples with apples.
Well, you do. This is the thing. This is how the $180 billion in gross savings tally is constructed, so you do add them up.
As I said when I was here before, we give them with caveats that they are not actually apples and apples.
That's not what the government says when it bandies it about.

We give the same advice when we put these up. I will tell you what the numbers have been over time, Senator. In the 2022-23 budget—the first budget of this government—it was $9,782 million. They are numbers that make the budget worse.
That is the $100 billion that—
No. This is just the first budget. This is the government's first budget in October 2023.
When Chris Richardson says $100 billion, what is it that he is referring to, in your estimation?
I don't know what Chris Richardson is referring to, Senator. I am going to give you these numbers because they are the ones that come out of the budget papers.
Okay.

We'll just give you what is in the budget. In the 2023-24 budget, it was minus $2,588 million. In the 2023-24 MYEFO, it was minus $5,266 million. In the 2024-25 budget, it was minus $24,439 million. In the 2024-25 MYEFO, it was minus $17,465 million. In the 2025-26 budget, it was minus $34,884 million. There were also numbers in the PEFO that came out. That was minus $1,109 million. In the MYEFO for 2025-26 it was $2,170 million. In the 2026-27 budget from earlier this year, it was $8,242 million.
If you add them up, what do you get?
It is $103 billion, Senator.
That sounds familiar. It is very Richardson-esque.
As we said, we would put caveats on that. They are not all quite the same.
Right. So that is $100 billion, or $103.122 billion—
I haven't added it up to a decimal, Senator.
of spending.

In terms of the big components of that, which I think is important, there's $27.8 billion on strengthening Medicare, which is the UCC's; tripling bulk-billing; and 1800 Medicare. There is $25 billion in the state agreement on public hospitals. There is $24 billion on cheaper medicines, including new and amended PBS listings. There is $16 billion into aged care. These don't completely line up with those. I am talking in general about where the big pieces of investment have been. They is energy bill relief, Services Australia, rent assistance, the prevention of violence against women and children, and expanding eligibility for parenting payment single.
I'm happy for you to table this list, if you like, Minister.
In any discussion of additional investment, we should consider what those investments are.
I understand that's what the budget is all about.
It's fine if people want to go out and say that is not quality spending. They need to say what that means for Medicare, for medicines, for hospitals and for payments.
All I am saying, Minister, is that you claim to have saved $180 billion—
Well, we have.
but you've actually spent $100 billion. For every $2 that you have claimed to have saved, you have spent $3.
No.
And it's the same calculation.
No.
So you can't be selective.
No. I don't agree with the way that you have outlined that.

We are at time for a break now. We will take a short break. We can release Fiscal Group now. Thank you very much. We will suspend for a short break and be back with Revenue, Small Business and Law Group.
The committee welcomes officers from the Revenue, Small Business and Law Group of the Department of the Treasury. Senator Whitten, over to you.

I have some questions on the CGT changes and their effect on junior mineral explorers. The CGT changes came as quite a shock to a lot of investors. One of the groups we've heard from who were particularly hard hit with this is junior mineral explorers. Was any consultation undertaken with this sector?

We're aware of the concerns of that sector. I might defer to my colleagues to understand if any specific consultations have been undertaken with them post the announcement, but we're certainly aware of the concerns that have been raised.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text:
We've met with a number of stakeholders in developing the design of the government's innovative-business CGT concessions, including with some representatives of junior mineral explorers. It might be helpful for me to step through the IBCC concession and the parameters that underpin it. The concession is a targeted concession to support early-stage investment in innovative Australian businesses. A number of the criteria go to that, including that it needs to be an unlisted business that is under 15 years of age with a turnover threshold of less than $50 million. They are quite important because they are directed at supporting businesses and having positive spillover effects for businesses.

I think the junior mineral explorers are sometimes concerned that they don't meet the requirement to be unlisted. It is a deliberate feature of the policy to target support for new capital invested in unlisted companies that would otherwise have challenges in attracting capital or have cost bases that are difficult to value. When you have a business that is listed, there is actually an identifiable cost base that can be used, so they fall out of the scope of that particular concession.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Chief Adviser, Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I am all for supporting all levels of businesses in this regard. The issue is that a lot of the explorers that are listed are the ones that probably have more chance of finding something. To attract investment, when you are an investor, your only upside potential is capital gains. Why would you invest in one of those businesses again?

The capital gains changes are about providing more neutral treatment across all different asset classes and returning the CGT regime to its original purpose of taxing real gains. Whether an investor is better or worse off very much depends on the particular facts and circumstances, including, for example, the period for which they've held the investment. So it will very much depend on their particular circumstances. But the regime as a whole is about providing more neutral treatment so decisions are made on economic considerations, not tax considerations.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Chief Adviser, Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: They are going to struggle to attract new investment, aren't they?
I don't think that's something I can answer, but my colleague in corporate and international tax division can.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Chief Adviser, Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: In our discussions with the representatives of the sector, they have spoken to us about the types of investors in this sector. I thought I would mention that, yes, there are quite a lot of individual investors who, if they are investing directly, would be impacted by the CGT changes. The sector does also attract some investment from institutional investors. If they are corporate investors, for instance, they are not impacted by the CGT changes. If they are superannuation funds—and that includes individuals who may choose to invest through a self-managed super fund—they are also not impacted by the changes. In this sector, as you can imagine, commodity prices are quite an important driver of investment. In fact, tax is one factor that might impact on investment in the sector. Historically, commodity prices have been a major driver of investment. Right now, with buoyant, for instance, copper and gold prices, they still in recent quarters have been attracting quite a significant amount of investment to the sector. As a whole, there are still a lot of factors that remain attractive for investment. As my colleague has said, whether or not you are affected by the CGT changes does depend on your circumstances. Not all investors will be affected.

Yes, I get that. I would suggest that a lot of people invest in junior explorers. They are pretty well gambling. They are not likely to be an institutional investor or somebody who is not affected. It is more likely to be somebody who will be impacted. Given that over 60 per cent of mineral discoveries have been made in recent decades and given that we have a declining manufacturing sector, we are increasingly relying on our mineral exports. If we don't have investment in exploration, we're in danger of a declining minerals sector. Was this sector specifically considered when making these tax changes? Do you concede that it will have a material impact on the level of investment?

I might just echo a couple of sentiments that colleagues have made already. The purpose of the changes was to provide a more neutral tax treatment of capital gains. It was not to set out to reward particular kinds of investment or investment where you have spoken about things that could be taken as gambling, speculation or luck or those sorts of things. It is designed to provide a much more neutral treatment such that capital flows to its most productive use. I hear your representations from stakeholders that may affect particular characteristics of certain sectors.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I'd suggest they are pretty productive use—

If they are very productive, then, despite the changes, it still provides a return on that capital investment should it be successful. It doesn't deny that there would be a return from that capital investment. It changes the base of it such that it's more neutral so investors choose to go to what they believe is most productive. I'm sorry; I don't want to be too trite, but, if that is something that is—to borrow your word—'gambling', then that is still available under the legislative regime.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I have some other questions on trust tax changes and small business. There is going to be a massive restructure cost for people restructuring their trusts. I think Treasury estimates 350,000 small businesses use discretionary trusts and 210,000 of them will either pay more tax or be required to restructure. Will these changes effectively end income splitting in small business?

It was certainly one of the objectives of the reform. Discretionary trusts have for some time enabled flexible timing and the allocation of income and capital gains and losses. I think the government has been fairly transparent about how that would impact the operation of trusts and how that works with income splitting. You are right that it would affect around 350,000 small businesses that operate through discretionary trusts, but we also want to be pretty clear: that is around 15 per cent of small businesses. We're not diminishing that that number is present. That is going to require restructuring. We sought to be incredibly transparent in the impact analysis of those costs. Nonetheless, that was an active aspect of the policy design. We have certainly heard the feedback through consultation from stakeholders. That is why the policy included rollover relief. It is why it also included the election regime. I might see if Ms Berger-Thomson wants to add anything to that.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text:
The government has been very transparent about a lot of the stats that you've outlined. In the explanatory memorandum of the bill that was introduced, we have our impact analysis. It goes through all of the compliance cost estimates that we have worked through, as required. We've been very transparent about those.

I will go to the purpose of the measure, which is outlined on page 176 of the explanatory memorandum. That document talks about supporting a fairer and more sustainable tax system by improving equity between income earned through discretionary trusts and income earned through wages or direct business activities by reducing the extent to which tax advantages can be obtained through these structures. It is about improving the sustainability of the tax system by reducing revenue lost from tax arrangements involving discretionary trusts and promoting the efficient use of resources by reducing incentives to spend time and resources on complex trust arrangements for tax purposes.

Ms Di Marco has gone through some of the transitional arrangements that the government has put in place to facilitate the transition to the new regime. What the impact analysis talks about is that there are some upfront costs. It very transparently goes through those. Those are largely transitional. The benefits of the regime, as outlined in the impact assessment, indicate that, particularly given the purpose of the measure and what it's aimed to do, those costs—if you look at a holistic assessment of what the measure is trying to do, the measure is still worth doing, even despite those costs.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

text: I understand your point about trying to make the tax system fair. That sounds perfectly reasonable. I'll put to you that, when you run a small business and you're putting it all on the line, doing 80 hours a week—blood, sweat and tears—maybe that's a bit harder than it is for somebody that just turns up and gets a wage. And, when you own a small business, just paying yourself a wage—why would you bother? You wouldn't; you'd just go and get a job. That's why there is a differential for that benefit. I'll give you a scenario.
Senator, I'm going to have to rotate the call shortly, so if you can—
I'll be real quick, please.
Yes, and then I can come back to you if I need to.

Okay. In many small businesses, parents play different roles. It might be that the dad runs an electrician business and mum stays at home with the kids. Dad couldn't do that if mum wasn't staying at home with the kids. In a real way, she is contributing to that business. These new rules would make that ineffective. Was any advice provided to the government around these sorts of scenarios? Was there any modelling of the economic contributions of stay-at-home parents when formulating the policy?

Obviously, the government had a lot of information as we were considering the reforms. This is something that has been looked at over the last 50 years. Every single review into the tax system in the last 50 years has recommended making some reforms to the way trusts operate. We have been very cognisant of some of the pressures that you have outlined and how they are being used for a relatively small percentage of small businesses in Australia—about 15 per cent. That's why we're doing the work that's being done now. The legislation is coming in. The start date is from July 2028. We are also looking at a range of options available for people using trust structures. We can support the restructuring arrangements, essentially, to give them the support because the rules are changing.

Based on all of those reviews, our desire is to ensure that people working for wages are treated fairly. Our tax system approaches wages earned through, essentially, labour—turning up and getting a wage—differently to the way it treats assets. Our decision overall has been to try and make that a bit fairer.

And, Senator, there were other elements of the package that sought to speak to specific things for small business. Obviously, the instant asset write-off has been made permanent. There've been changes to the CGT active asset rules. So there've been a range of other changes that have sought to support small business. But, as the minister has outlined, it was a clear intent of the policy that you would more clearly align tax rates on income from discretionary trusts with other labourlike income, including salary and wages.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I will have to rotate the call.
Just one question.
One more.

Was there any consideration or advice by Treasury around the High Court case that ruled a month after the budget that bucket companies were not subject to division 7A rules? Bucket companies could be used to defer tax liabilities.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

The High Court decision?
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I'm out of time and want to hand back, but I believe the issue is around the bucket companies.
Senator Nampijinpa Price.

My line of questioning continues around discretionary trust changes. I would like to understand who signed off on the decision for the consultation of the exposure draft legislation to be a window of only 12 business days.
We'll see if we can provide that. Who signed it off as being the timetable?
Correct.

Consultation times are done in consultation with decisions of government. With the trust policy, we'd been trying to manage both trying to give industry and the sector certainty around the direction of policy and also undertaking consultation. witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Are you able to provide me—you might need to give that on notice if you don't have the answer before you now—specifically who made the decision to provide a window of 12 business days only.

witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

Again, we appreciate the consultation period was not long. It is why we decided to have a two-stage process. As I said, we are trying to manage the confluence of wanting to give industry certainty about the policy direction—that way, stakeholders can undertake work with their clients and work with businesses to understand those implications—and trying to consult and make sure that those laws are in place and have been well socialised. There will be future tranches of legislation. We will continue to work with stakeholders and the sector through them.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: You acknowledge that it was quite a complex package. Do you think that 12 days is a sufficient amount of time for stakeholders to consider that package?
Senator, I'm not going to proffer an opinion on the length of consultation times.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: The impact analysis statement states that the consultation paper released in July and the exposure draft consultation received 595 submissions. How many submissions were received for each respective consultation?
I might hand to Ms Berger-Thomson for that.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

It's not up to officials, I think, to answer questions about that. The consultation timetable is agreed with government.

I note that former deputy secretary Diane Brown signed off on the statement of sufficiency for the impact analysis statement. Ms Di Marco, would you be comfortable signing off on a statement of sufficiency for an impact analysis on such a complex piece of legislation that was only out for exposure draft consultation for 12 business days?
With great respect, I'm not going to answer that question.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Presumably, an official would make that decision based on the information before them. And I would say there was also a period—I've got it in my notes—of consultation of the implementation of a minimum tax on trusts from, essentially, 8 to 31 July that led up to the exposure draft. There has been quite a lot of work done in consulting in preparation for that exposure draft, which we should also take into account.
Specifically with stakeholders.
It would have involved stakeholders, yes.

I think Ms Berger-Thomson outlined the number of submissions we received in response to that consultation paper. While I'm not going to answer that question, given that it is requesting an opinion, I will say that Ms Brown and Ms Berger-Thomson have been actively engaged with stakeholders since budget night. They have had a huge number of meetings to discuss these issues. I have great confidence in the fact that it was signed off with knowledge of what the stakeholders' concerns were.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Are you able to provide a list of who those stakeholders were?

witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Thank you. More broadly, what modelling, research or analysis has been completed by the department on the impact of the proposed discretionary trust changes, if any? Has any been done?

I might ask my colleague Shane Johnson to outline some of that. There was quite a lot of material provided in budget statement No. 4. I think we spoke about it at the last hearing. It went to the use of discretionary trusts, some of the distributional analysis around who uses discretionary trusts and what the impact of that is on the equity and efficiency of the tax system. That is provided in Budget Paper No. 1, statement 4.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

text: That precise modelling. Is there any further modelling? Was there any further modelling done besides what was provided within the budget papers that speaks to the impact of the proposed discretionary trust changes?

Well, there are two sets. There is the analysis done as part of the budget papers, which Dr Johnson may wish to talk through. There is also extensive analysis on the implementation aspects of it that is contained within the impact analysis. I think the department has sought to be very transparent about those transition costs and how it expects to affect different kinds of trusts. It distinguishes between those who are in business and those who are not in business.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Specifically small business modelling?
The majority of trusts in business are small business. I think that is outlined quite clearly, actually, in the impact assessment as well.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Experts have suggested that Australian small businesses could face tax bills as high as 77 per cent thanks to these changes. The Assistant Treasurer hasn't wanted to get into specifics or rule out rates over 60 per cent. Can you confirm what the highest effective tax rate is that a small business could face with these changes?

I'm happy to talk about that. The policy is designed to discourage the combination of discretionary trusts with corporate beneficiaries. This is outlined actually in the impact analysis. It is designed to do that because that combination gives the most flexibility to split stream and defer income to minimise tax. That is deliberate. I think what you are talking about is the fact that corporate beneficiaries are not eligible for the credit for the minimum tax paid at the trust level. The government has outlined—indeed, it is in the impact assessment—the purpose of that feature of the trust legislation.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

text: More specifically, though, you can't rule out that it could be over 60 per cent?

I think the purpose of this feature is to reduce the incentives to undertake some of that—utilising some of those opportunities to minimise tax through those types of structures. It deliberately disincentivises the use of—
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Individuals and Indirect Tax and Superannuation Division

text: Minimising tax?

It deliberately disincentivises the distributions to corporate beneficiaries. In terms of who pays some of those rates of tax, we actually don't expect a large number of businesses to pay those rates of tax because we expect them to restructure, take advantage of the election and to, in some cases, depending on their circumstances, actually pay the minimum tax. That will depend on individual businesses' facts and circumstances.

I might start very briefly and hand over to Dr Johnson. The projections contained in the IGR are very long-run projections. These projections are not built off individual export categories or individual sectors. We model these based on forecasts from our macroeconomic group around GDP and around components of GDP There are particular heads of revenue, which Dr Johnson can talk through, where we have outlined particular impacts, fuel excise obviously being the most obvious of those, but we do not model export revenue or expected tax receipts from any particular sector. I might hand over to Dr Johnson to add to that.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Just before we move to that, Dr Johnson, Australia's net zero transformation Treasury modelling and analysis very specifically does do exactly that.
