There is a difference between how you think about how you model these things at a macroeconomic level and then how you translate that into revenue. What I'm saying—and I'm happy to pass over to Dr Johnson—is that, when we model the revenue estimates, we do so off macroeconomic aggregates. We do it off nominal GDP, and compensation of employees in case of wage and labour income. We don't do it based on specific exports or specific industries. To the extent to which Macroeconomic Group has taken account of those projections that you've talked about around different export categories, and that feeds into the aggregates that we use for revenue forecasting, it'll be incorporated in that, but we don't do a bottoms-up accounting of how revenue is going to change over time in terms of corporate taxation. I'll hand over to Dr Johnson.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: I'll ask for one further clarification before you speak, Dr Johnson. As Ms Di Marco mentioned, the way we do the projections in the intergenerational report, and as we do any forecast, is we take the parameters from our economic parameters and then we map them through to revenue. In the IGR, because we go to a projection period—we're going out 50-odd years—we also make a technical assumption that the tax-to-GDP ratio hits a particular cap and stays on that. We do that because that's being consistent all the way through, and without doing that you'd end up having increasing tax-to-GDP rates. We then look at how that maps to different types of revenue heads, and then try to overlay where we think there might be some structural changes in the economy so we can get a better understanding of how it might affect different types of revenue. As Ms Di Marco said, probably the clearest one is around the excise from petrol. In fact, most of our consumption taxes fit with this model as we're seeing changing consumption patterns. Excise from fuel is certainly one. Over the IGR, we see a reduction in that particular one. What we don't do is go through a bottoms-up process looking at every single sector. We take the aggregates, we then put a cap, and then we look at what might happen to particular revenue heads, knowing where future trends are likely to go.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Tax Analysis Division

text: Good evening, folks. I'm hoping there's someone who can assist me on Treasury's engagement with the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation.
I'll ask Mr South to come to the table.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

text: Obviously, negotiations are underway. My first question is: what is the nature of Australia's engagement with those negotiations? I understand Treasury is the lead agency. Have we made submissions to those negotiations? What are the benefits for Australia, if any, of securing a strong global tax treaty?

You are right. The UN is currently negotiating a new framework convention on international tax. This is intended to establish broad principles and arrangements for cooperation on international tax. The negotiations are underway. They are scheduled to run until the end of 2027. Progress, I think, is still ongoing. Australia's engagement is continuing. We continue to monitor and participate in those negotiations. We have not yet made a submission. Australia has not made a submission to those negotiations, but we continue to engage on those.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Corporate and International Tax Division

text: Alright, thank you. Australia has strong—or relatively strong, in the international context—public country-by-country reporting laws. Is that something that you might consider driving or lobbying on during these negotiations? As a corollary to that, given that we haven't yet made a submission, is it our intent to make a submission? If so, what would the process be around formulating such a submission?

We would continue to consider if and when to make a submission based on the progress of negotiations and whether there is a clear position that the Australian government needs to make to express its view or to influence the progress of those negotiations. As I've said, they are still ongoing, and progress, I think, has been widely considered to be quite slow. In regard to public country-by-country, that's a domestic measure that the government announced as an election commitment and has implemented. As you know, it's currently in the early stages of implementation, and the ATO is working through that. At the moment, with first lodgements of information being made—and that will be published in due course—that's a transparency measure that I think has got attention from a number of other jurisdictions, and the EU has a similar regime that it is in the process of implementing. I think there is international interest out there, but that has not, to my knowledge, been a matter that has been part of the negotiations within the UN on the framework convention.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Corporate and International Tax Division

text: Thank you. Under the OECD's Inclusive Framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting, pillar 1 seeks to regulate transfer pricing arrangements for multinationals. Are you aware of any progress that's been made on that through these negotiations? As a corollary, are you aware of any countries that are actually pushing back against any progress?

The OECD pillar 1, amount B arrangements deal with transfer pricing and amount B is an optional measure whereby countries can take simplified approaches to transfer pricing. As simplified approaches, they're typically opted into by developing countries, which have lower capacity, I guess, to engage with complex arrangements that multinationals might engage in in transfer pricing. That was an agreement and work that has been done under the OECD. The OECD process is operating, I guess, in parallel, and to some extent has overlapped with the work that is being done by the UN Framework Convention. The UN framework convention and its two protocols that are being considered at the moment don't directly consider the transfer pricing issues at the moment, but that work, as I say, is still progressing and in some ways continues to evolve and is still in its early days.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Corporate and International Tax Division

text: Alright. That would be of benefit to Australia, would it not, if there could be some international cooperation on transfer pricing?

There already is international cooperation on transfer pricing through the OECD. I spoke about the amount B work, but that is a very particular part of transfer pricing arrangements and international standards. The OECD transfer pricing guidelines have existed for many years, and Australia and other jurisdictions have agreed on those and we implement them.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Corporate and International Tax Division

text: Senator, could I add a couple of things. On the transfer pricing question, international cooperation could be of benefit, but it would depend very substantially on the design. The ATO is widely regarded as fairly effective when it comes to considering issues around transfer pricing, and any cooperation that would seek to change the existing arrangements under which we operate may or may not help. Cooperation may or may not benefit us, depending on the design is, I suppose, what I would say.

text: Pillar 2 focuses on fair taxation of income. How would you characterise progress on that through the negotiations? Specifically, how did the OECD and the US negotiating a deal to exclude US-based multinationals from the 15 per cent global minimum tax impact on that framework?

As you referenced in your question, pillar 2 work is about a global minimum tax. That's about a widely adopted and accepted approach to setting a baseline to the effective taxing of very large corporates. The agreement that you're referring to, the so-called side-by-side package, recognised that the United States had a pre-existing minimum tax arrangement, which substantially reflects the same outcomes as those achieved under the pillar 2 arrangements that are being implemented by other countries. The side-by-side arrangement recognises that and allows those two sets of rules to operate, as the name suggests, side by side. The US continues to apply its own pre-existing minimum tax arrangements whereas other implementing countries, including Australia, choose to implement the pillar 2 rules as agreed by the inclusive framework of the pillar.

witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Corporate and International Tax Division

text: Are you suggesting that the deal to exclude US-based multinationals from the global minimum tax has not impacted on the framework at all?

text: I have some questions around credit card surcharges. Commissioner, it was in March 2026 that the RBA announced its decision around credit card surcharges, and it was in July 2026 that our federal Labor government knew that the ATO was intending to stop taking payments of tax by credit cards. You kindly let us all know on 1 October. Why didn't you tell us earlier than that?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
The timeline is probably not quite correct. Just going back to the RBA's announcement, we went through the process of a consultation paper and through the consultation, which, of course, we were involved in with our colleagues at the Treasury. Once Minister Mulino, as the minister responsible, wrote out to all agencies and all ministers, I think at the end of April, to say that the surcharge ban would be in place, that brought it to a sharp head. We had been working on this in the ATO for quite a while, with our colleagues in the Treasury. We then discussed with our colleagues in the Treasury about possible ways forward. On 20 July, I met with the Assistant Treasurer and discussed those. As you would expect, there was a range of options. It's still possible, of course, for the ATO to continue to surcharge. The minister, of course, is the author of the letter to portfolio ministers to say there is no surcharge from government. That was off the table. We approached it in a somewhat binary way, that either we continue to accept credit cards and seek some additional funding for the costs that we would bear or we'd cease the credit cards. Discussing this with the Assistant Treasurer on 20 July, he understood the gravity of it. He said, 'We need a lot more detail.' and so he asked me to follow up the experience with the states and territories, which are revenue agencies are in a similar position, and also the international experience.

I went through that process. As it happened, I had a meeting with the state and territory revenue officers the next week. I discussed it with them. Many of them were still at the preliminary stage of thinking what to do. We'd all gone through the debit card issue. Some had taken a step forward on the credit cards. Armed with that information, I went back to the Assistant Treasurer a few weeks later, and said, 'Actually, from what we've discovered from our conversations to understand what's happening overseas and with state and territory colleagues, we think the idea of having to limit the use of credit cards is the preferred way.'
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, who said that?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I said that.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: You said that to him, yes.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I said that to the Assistant Treasurer. He was still seized of the importance of this. Through this process, the RBA, which is our banker, would have been having the conversations with the three credit card companies.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: This is in August 2026, we're up to, in the timeline?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
Yes, and the RBA had been doing this for quite a while. Part of the overall package was that, with the surcharge ban put in place, the lower interchange fees would come into force, and so the lower interchange fees would provide that proper competition in the market to reduce the overall costs in the economy. I said, 'Go back to them. Can you get a better deal?' The ATO was quite a presence. At that stage, we had the calculation of about $700 billion we collect, and about $14 or $15 billion was paid through credit card. In the scheme of things, it was a quite small proportion but, in absolute terms, quite large. I wrote to the credit card company at the start of September to say, 'I'd like to meet you with your best and final offer. I know you've been working with the RBA.' With colleagues from the RBA, we went through those meetings in mid-September.

Going through that process, we were still at the stage where, while the credit card companies engaged in that discussion very constructively, the price that they could provide us was still such that we felt it was difficult to afford. Accordingly, we went through the process of advising our minister that we felt this was something that we would have to cease, recognising there would be a need for some transition for people who use credit card. We then proposed a two-month transition and, as I think the public record shows, the Assistant Treasurer discussed that with his colleagues. That was the first announcement, and then, of course, it turned out, with the feedback that was provided, the government has asked us to extend that until the end of June. Sorry, that was a context I thought would be useful just for the committee's understanding. In July, a decision hadn't been made.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: In July, it was an option, but your evidence is that a decision wasn't made until shortly before 1 October, which is when it was announced. Have I got it right?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: We came to our decision—I had better not use 'we'; I came to the decision, based on advice from my senior executive, on 25 September, that was the point at which we would propose the not accepting credit cards anymore after 30 November.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: A lot of small businesses are complaining about the ATO not having told them earlier, so let's hope you just cleared your name with all of them.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Could I add to that. Hindsight is a wonderful thing.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Always is.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
I think, to be fair, with the benefit of hindsight, if I had this time over again—of course, I won't because it's a different world, but I mean in a similar situation. When we had the numbers about who paid by credit card—I know it's in the public discussion—that about $15 billion is paid on credit card, so a relatively small proportion of the overall tax revenue of small business, as five per cent of small business would use a credit card and two per cent of individuals—we saw that around 60 per cent of the value of credit card payments is from large corporate and private and wealthy taxpayers. On the that basis that only five per cent of small business would be affected, we went down the path we went down. As I was saying, with the benefit of hindsight—one always hopes to live a bit longer to get a bit wiser—at an early stage, we could have had a much more open conversation with relevant stakeholders to really put the position and say: 'With the surcharge ban, obviously, we can't pass the surcharge on. That leaves us with a bit of a problem.' Now, it's a relatively small number of taxpayers, and I think maybe that conversation could have operated in such a way as to not quite crowdsource but get input from stakeholders who want the system to work well to then say, 'What are these other options?'

Particularly, one of the things we've heard is that people would use their credit card to manage their cash flow. When I heard that, I had jumped to the conclusion that managing cash flow related to a situation where a person or a business might be struggling and they needed the credit card to help them through that struggle. I thought, as a lot of others would think, if you're struggling and aren't going to be able to pay what's owed on time, a credit card would be a pretty risky way to finance because, if you're waiting for something to come in and it doesn't come in, you are then subject to the very hefty interest charge on the credit card. Of course, now I've learnt that managing the cash flow is not about people who are necessarily struggling, but it's about people who simply can get the use of the interest-free period on the credit card to help them manage their cash flow better.

Had we had that discussion earlier on, there may have been things we could do in the payment system—deferrals of payment, automatic remission of the general interest charge and so forth that happen in other circumstances when businesses are in trouble. I'm not suggesting that would necessarily be a path to go down, but it's just to make the point that, with earlier engagement with affected stakeholders—not on the basis of, 'Here's a solution and you have some time to adjust,' but rather on the basis of saying, 'Here's a problem, and it's a system problem,' and trying to engage people in how to have that solved—and if we got the right stakeholders, including, of course, ASBFEO, the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman, we may well have been in a different situation. Of course, we didn't, and things show that we're not in that situation, but I just would like to say that, with the experience we have now, if we had a similar thing happen to us again, I think we would be more active in trying to engage with people earlier—and, rather than coming from the point of view of, 'Here's a solution, and you have now time to adjust, actually engaging in the problem-solving activity itself.'

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: In short, it was not as a result of a change in ATO stance. I think what happened was that a couple of matters which came up during ordinary reviews and audits came into the public domain and caused many participants to review their affairs.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay. These are effectively historical mistakes that have been made. Is that right?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes. To give a bit of context, there have been various integrity rules over time which have been introduced in relation to the abuse of trusts for tax planning purposes. The family trust election regime was brought in as a regime for genuine family trusts to effectively stay outside those integrity regimes, to be unaffected by them.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The idea was that they wouldn't be able to take losses outside of the family; is that right?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: As long as you were genuinely a solid family trust, clustered around an individual, so there's a concept of a core individual. A perspective would be that, over time, groups got more complex. Sometimes groups and their advisers forgot past elections and did things which were contrary to the elected family group and triggered consequences. Those consequences were deliberately set at a harsh level to stop people abusing the family trust election. What has become clear over the last couple of years is that many family groups and their advisers have done things inconsistent with their family trust elections and have potentially triggered those harsh consequences.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Have any been bankrupted?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: To the best of my knowledge, nobody has been bankrupted.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay. How much revenue has been raised through these initiatives?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'll have to take that on notice, but I would say that the ATO does not have some sort of compliance strategy or project in relation to family trust elections and the distribution tax. There have been a sporadic number of matters which have come up through other ordinary reviews.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay, so is there no target of revenue you're trying to raise?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: There is no target of revenue we're trying to raise.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Have there been cases where people have made honest mistakes?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It's an interesting question. People have planned parts of their group around a certain person being the reference individual. They have then done things which have been inconsistent with that. I think there's a question about why. In some cases, that's sloppiness in affairs, either by them or their adviser. In some cases, it's directly contrary to the spirit of the family trust election rules. I think some of the angst in the public domain is that perhaps taxpayers who have entrusted their affairs to their advisers, and maybe sometimes on a change of advisers, have not deliberately been trying to avoid or get around the rules but they have done things which have triggered the rules.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: You don't have any discretion in these matters, do you?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The way the provisions work, if somebody has breached the rules, they have breached the rules, it has triggered the liability, and the onus is on the taxpayer, as it is ordinarily in a self-assessment system, to self-assess, notify us and pay the tax. We do have discretion around the level of penalties and interest.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay, but there has to be a penalty, and it could be very substantial. The general interest charge is cascading over many decades in some cases, isn't it?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: If we do not remit the general interest charge, it compounds and the general interest charge is, by policy, set at a level which makes the ATO, let's say, not the most competitive of banks. Recognising, that the recent, I suppose, awareness of these issues has caused a lot of taxpayers to look into their affairs and realise that they might have made mistakes or done things inconsistent with the rules, we have announced, effectively, a general interest charge amnesty of sorts, for people who come forward and self-assess, as is their obligation.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: How long for?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It has recently been extended, I think, until around June next year. We will remit 80 per cent of the general interest charge.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think you've referred to the angst. To use your own words, Mr Hirschhorn, I think some of the angst comes from the fact that this never ends. If people have made a mistake decades ago, it never ends for them.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, I would say that, to the extent that they don't come forward, the general interest charge accrues, so, to the extent that it's a general interest charge question, yes, it would accrue. We do have the power to consider remission requests and we have offered this amnesty. In terms of ongoing—
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's it, right? It ends this year.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That ends this year, but really there is an element of, 'You can, in a sense, cleanse the past and, going forward, having looked at your elections, make sure that you do not breach or trigger the rules again in the future.'
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: One of the reasons I'm asking about this that we're about to have a lot more people in day-to-day, more typical businesses in the trust world, if this legislation passes parliament. Have you given any thought to advising the government that there should be discretion for the ATO to deal with mistakes that will be made? As the Commissioner just said, the ATO itself bungled, in some form, the consultation on the credit card issue. A lot of small businesses are going to make bungles. Have you given any thought to this massive new population of people and organisations that are going to be using trusts that might not be able to afford expensive advice? What sort of discretion do you think would be helpful for the ATO to help the typical Australian that might make a mistake on one of their trust elections?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
You know it's not my job to talk about policy. I would say that, in terms of thinking about policy changes, we support our colleagues in the Revenue Group and give them the best evidence we can in relation to the operation of the tax system, including where it may be operating in a way which is perceived as unfair by taxpayers. I would also say, in relation to the family trust election, the taxpayers with that problem generally are not the average small business running their operations through a trust and a company. These issues arise, generally, where you have multiple trusts and multiple companies in a complex private group. Often it happens where people have multiple trusts and, in a sense, designate different family members as the key individual in different trusts, but think of it as one family group when, in fact, for tax purposes, it's really two family groups.

In terms of the elections proposed under the new legislation, of course, we will provide the absolute best guidance we can to taxpayers, both on how to make the elections and, to a degree, how not to forget that they've made the election and the consequences of making the election.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: There are half-a-million building companies in Australia. The housing industry association says that three in five builders use a trust. Let's say you've got a couple of hundred thousand new trusts coming in, just in that sector. They are going to have to make elections. I understand you don't want to give legislative advice, but I think there are already a lot of Australians that are facing this situation of never being able to resolve these long-term issues because there isn't a time limit, or you might not have as much discretion as you might need to resolve honest mistakes. What kind of engagement do you think you will have on this new proposal, either through the Senate committee or directly to the government, about trying to give the many more taxpayers that are now going to be facing these complex and quite convoluted trust structures some comfort that they're not going to face potentially bankrupting tax bills down the line because someone made an administrative error a decade ago, or two decades ago, which has cascaded into a huge bill, and maybe in the circumstances where they were relying on an accountant? Everyone makes mistakes, as we just heard from the commissioner. I'm interested in what you can do to help protect some of these people.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: As I understand the measures, they apply to discretionary trusts, and there are about 800,000 discretionary trusts in Australia at the moment. Many trusts used for commercial purposes are fixed trusts already and so are not really caught up by these. They have their existing fixed trust arrangements so they can't be used for streaming. That's why they're not in, because with a fixed trust you can't, in a sense, choose who gets the benefit of the trust; it goes directly to people. Again, when the legislation is passed and fully implemented, we will be giving, again, the best guidance that we can as to how these rules apply and how to make sure you are monitoring them so that you're still compliant. We're still exploring exactly how we will do that. Under the family trust election regime, this was considered, and originally the requirement was put on taxpayers to advise the Tax Office of their family trust election, and that was one way it was thought that the ATO would always be in a position to remind people that they had done an election. For various reasons, which are lost a little bit in time, that requirement was subsequently repealed, and so the commissioner was not in a position to be able to advise people whether or not they had done a family trust election. I think there is an element of how advisers to families running a family discretionary trust and the Tax Office will have to work together to, in a sense, ensure against forgetfulness.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Well, you're going to have a lot more people to deal with very soon.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm going to rotate now to Senator Pocock, and I'll just let everyone know I've got five new senators on the list to ask questions for one block each, and we're running behind time, so I'd appreciate everyone being as efficient as possible in their questions and answers.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I want to go to a complaint letter lodged by Mr Michael O'Neill, former CEO of the Tax Practitioners Board, during the investigation of PwC in relation to that tax leaks scandal. The complaints letter was lodged with the ATO on 1 September 2025. You're nodding, Commissioner. You have memory of it, perhaps?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I do.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Mr de Cure, you're also familiar with the document?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I first became aware of it yesterday.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay. I've got copies if you want to have one in front of you. I'm not seeking to table it, but that's just if it's useful for you to have it in front of you—perhaps just to the commissioner and Mr de Cure at this point. I'd like to ask some questions about this matter. Mr O'Neill makes five allegations in his complaint. The first of them relates to the action of some APS officers and officials and raises significant concerns about the adherence of those officers to the APS Code of Conduct, and then there are four other issues: firstly, the independence of the TPB and its operation in relation to the PwC matter; secondly, the TPB's investigations in relation to PwC and Peter John Collins; thirdly, evidence provided at parliamentary hearings and in responses to questions on notice; and, fourthly, the ongoing bullying, harassment and threats against him as he exercised his powers as the TPB's CEO and secretary. Mr Heferen, this was a document that went to the ATO on 1 September. Can you outline the processes undertaken by you when you received it? I'm not asking you to name individuals, just a sense of the shape of what you did.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
When that was provided to me, given the nature of the allegations raised by Mr O'Neill, I thought it prudent to ensure that it was appropriately investigated by someone external to the ATO, so I referred it to the Public Service Commissioner, during the time of the previous Public Service Commissioner. I referred my powers, as an agency head to deal with this, to the Public Service Commissioner. The Public Service Commissioner then asked the ombudsman to conduct the examination of the complaint. That has been completed. I have I have been told the outcome of the ombudsman's review. From the Public Service Commission, I got some guidance about handling the information. It says:

The contents of the document which has been provided—

that is, the complaint and the outcome—

are strictly confidential, sensitive and contain personal information about individuals that is protected by the Public Service Act and the Privacy Act. Both Acts impose strict limitations on the disclosure of the protected information provided. You should not disclose the document or the information contained in it without first seeking approval from the Commissioner or an authorised delegate.

On public commentary on the matter, it says:

The documents and any of the information contained therein must not be disclosed publicly. Release of information concerning the exercise of the Commissioner's functions—

that is, the Public Service Commissioner's functions

—under sections 41(2)(m), 41(2)(n) and 41(2)(p) of the Public Service Act and information referred to in the documents may risk the integrity of future processes related to these functions. In particular, such disclosure may send the message to the public and the whole Commonwealth public sector that conduct of processes can be made public and this could undermine the effectiveness of the hundreds of investigations that occur every year and potentially jeopardise workplace integrity, conditions and performance.

Given that advice and guidance to me, I am concerned that, if I step into a discussion of any of the matters—given that I've been given an explicit instruction not to publicly disclose—I could be operating in breach of the code in that I'm failing to protect confidential information.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Let me go to one of the five matters, which is an employee allegation that they have been bullied, harassed and had threats placed against them. That's something in respect of which you are the officer in charge of the employment of that person and they have come with a complaint about bullying and harassment. What did you do in relation to that element of the complaint, which is not an infrequent occurrence for an exchange between an employee and their employer?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The entire complaint I referred to the Public Service Commissioner. I didn't go through the complaint and say, 'Some I can deal with, some others.' I'm conscious of my obligations to keep this information confidential and not disclose it publicly, but I was satisfied that, taking the complaint as a whole, it should be dealt with as a whole, and so the entire matter was referred to the Public Service Commissioner, who then asked the ombudsman to do the investigation. That being complete, and having received the outcome of that, that has to remain confidential.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm going to go to an element of the document in front of you. You can see that I have Mr O'Neill's permission to publicly discuss the document. One of his allegations about false and misleading information—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, Senator. We're under strict requirements. In fact, Mr de Cure having a copy of it, unfortunately, could be in a position of actually being in breach of the requirements.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: If Mr de Cure wishes to surrender the document, please feel free, but I am exercising my rights and responsibilities as a senator to pursue an element of this complaint. One of Mr O'Neill's allegations—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: If I might interrupt very briefly, I can see that the position that Mr Heferen has been advised to take in relation to these issues, not just here but in the broad, conflicts with you asking him questions, which you're entitled to do. I can see, just from watching, that you are trying to ask questions that he is able to answer. At least, that's what I thought I observed. It may be that pretty soon we are in a position where Mr Heferen has to take these questions on notice in order to get advice.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Absolutely. My question is not to Mr Heferen.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Anyway, I'm just watching. We'll see how we go.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
Thank you. One of Mr O'Neill's allegations is about false and misleading information being provided at parliamentary hearings and in responses to one of my questions on notice, QON AET031, which was made at estimates in February 2024. I want to go to the QON. It's obviously in the public realm, and it's on page 20, I think, of the document in front of you.

On notice I ask the ATO, Treasury and specifically Mr O'Neill, as CEO of the TPB—not the board and not the board chair, because there were diverse opinions in that board, so I'm asking you, Mr O'Neill—to provide not only all documents, records and notes related to the contract change which was announced by Mr Sukkar in March 2022 but any documents, records or notes related to the other four processes that I have just referred to.

That is a quote of my QON, and there are four processes that are implicitly spoken of in there. I'm going to come to you, Mr de Cure, and ask you in a moment whether you think my request was clear. The four processes—in fact, there were five, and they were all processes which had the effect, and it's been widely canvassed in reports before the Senate and so on—raised allegations that Mr O'Neill had bullied ATO staff. These were allegations made as Mr O'Neill was the investigator on this key case of the PwC event. Excuse me for going through it in detail, but I think people need to understand why I am paying attention to this. It is not an individual matter where I am protective of Mr O'Neill. It goes to the functioning and regulation of our system of tax and tax advice, but it also goes to the question of how we treat public servants when they are regulating. Allegations that Mr O'Neill had bullied ATO staff were not substantiated. An inquiry into the way the TPB officer, Mr O'Neill, had conducted the PwC inquiry: clean bill of health. There was a workplace assessment, so-called Oliver review. These were very extensive processes, with a lot of public service time spent on them. Once again, clean bill of health. A fraud investigation into Mr O'Neill: clean bill of health. Finally, an attempt to change Mr O'Neill's contract of employment, which also failed. There were five pressured events which are documented in documents of the Senate as processes that occurred. I want to come to you, Mr de Cure. Do you think my request was clear?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I believe so.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Why did you take over the processes of preparing the response to the question on notice and not allow Mr O'Neill to complete that response, as I was so clear about requesting?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I don't believe I did take over the process, Senator. Whatever is in this document, I have not seen before today. I think the commissioner has explained that I probably shouldn't see this document, and I haven't asked to see it. I was informed that the complaint existed yesterday, so I'm not aware of the detailed contents of this document.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: My question is not about the document. My question is: were you clear on what was requested?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I believe so, yes.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Do you have a recollection of seeing Mr O'Neill's response to my question on notice, Mr de Cure? I just remind you of the words that are read out at the beginning of every one of these estimates committees about being very clear and truthful.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I don't have a specific recollection, Senator, but it's very normal practice for the Chair of the TPB and the Secretary of the TPB and the senior officers to prepare these responses together. I don't believe it is an unusual practice that the Chair of the TPB wouldn't be involved in responding to these questions.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: My question on notice was very explicit, Mr de Cure, because of the political complexities that lay behind it. On notice, could you please provide Mr O'Neill's original response to my question on notice, No. AET31 from February 2024 estimates, unchanged from the way he wrote it?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, we can take that on notice, Senator. I don't have that available tonight.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I have to rotate the call, and we will come back. I have now Senator Nampijinpa Price.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Commissioner Heferen, can you tell me, have you ever run a small business?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, I have not.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Worked in a small business?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: What about your executive team? Have any of them ever run a small business?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm not aware of that. I know some have partners who run small businesses, but I'm not aware of that.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I only ask because I found it concerning, I suppose, that you hadn't realised or understood the small business use of credit card payments as a cash flow tool. What is your annual salary package, Mr Heferen?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I know this is going to fall short, but I'm not entirely familiar with that. I mean, it's a lot. I get paid a lot. I'm very well remunerated. We have something in the annual report, which is not actually a reflection of my salary package. The Remuneration Tribunal determines my salary and conditions. I can take it on notice to provide the precise figure, but I'm pretty sure in saying that my cash salary is over $800,000. As to the precise number, I'll need to take it on notice.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Would it be about $928,980?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Well, it sounds like you know what it is.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I just wanted to confirm, I suppose.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: One little trap with that, though, is that takes into account the cash salary plus superannuation. Given my age and being a long-term public servant, that superannuation is probably, in one sense, for an annual salary, inflated, but I don't want to quibble. It's a lot. I'm very well remunerated.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay. Are you aware that nearly 40 per cent of small businesses pay themselves less than $40,000 a year, sometimes nothing at all, to stay afloat?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I haven't looked at the data of salaries for owners of small business who pay themselves a salary. I could apprise myself of that if you would like me to.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I suppose I just want to understand that there is an understanding of the significance of the decisions that are made and how they impact—obviously, cash flow for small businesses and their viability, whether they can stay afloat, whether the owners themselves can actually pay themselves a wage as well.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm certainly aware of the financial difficulties that a range of businesses are in. I mean, I don't know if you've attempted to make the link because I have, by public service standards, a very high salary and that I don't recognise that others don't have as high a salary. I do understand that. I understand the pressure that people are under, and I think it goes to the question of the use of credit cards. Certainly in the consultations that we deal with, people who work a lot with people who are struggling are concerned about the use of credit cards, because if a credit card is used and a payment is missed, obviously the interest rate on the credit card is quite punitive, far more so than if they come to speak with us and say, 'We can't make a payment.' If people are in genuinely difficult circumstances, we'll inevitably waive the GIC, but, even if the general interest charge is imposed, that's only imposing the long-term bond rate plus about, I think, seven points, so about 11 per cent, which, of course, is much lower than the 20 per cent or 25 per cent with whichever card system they're in. The point I was making before about managing the cash flow was that, as it's put to me, a very common arrangement is that businesses that are liquid use the interest-free period on the credit card to effectively manage their cash flow more effectively. It's not a question of not being able to make the payment; it's being able to use the credit card because they know that, when the payment time comes, they'll be able to meet it.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Absolutely.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's an issue about the constructive use of the interest-free period that the credit card offers to manage the cash flow of their business better. When we had the discussion about managing cash flow, I jumped to the conclusion of people who are in financial difficulty using the credit card, and, of course, that's a very different situation. As for people in difficulty using a credit card, obviously, that's not the optimal time to be using a credit card.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I suppose you've come to realise now, though, that not being able to use a credit card is going to cause financial difficulty for a number of small businesses.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Certainly, to the extent that they couldn't use a credit card and have that interest-free period, that changes. I might make the point that's not just a small-business issue. In fact, we're hearing that loud and clear in our consultations from large business. Many large businesses use their credit cards in exactly the same way.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Is it good to make decisions by jumping to conclusions, or did you consider perhaps consulting small businesses during that time?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I wouldn't say 'jump to conclusions'. There was a lot of work done, a lot of analysis done, a lot of thought put into it.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Were small businesses spoken to during the analysis and thought?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, sorry, you might not have been in the committee room when I spoke before and answered Senator Bleyer's question. I was quite clear when we went through the process, and I outlined the process in quite some detail, so for the benefit of the committee I won't go through it again, but we had a series of points we went to the minister with to determine the path forward. At each point, Minister Mulino would say, 'I'd like you to check this, I'd like you to check that,' so we went through that process. As I said to the committee before, if we had our time over again, knowing then what we know now, we would have had a more open conversation early with small businesses—
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I suppose—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Could I finish, please, Senator. We would have had a more open conversation with business and their representatives, essentially, to share the problem that we'd faced, rather than coming with, 'This is what we're going to do and here's a transition period.'
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I suppose you said, and when I heard that, 'when we had the discussion about managing cash flow, I jumped to the conclusion of people who are in financial difficulty using the credit card,' so jumping to conclusion was my reference to your statement.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Oh, I beg your pardon. Forgive me, that's probably a bit of loose speech on my part, so I apologise for that. I hope you appreciate that someone in my role, and my stature, fairly rarely jumps to anything.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Thank goodness for that! I just want to be really clear to get the time line right. The government flagged it would look to ban the surcharges in October 2024, and on 30 March 2026, the RBA confirmed it would do so from 1 October. When did the ATO first become aware that the surcharge ban would have a significant financial impact for the ATO?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The complete understanding of what we'd be facing emerged over a period of time. From when the RBA first commenced the review of surcharging and put out the consultation paper in 2025, we had some internal discussions about what this might mean. We then had the conversation with the colleagues in the Treasury and working through information that would give light to what the cost for the government would be. I think it's fair to say that, after the letter from the Assistant Treasurer went out to all ministers on 28 April, that's really the point at which we homed in on the issue to say, 'This is a real issue that we need to grapple with.' At that time, we formulated the options about, 'If we accept credit cards, it needs to be funded,' and ceasing credit cards will have an effect on people who use credit cards, and so our discussion was, 'What's the appropriate transition for people to transition through?' That awareness, it's fair to say, was around June or July. We had staff before that who were already thinking about the issue, and already formulating proposals, but I guess I'm just thinking from my perspective, when it was raised to the senior levels of the organisation, probably around that June/July period in 2026.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: When did you let the Treasury and the government know and which ministers or their offices were informed?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: As I've answered before, my first discussion with the Assistant Treasurer was on 20 July 2026, and then I had a series of meetings. I have a regular catch-up with the Assistant Treasurer. He's the minister responsible for the Tax Office. It's a very constructive working relationship. I'm very appreciative of having him as a minister. We would meet monthly, sometimes a little bit more regularly, but we had a series of discussions in July, August, September and then into October about him wanting more information, us providing more information, and then him formulating the way forward. He would then take the position of what we wanted to do so he could take it to his ministerial colleagues. The Assistant Treasurer is the only minister I spoke directly with up until the point at which we made the announcement on 1 October.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Not the small business minister? The small business minister wasn't informed at any time?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, I only spoke to the Assistant Treasurer, and, of course, the Treasury. Then, when it came to the point of decision-making, then colleagues and obviously the colleagues in the Department of Finance.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Are you able to table the letter from the Assistant Treasurer on 28 April?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Certainly.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think it's fair to say that, after the letter from the Assistant Treasurer went out to all ministers on the 28th, that's really the point, so that's what I'd like you to table, if that's okay. Can I ask a couple more questions?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: We are running really short on time. I'm going to rotate the call. I can come back. It's been 12 minutes, and other senators have got questions.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Thank you for appearing tonight. Are you familiar with the judgement of the Supreme Court of Queensland in the case R v Clark?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, I think I am.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: This is a case dating back to 2017 in which the ATO alleged fraud in a research and development application and in which the ATO referred the matter for criminal prosecution. The Queensland court found there was no criminal case to answer on the initial allegation, but the ATO persisted. In the recent court decision on the final matter, this was again thrown out and the court found the ATO officers concerned deliberately altered expenses statements. The ATO was involved in the preparation of false statements. The ATO officers provided misleading information and affidavits to obtain search warrants. The ATO officers lied in a briefing note to the Queensland bar, failed to disclose emails, and ignored the fact that the R&D funds were spent on legitimate expenses. The court also found the ATO undermined the fundamental right of the defendant to remain silent. The conduct of the ATO amounted to oppression of the defendant. The conduct of the ATO has brought the administration of justice into disrepute and has the tendency of undermining the integrity of the court. The defendant self-represented for more than four years. I understand that, for some days during the trial, the CDP and the ATO and the Attorney-General's Department had some 12 in the combined legal teams, including three to four barristers plus numerous ATO staff and attendants. Would you agree, Commissioner, that, on the basis of this case alone, and the court decision, that senators could readily form the view that there is something seriously wrong, possibly sick, within the ATO to go to such lengths of persecuting an innocent person?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No. I don't think that's a fair characterisation. I make the point that, when matters go to court, we work with the CDPP. The CDPP actually is the one that takes people to court, not the ATO, so the ATO didn't, in this case. There is a very narrow range where we would take the prosecution. He was not one of them. It's the CDPP. The other thing I just might note is that, as I said, the CDPP has appealed that decision and we're awaiting the outcome of the appeal. Until such time as we get the result of the appeal, I think it's probably best to wait and see what happens and then, on outcome of that, we're going to be in a stronger position. The facts, in the first instance, referred to actions of the Tax Office, and that was named in the case. It would be prudent to wait for the outcome of the appeal to see what the appeal court says. I shouldn't step into the world of speaking hypothetically, but, if it is the case, that officer behaved poorly, I think taking the actions of one officer and spreading it over 20,000 would not be a fair assessment.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I just wonder how much of that could have been done by one person alone. Let's move on. Are you familiar with, or aware of, the case of Mr Jae Jang reported on A Current Affair on 14 and again on 15 July 2025?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Reasonably familiar.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The Jae Jang case has similar patterns to the Clark case that I just mentioned. That is, the ATO caused criminal charges to be brought against Mr Jang. His case dates back as far as 2011. After protracted legal activity, the case against Mr Jang was dropped because, 'The prosecution had no evidence to offer.' Similarly, charges against employees of Mr Jang were dropped because there was no evidence to offer—yet in this period Mr Jang spent time in jail and his sister suicided after her bank accounts were falsely frozen by the ATO. Has the ATO got blood on its hands over this?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No. When that TV show aired with those serious allegations, I referred the matter to the Tax Ombudsman. As it turned out, I didn't need to refer it to her because she was going to take her own-motion action. She did that. She looked at it very thoroughly. Mr Jang was involved in that. Mr Jang, I believe, got copies of the report that the Tax Ombudsman Did. Because it was about a single case, I don't think that was made public. Nonetheless, the results were, and I can say as the commissioner, the allegations of the actions of my officers leading to those tragic outcomes were not established.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Do you see any parallels between these two cases and the behaviour of the ATO in the Robodebt scandal—specifically, the false income assessments by Social Services were based on incomplete and arguably misleading income data provided to it by the ATO, and the ATO knew, or should have known, the data was unreliable for the Robodebt exercise.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, I see zero parallel.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: In the Clark and Jang cases, do you accept that the behaviour of the ATO has resulted in major financial, emotional and business harm to the persons the ATO had in its sights?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think 'had in its sights' is unnecessarily inflammatory in the context of what ATO investigators need to do when they are undertaking audits. As I said, in the Clark case, the matter is under appeal, and so I think it would be prudent to wait for the outcome of the appeal before deciding on a concluded view.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Chair, in the interests of time, I'll continue with another set of questions and put the rest of this set of questions on notice.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'd be most appreciative, thank you, as will your colleagues, more importantly.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The ATO website states that the pre-2018 member contribution statement archive is used to check employer compliance with the super guarantee, meaning that directors have paid super for their employees. I'm advised that when affected employers attempted to resolve these matters, your own officers freely admit they're only checking the modernised Australian tax system and have no knowledge of the earlier member contribution statement archive whatsoever. Those officers are searching a system that contains no data before 1 July 2018. If the search returns blank, that does not mean that the superannuation was never paid. It means your later system does not hold that data, so it seems that directors were wrongly charged. Why have ATO staff not been trained to understand that the modernised Australian tax system only contains records from 1 July 2018, that a blank result does not mean non-payment, and that the member contribution statement archive must be consulted before any pre-2018 debt is raised? On that basis, how can any of these debts be considered lawfully raised?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'd like to take that on notice. If there are particular cases that have been raised with you by constituents, it would be very useful if, on their permission, you could share those details with me. What you described does not sound to me like what is happening, but I would be very happy to look into it, and it makes it a lot easier to look into things like this if you can share specific complaints.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I would appreciate that. We have in our possession correspondence from ATO officers to affected taxpayers directing them to authorise the ATO to apply to the Department of Finance on their behalf for debt relief in relation to these director penalty notices. Can you confirm that, when a taxpayer receives resolution through the Department of Finance debt waiver process, they are required to agree to confidentiality conditions as part of that resolution?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: There are some circumstances, when we look at taxpayers, particularly in some vulnerable situations or circumstances, where we think it may be appropriate to seek a waiver from the Department of Finance. There's a very tight process available through the Department of Finance to seek waiver of tax debts, and we will, in very limited circumstances, support that. Ultimately, it's a decision for the Department of Finance as to whether they waive that debt.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think any conditions that are put on the taxpayer after the debt is waived—I think you mentioned a condition was placed—would be a matter for the Department of Finance, but I think it might be prudent if, again, we could take that one on notice to be sure of our response.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I have two short questions left. How many taxpayers have been treated by way of this debt waiver mechanism where they never in fact owed a debt? I think that's the key point. They never owed a debt because it was the Taxation Office that was at fault, but then they're levied a debt, and then they're waived, so it's on their record. How many? Would you like to take it on notice?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I will have to take it on notice, but I would hazard a guess it would be zero.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: My last question is: why is an Australian taxpayer who has been wrongly treated, wrongly pursued for a debt they never owed, being silenced as a condition of receiving that relief?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: As I mentioned, any requirement or condition of receiving the waiver would come from the Department of Finance. It wouldn't come from us. The waiver comes from the Department of Finance. We don't have the capacity to waive tax debts. That would come from Finance. I must confess, that sounds unusual, but I've been surprised before. We will take that on notice and make sure we get a response.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: You'd be pleased to hear that a lot of this sounds unusual, but we'll leave that to the questions on notice and the appeals.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, could I make one addition. If we think a debt has been unfairly levied after we've got more evidence from the taxpayer, we do not send the taxpayer to the Department of Finance. We amend their debt. By definition, if we are sending a debt to the Department of Finance, it's because we think it is a real debt, but we think that, because of the vulnerable position of the taxpayer, the Minister for Finance may choose to exercise her discretion to waive the debt.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Hello. Without going into any specifics about charities or individuals, could you outline the number of charities that have had their DGR status revoked in the last five years?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Over a five-year period, I'd need to take that on notice.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: What about three years? Is there a period that you would be aware of?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I don't believe I have that in my data, partly because there are different ways that charity status can be revoked. Some apply voluntarily for revocation. With some it is revoked, for example, for persistent non-reporting. We call those, loosely, double defaulters. There's a bigger number of those. Then a smaller number are revoked as a result of our compliance action. Putting those together, it can be a couple of thousand in a year, and then I'd need to get the analysis done to divide that by the DGR category. We can take that on notice.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Thank you. If you could break them into those categories, that would be helpful. How about under the ACNC governance standards? Is that a separate category?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Are you asking how many have been revoked for breaching the governance standards?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Again, we can try and do that analysis, and it would be helpful to know over what period you wanted it. Predominantly, we could categorise the revocations by those that were voluntary, which, of course, would not be the governance standards, and then we could categorise them by those that were for non-reporting, which is one of their obligations to the ACNC but not perhaps the governance standard in the way that you're talking about, and then, when we could look at those that we've done for compliance reasons, we could look at where that's been the predominant reason. Sometimes it will be a combination of breaches, really, if that revocation has been exercised, but we could try to get you some more detail.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Do you do this process annually? I'm just trying to be helpful in picking a timeframe that would fit within your usual cycle.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
