text: We could do it most easily from the annual reporting period. We do report these numbers in our annual report, which has just been tabled in parliament. In our annual report, we indicate the different categories of revocation, but if you wanted further detail about the DGR category and the governance standard point, I would need to take that on notice.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: What about having their status revoked for breaching the law with more than 60 penalty units?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's governance standard 3. Within governance standard 3, there are two elements of breaching the Australian law. One is breaching it because of a breach by the charity of an indictable offence, and the second element would be a breach by, again, the charity of a civil matter that had the 60 penalty units. Even within that governance standard, there is both the criminal aspect and the serious civil action. We could try to do that. It gets quite complicated because, as I say, it might be that they haven't done their reporting and they haven't done this and they've breached, or financial mismanagement. It's not always as neat as one particular governance standard.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Would you say that breaching the law with more than 60 penalty units is something you would see frequently? Would that be something that would stand out?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It can be quite rare for us to see a breach by the charity. There might be individuals associated with the charity that have committed criminal offences or serious civil offences. It's not a common thing, but obviously the governance standards is something that we look at in our compliance work.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: You mentioned that there had to be proven behaviour by the charity rather than an individual, and those situations raise a question whether the charity should remain registered. How many instances has the ACNC investigated and found breaches to have occurred—again, let's pick the five-year period?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, Senator, can you just say, was it how many instances has the ACNC five-year period seen of charities—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Breaching the 60 penalty units.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I would have to take that on notice, again, with the caveat that sometimes it's not as easy as saying that is the only reason that they were revoked. There could, of course, be other regulatory action that we may have taken that's short of revocation. Certainly, revocation is the most serious action we can take, because obviously it removes their registration and their access to taxation concessions and can, in fact, mean the charity will struggle to continue. We may have taken other enforcement action. That can include regulatory advice to get them back on track. It could include an enforceable undertaking. It can include other actions.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry to interrupt you, but at the last estimates, we had a discussion about this, and my recollection was that 60 penalty units would be a revocation threshold.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It's not an automatic revocation. It will constitute a breach of the charity's obligations to the ACNC under the ACNC Act. Not every single breach that someone commits will end in revocation.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Could you outline the breakdown in behaviour by a charity versus behaviour by an individual? You touched on that earlier. Would that be an individual who's employed by a charity, or what was the difference that you're making there?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, the easiest way to explain it is the ACNC does not regulate individuals. Our job is to regulate charities, and sometimes, obviously, the individuals, employees and volunteers associated with the charity will do acts that are in the name of the charity and therefore are attributed to the charity. There will be other situations where it might be, when we look into it, that it's a volunteer who's done something and it's been in their personal capacity rather than with the authority and authorisation of the charity, so it's case by case and there are situations where it's a penalty against the charity and we have to establish that the charity has committed the breach.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: All right. Well, I would note that there are approximately 24,800 penalty units in a $9 million court-ordered indemnity cost. Has the ACNC ever had to deal with cases with such a high number of penalty units accrued?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, I don't think I quite understood how the penalty units you supplied from a court-ordered decision.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: My understanding is that penalty units are also attached to a financial amount. If you've had a court-ordered fine or penalty, the quantum of that penalty will equate to a number of penalty units.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: All I can refer to is the actual provision in the Act, which, by my recollection, talks about civil matters with a penalty of at least 60 units. Obviously, there are situations where legislation will provide that the civil penalty is greater than 60 penalty units.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: If a charity had a court-ordered penalty of $9 million in a civil action, would I be right in assuming that would incur more than 60 penalty units?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I might get my assistant commissioner, legal counsellor, to come forward on that point. My understanding would be that a court-ordered decision, where it's an award of damages or compensation, is different to civil penalties in legislation. But I might seek my legal counsel's assistance.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sometimes a court fine can be based on a penalty unit, but without the exact case it's hard for me to answer that question.
witness_position: Assistant Commissioner, General Counsel and Regulatory Services

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Specifically, I'm referring to the Environmental Defender's Office and their court-ordered penalty of $9 million, ordered by Justice Charlesworth in a trial relatively recently.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, you're at 10 minutes.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm not familiar with the orders off the top of my head, but I'm happy to take that on notice to confirm whether that fine was based on penalty units or not.
witness_position: Assistant Commissioner, General Counsel and Regulatory Services

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That would be terrific. The Environmental Defender's Office, a DGR status registered charity, which received a court-ordered penalty of $9 million. I'm happy to provide you with dates if you can't Google that, but I think you'll find there's a significant amount of media around it.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sure.
witness_position: Assistant Commissioner, General Counsel and Regulatory Services

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's all my questions. Thank you.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think I see Assistant Secretary Janette Luu at the back. I would ask her to come to the table. I have a question. You would have heard the earlier discussion.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, I did.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: You would. Did you prepare a draft answer to question AET031 that we were discussing earlier?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'd have to refresh my memory in particular in relation to that particular question on notice, but generally, yes, that would be the case, when it comes to questions on notice more broadly.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: And who directed you to prepare that draft?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That would have been Mr de Cure.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Mr de Cure, do you recollect asking Assistant Secretary Luu to prepare that answer, the draft?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Specifically, Senator, I don't have a specific recollection of giving a direction. But I will say that I think there's an interesting discussion here about the operation of the Tax Practitioners Board, which is a creature of the Taxation Services Act of 2009, and the board comprises individual board members, and the act obliges the commissioner to provide ATO officers to assist the board in their work.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I understand that.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It's our normal procedure that we will work with our team in relation to matters of answering senators' questions and questions on notice. We work together to craft those answers in response to the questions, so it's a perfectly normal part of what we do for Ms Luu and/or now Mr Orme, as the secretary, to be engaged in drafting and preparing answers and checking our records and systems to make sure that the answers are factually correct. We do our best to make sure that we take care to answer the question that is put to us. I note your question today asking for an initial draft—a previous question in relation to Mr O'Neill's initial draft.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, that wasn't it. The question on notice, to be explicit, that you said you understood—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I believed I did.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: May I finish. Do you want to finish what you're saying?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No. You go.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Well, it was very specific. It specifically said I don't want an answer from the TPB. I don't want an answer from the board. I don't want to read it again. It's boring. I'm being asked to be quick, but I asked you specifically, given the controversy, and the pressure on an investigator in the middle of an investigation—I wanted his account of the events that were indicative of pressure he felt as an investigator. You said you understood that, and that is not what has happened here. I asked him to prepare it. That's the Senate asking you to prepare it.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, I agree with the answer I gave. I do understand that question tonight, absolutely, so we'll take that on notice. I'm not sure I understood it as specifically as you've outlined it tonight on that previous occasion.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It was in black and white and supplied to you.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I accept that to be correct. You've been very specific tonight—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, I was very specific on 14 February 2024, Mr de Cure, and it is a matter of considerable weight that you did not respond, you did not give the parliament the answer that was sought, and it is not a mere coincidence and misunderstanding, for my money. It is a very significant outcome, because Mr O'Neill, as I understand it, had no role, did not read, did not see what you submitted against the specific request. It's important.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, I'd like to go back and check.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I have the documents in front of me. I'm telling you.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: And I'd like to check our records.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Do you accept that you have misled the Senate in not complying with my request to provide Mr O'Neill's version of events, which he did prepare. You have agreed to supply them to the Senate. They weren't supplied to the parliament. Do you agree you have misled us in not responding to a very clear request?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I would like to check our records before I answer that question.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I will go to another question, and I look forward to that answer. It's very evident to me that the question that was posed to you two years ago was very clear and was not answered, and Mr O'Neill wasn't able to give his response to the various pressures he felt, through five different mechanisms, while he was trying to investigate a very significant failure by a very large partnership. The PJC for Corporations and Financial Services, under the signature of my colleague Senator O'Neill, wrote to you, Mr de Cure, on 10 July 2026, seeking assurances that your former 25-year career as a KPMG tax partner would not compromise the TPB's investigation into allegations against KPMG. You will recollect that letter?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, I do.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: In your response, you said you recused yourself in late June after discussions had already commenced about a KPMG investigation. After that, you did not attend formal meetings with KPMG. On your contact and conversation with a KPMG audit partner, through your position as chair of the Royal Flying Doctor Service, of which KPMG is the auditor and you are the chair of the audit committee, you had a conversation?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, I'm not the chair of the audit committee. I'm the chair of the RFDS.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry. But you had a conversation, I understand, in connection with KPMG as the auditor for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Is that correct?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's correct, and can I give you detail of the conversation?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Can I finish my question first?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: So the scandal was that you had that conversation and you did not declare the conversation. You used the word 'disgruntled' to describe the whistleblower from KPMG and you provided in that letter—I'm talking about everything that was in the letter of your reply—a plan to manage conflicts of interest. Mr de Cure, you initially decided you could continue engaging with the KPMG matter, including answering questions at Senate estimates, despite your long 25 years with KPMG. Why did you think it was appropriate, given that long career with KPMG, to persist in that matter in that way?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
Senator, I will say very clearly that I did have a long career with KPMG. I left KPMG of my own volition. I retired as a partner on 30 June 2012, which is some 14 years ago. When these matters became part of the public interest earlier this year, they were emerging through various inquiries, newspaper articles and the work that you and Senator O'Neill have done. They were emerging in small pieces of information. At the outset, we were in a set of circumstances where we were seeing things in the paper. We were appearing before the PJC and Senate estimates and, at that stage, things were quite preliminary. In previous matters in relation to KPMG, I have always recused myself from being part of the Board Conduct Committee at the stage when there's been an investigation. I've recused myself from any involvement in the decision-making in relation to KPMG matters. In this matter, we were in a set of circumstances where there was the matter emerging. It appeared to largely relate to the conduct of people in the audit practice. We had internal discussions at the TPB to note that the issue was there, to talk about how this relates to our work, and we had pretty much reached the internal conclusion that it's a large firm, there's an issue in relation to honesty, integrity and ethics, and it's also a registered tax practitioner firm.

At that point, we were in front of a PJC inquiry, and I responded to a question, saying that I was aware that our team had engaged with KPMG. I was aware that our team was making inquiries in relation to this matter. I was aware that we were making inquiries into some other matters, but I was not involved in any meetings with KPMG. I was not involved in any of the actual inquiries. As Chair of the TPB, I was briefed by the team that these things were happening, and as this matter emerged I spoke with Mr Orme, the secretary, on a number of occasions about the appropriate action and I concluded, in the course of those conversations, to make the decision to recuse myself from any involvement in the KPMG matter. It subsequently came to be—I think it was on 29 June—that we talked about it. I decided it was appropriate to have a formal conflict management plan that we documented and that I signed and put on the formal record of the TPB that I will have no involvement in anything to do with this KPMG investigation. We appointed another board member to liaise with our team in relation to those investigations and, genuinely, that is about making sure that the external perception of procedural fairness and equity is there. I can honestly say to you I accept and understand why people might think that there is a perception of potential conflict, but there is no actual conflict of interest.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Mr de Cure, you acknowledge that a KPMG audit partner spoke to—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: May I explain that?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Can I finish?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, sure.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: A KPMG audit partner spoke to you about the whistleblower and you did not formally disclose the conversation and it was not recorded in the minutes. Why not?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I would like to say, on the context of that happening, I received a phone call from a KPMG partner who was the audit partner of the Royal Flying Doctor Service in my capacity as Chair of the Royal Flying Doctor Service. The phone call went along the lines that he rang to assure me. He said, 'I'm just ringing to assure you that this is not affecting our services in Adelaide,' and I said to him, 'This is an unfortunate set of circumstances, but we shouldn't be having this conversation.' That's pretty much the end of that conversation.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: On what did you base your statement that the whistleblower in KPMG was disgruntled?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The context of that discussion was that—that discussion happened at the end of a board meeting where people were packing their bags and about to walk away, and I was talking to, I believe, another board member in particular, and we were just discussing the surrounding circumstances. It was at a stage where KPMG had publicly acknowledged that they'd made errors in the way that they'd handled this, and we were talking about how things got to this point, and I made the remark in the context that these things generally don't get this far if the complaining person isn't somehow disgruntled. That was not an expression of any judgement as to whether the complainant's grievances were genuine, legitimate. It did not include any judgement or any indication that person's honesty was in question. It was just simply to talk about the circumstances, and how do these sorts of issues get to the point that this one was at?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The term 'disgruntled'—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator Pocock—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Can I just finish this? That way I won't have to return to it maybe. Many people in this room will have followed the KPMG matter and will have seen the successive parts of KPMG and the ecosystem within and around, including the attempts by the whistleblower to go through a range of pipes to try to get a very serious set of concerns, now validated, listened to. They lost their job. They paid an enormous price, as whistleblowers always do, almost invariably, and they were characterised as disgruntled. That was a clear narrative, and it's a common narrative for whistleblowers, and I think it's nothing—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm not suggesting—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: if I may finish—it is nothing for you as the chair of a board at the end of a board meeting, with other people in the room, to use that characterisation. It is a real concern to me that has occurred and I think it is a terrible disservice to the whistleblower.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, can I genuinely say that the spirit in which I used the word was not to make an accusation about that person and not to do anything to undermine that person but simply to record what I thought their state of mind would be in relation to their relationship with KPMG as their former employer. It obviously hadn't—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think the whistleblower was insightful, not disgruntled. When I made my speech on 30 March, I didn't do so lightly. That was a serious consideration by a senator of the Australian parliament—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: A last resort.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: And it took three months for you to come to a decision that I think accords with public standards, so I just think we should put that on record.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: And it's nothing, Mr de Cure, because you are chair of the board of a significant regulator, where this really matters. People take their tone from their regulator, and there you are characterising someone in that way when you are regulating them for their ethical practice as a firm, and that is your off-the-cuff characterisation of them. It shocks me, and it's not appropriate for you as a regulator to speak like that.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'll accept your judgement on that, Senator.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: And what's your view of your behaviour?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Last question, Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: With the benefit of review, I probably would have chosen my words more carefully. I really genuinely want to say that nothing that I've said is intended to be a judgement in relation to that person's honesty or integrity.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: If we're going to keep ploughing over this, I will need to reply to that.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I will need to rotate the call.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm genuinely not trying to cast any aspersions.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think we've heard you, Mr de Cure. Thank you very much. Thank you, Senator Pocock. Senator Smith, did you have any final questions?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I do have some questions of the ACNC. Ms Woodward, welcome. How are cost-of-living pressures manifesting themselves in the experience of charities and not-for-profits in Australia?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator, probably the best document to refer you to—and I'm sure you're aware of it—is the most recent edition of our annual Australian charities report, the 12th edition, that we released at the end of June. It does show that expenses grew significantly and, in fact, outpaced revenue growth—so there was growth in revenue but a greater growth in expenses. It does affirm a lot of what we see and we hear from the sector, and you've summarised there that the sector is under quite significant pressure in terms of many charities finding that their expenses are growing and the demand for their services is also growing. In a sector where it's not a matter where you can just increase your price to meet greater demand, they are under pressure.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: How are they managing that pressure?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It's a very broad sector and, as you know, comprises some very large organisations right down to some very micro organisations. They range across so many different activities. For some, they will be able to continue in the normal way, and for others—perhaps more at the front line where you see regular reports, for example, about food relief services and homelessness services—it can be more difficult for them to manage that pressure, and they continue to do the best they can with the funds they have.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: At the beginning of that report, you highlight the year in review, and you identify that 1,298 charity registrations were revoked either voluntarily or due to ACNC action. Of those 1,176 that were voluntarily revoked, how many do you think might be acting in response to the growing cost of living or the growing cost of doing charity business?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: We could get you a more detailed breakdown. There's a voluntary question when they apply—not all of them complete that question. We do, I think, summarise in the report the types of answers given. Sometimes it will be that the work that they were doing or a project has been completed. Sometimes it will be that they've merged and sometimes it will be that they've had to close.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
But the experience must be—because this is what you say in your opening statement and also in your annual report:

Charities generated $239 billion in revenue, a significant 7.5 per cent increase that surpassed growth in the wider economy. However, total sector expenses rose by 8.6 per cent, to $231 billion.

If I recall correctly, that has been a common feature over a number of years now, so would it be right to assume or expect that some of those 1,298 charities that are no longer registered with the ACNC might be closing their doors because of the cost of living and the cost of doing charity business?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, definitely some of them would be closing under that pressure, and you see reports of that. That trend has been fairly consistent, although there was a year fairly recently when growth in revenue did exceed growth in expenses, but I think as a general comment that's fair.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I was interested to read the chair of the advisory committee's report and I thought how valuable her comments were about the ongoing matter of the self-assessment income tax exemption reform. I noticed that the ATO commissioner had been to a meeting of the advisory group in July. Can you, from the ACNC's perspective, give me an update on the impact of the self-assessment income tax exemption reform, and I might ask the ATO to give me an update from their perspective.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: From the ACNC perspective, you will understand that, if an organisation is eligible to be a charity, they need to register with us, and, if not, then it falls to the ATO and the new reporting regime. The number of charities that are still indicating to us that they're seeking registration with us because of that measure has levelled out or even slightly declined as a percentage. I think it's about 42 per cent that indicate that, again, against a voluntary question on the registration application. We've certainly seen that the number of organisations applying indirectly because of that measure is there. We have had very generous support from the ATO commissioner, in terms of staffing support, to meet the extra demand. That demand has flattened out a bit, and the resourcing has reduced appropriately with that.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Has it flattened out from a low level or flattened out from a high level?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It's flattened out from a fairly high level.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text:
That's what I would have thought. In the Advisory Board Chair's Report, she says:

The board remains alert to the continuing impact of the SAITE reforms and subsequent increase in ACNC registrations, a considerable contributor to the 3.8 per cent increase in the number of charities regulated by the ACNC as of 30 June 2026—

meaning that many are moving to the ACNC to get registration, so not necessarily organic charities.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes. Perhaps just to explain that, over the period since the measure was first introduced, the number of charities in the years prior to that had been fairly stable at about 60,000. Some would come off the register and some would come on, and it would level out at about that. It was fairly stable. Over the last three years, I think it would be, we're now up to 66,500 charities, so that's a growth of over 10 per cent. That has really primarily, as far as we can ascertain from our data, been as a result of that reporting measure. These are organisations that are eligible to be charities and are now taking that step.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: That's right. I've calculated that, on average, anywhere between 1,200 and 1,400 charities might have their registration revoked voluntarily over the most recent period. Commissioner, can the ATO give me an update? Perhaps you might be able to populate the commissioner's comments with some raw data.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: We may be able to, fingers crossed. I will see if Mr Hirschhorn can help.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: At the time of the measure—I might be a little bit rough because I'm trying to work out my arithmetic on the fly—maybe there were about 160,000 not-for-profits that were self-assessing as exempt without providing any information.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I thought it was 200,000, but I'll trust you.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Since then, close to 50,000 of those not-for-profits have lodged their self-review return, so confirming that they are exempt not-for-profits.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: A third.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: About a third. Across the remainder, the numbers I have in front of me are that around about 6,000 of the not-for-profits, on the prompting, cancelled their ABNs. They effectively said, 'We no longer operate; we are defunct.' About 3,000 have effectively acknowledged that they are not tax exempt, and they either don't have enough income to have to lodge or they've been lodging tax returns. According to my records, about 7,000 organisations realised that they actually had to be registered as charities, not self-assess as exempt not-for-profits, so I think that 7,000 aligns quite nicely, not precisely but certainly in order of magnitude, with Ms Woodward's evidence. There are still around about 100,000 not-for-profits that have not yet engaged with us, which we are continuing to reach out to and ask to resolve their status one way or the other.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: This was an integrity measure, correct?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: It was indeed an integrity measure, because we had no visibility.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: How much has it cost the ATO to implement this integrity measure?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, please. How much integrity has been restored to the tax system, in a dollar value, thus far, as a result of this initiative, because it's captured 7,000?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'd say it is 3,000, to acknowledge that they are now part of the tax system, are not exempt, and 7,000 to appropriately engage with the charity system where they should always have been registered.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Very briefly, the catch-all was about 160,000, and 10,000 got caught—not caught—

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: So far, for 10,000 their status has been resolved differently from how they had self-assessed. As previously given in evidence, given their nature—that many of these not-for-profits are small and volunteer run—we have been taking a very gentle stance, and I suspect that many of the 100,000 are genuine, small not-for-profits.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Is that gentle in an ATO sort of cultural sense or gentle in a senatorial sense?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'm going to say gentle even as understood by the ordinary citizen.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: The common understanding of the word.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Particularly gentle for the tax office perhaps, but I suspect that some of the most deliberately non-compliant organisations will actually also be residing in that 100,000, and so, gradually over the course of this next year, we will probably be becoming a little bit more insistent with those 100,000 to resolve their status.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Okay. With your cooperation, perhaps we can do a follow-up private briefing just in regard to this specific matter and, Commissioner, perhaps we can have a wider conversation about other matters in the ACNC. Very briefly, I wrote to you in regard to activities of Greenpeace—illegal activities, storming an offshore rig. You were quick to respond to that—less than 24 hours, thank you—but you did say you weren't able to provide me with any information. Is that still the case?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Yes, Senator.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Thank you.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Senator Pocock.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I will try to be very succinct. We'll see how we go. I want to turn to a related matter exposed in the QON that I've already referred to, AET031, where there were bullying accusations by an AT officer, it was alleged, against Mr O'Neill. In relation to that complaint, Catherine Willis, ATO general counsel, is on the public record as saying, 'A quick read gives the impression that the authors of the complaint have been invited to give negative feedback,' and the nature of them related to conflicts over operational business issues between agencies. Mr O'Neill has said on the public record he was never offered a chance to respond or had any accusations put to him. Is it the case that there was, in fact, no allegation of bullying against Mr O'Neill?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, Senator, I'm not familiar with that. When was that question on notice?
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: No, no, it's a question to you now. Mr Hirschhorn may be able to illuminate that. You may take it on notice if you want to. It's your prerogative.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I think it's a matter of public record that a staff member who reported to me made a complaint, a bullying complaint, about Mr O'Neill's behaviour, which went through the normal course to our corporate area, and it was considered, and no further action was taken, and that is where the matter was left.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Was the complaint upheld or not?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: As you've said, the information which was provided under previous notices was that complaint was not upheld on the basis of the understanding of Ms Willis that, effectively, Mr O'Neill was an employee of a different agency and it was a dispute between agencies. I would just say that because a complaint was not upheld does not mean that the complaint was not honestly made.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Do you ever deal with a complaint of that form between two individuals in an agency, or between agencies, where the person complained against has no knowledge, is not consulted and has no place, no voice in that process? Is that common? Do you usually do that, Mr Hirschhorn?

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: This is an ATO thing, not a Second Commissioner, CEG, thing. Complaints are made. They're considered by our corporate function, and they go through various processes. I might pass over to my colleague. But of course there is natural justice given to those who are complained about if a complaint is being looked into.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group
witness_position: Second Commissioner, Compliance and Engagement Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: I'll mention just one thing. You mentioned a complaint between officers in two agencies. It's just the one agency. It's the ATO. It's all the one agency.
witness_organisation: Treasury Revenue, Small Business and Law Group

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
text: Sorry, Mr Hirschhorn said that, not me.

agency: Australian Taxation Office Tax Practitioners Board Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission

text: The ATO, for many years—decades—has used what would be described as AI in terms of its operations but with very limited, very tightly defined scopes. A touchstone which we often talk about is that AI, or computers, should not make a decision which adversely affects the rights of humans. Without getting ahead of your questioning, we do run data-matching programs. We would not describe that data-matching as AI. Generally, when we do run data-matching programs, we do our best not to fall in the trap of what I've described as data hubris. The data is just data and it can have errors in it, and so our general posture or stance, when we see what look to us like taxpayer errors in our data, is to show that data to the taxpayer and to give them a chance to understand what we know, or what we think we know, about that person and to either take action or explain the discrepancy.

They must be made by a human, because a human is accountable. Computers can never be held accountable. On a spectrum, automated decision-making maybe goes up to what we would have historically described as machine learning, which is where a model will learn from what it looks at, and then to what maybe now people would call AI and getting into generative—well, generative text is a completely different thing again. Before we move to this witness, I will let all the people who are very intently following along on screen somewhere and at home know that we will be releasing the National Competition Council witnesses, who are not required this evening. There will be some questions on notice for them, though. I now welcome representatives from the Productivity Commission, including the chair, Ms Danielle Wood. Do you have an opening statement?
No.
Fabulous. We'll go straight to questions. Senator Hume.

I'm going to try to do this very quickly tonight, so we'll try to help each other. First and foremost, your September update calls the picture of the June national accounts 'stagnant'. Is that the commission's assessment today?
I think we were making the observation that productivity has not moved over the past year and that was the term we chose to describe that phenomenon.
The June national accounts say GDP grew by 0.4 per cent in the quarter. GDP per hours worked—what happened there?
From memory, it moved by the same amount. Oh, no—in the quarter it would have grown by less, from memory, because productivity went back by 0.3.
I'm just trying to interpret that data. That means we produced more in total but not more per hour worked. Is that right?
That's right. Another way of thinking about it is that our working hours went up by more than our output did.
So we're working harder but getting less?
We're getting less per hour, yes.
Over the year to June, GDP increased 2.1 per cent but labour productivity fell two per cent. Are those figures in the ballpark?
The two per cent doesn't sound right.
GDP increased 2.1 per cent in the year to June. Labour productivity over the same period fell 0.2 per cent.
Oh—0.2 per cent. Yes, that's right.
Would it be fair to say, then, that the growth in output over that year is driven more by labour hours rather than producing more per hour—effectively, more participation rather than productivity?
That's right.
You also reported a 0.6 per cent decline in the March quarter. Can you identify for me just how much of that June result was a rebound and how much of it reflects a sustainable change in trend?

The quarterly data, I think, as we've talked about before, does bounce around a lot. The other challenge with the quarterly data is that we know, going back through history, that there will be revisions that can substantially change those numbers as well. When we tend to look at the data and draw conclusions about trends, we tend to use a longer time series; we don't really focus on the quarterly numbers.

Can I ask about the labour productivity and the industries that make positive and negative contributions to whole-of-economy labour productivity. Do you know the top three, four or five industries that made the largest negative contribution to labour productivity?

I think over the 12 months it was mining and construction that were the big falls. Mining moves around a lot according to capital cycles, and construction has not performed well over an extended period.

In the June quarter, real unit labour costs rose 0.9 per cent. With all else being equal, does that mean that weak productivity growth makes it harder to accommodate wage rises without cost pressure? I know that the governor of the Reserve Bank has spoken about that before, saying that unless you have productivity rises you can't have wage rises or growth without causing inflation. Is that right?

The way the governor talks about it, which I think is a good way to think about it, is that productivity sets the speed limit of the economy over time. Over the long term we expect to see a relationship between productivity and wage rises, so if productivity is stagnant over an extended period it does make it harder to have wage rises without cost pressures, as you say.

I have some questions that I want to get into on that data, but I'm not going to do them today. I will put them on notice just for the sake of getting through some of these questions a little quicker. I want to talk to you specifically about the productivity benefit of the mandatory climate reporting that's coming in, and specifically about the compliance activity that's involved with that. Would the Productivity Commission agree that compliance activity uses labour, it uses capital and it uses management time?

Yes, we would agree with that. It might be worth noting, for the record, that we're currently doing a review into non-financial corporate reporting, which will pick up the scope 3 emissions reporting.

Yes, I read about that in the Australian Financial Review in August. That's part of the 'tell us once' approach for all non-financial disclosures to government. I'm interested, though, in the reporting regime for group 3 entities that starts on 1 July 2027. Have you looked at how many group 3 entities will be required to report and the average cost that will be imposed upon them—the set-up and recurring costs—for that scope 3 reporting?

As part of that inquiry that I mentioned into non-financial corporate reporting, we are considering the burden on the group 3 companies. That's a review that's underway, so there's only so much I'm able to say, but it's certainly part of the scope of that review.
That is something that you are looking at as part of that review. When is that review due to report?
We have an interim report coming out in the next month, in November, and we'll provide a final report to government by 24 February.
Is the interim report going to the Treasurer, and is it going to be made publicly available?
Yes. For interim reports we put them straight out.
Straight out—so it goes public immediately?
We give it to the Treasurer a few days in advance, but we control the timing.

I'm assuming you're aware that Mr Longo, the former head of ASIC, said that this scope 3 reporting was going to be the 'biggest change to financial reporting and disclosure standards in a generation'.
Yes, I have heard that quote.

Is there an understanding or a recognition from government that has been expressed to you that, at a time when productivity is going backwards—or, in your words, is stagnant—adding further compliance and red tape, adding further burden of disclosures to government, is probably going to make the situation worse rather than better and that something needs to be done about that?

I think there was recognition in the budget. There were some changes that were announced, including changes to the threshold, to try to reduce some of those compliance costs. I think, sending us this inquiry—it specifically asks in the terms of reference for ways in which some of the compliance burden, not just of scope 3 but of other non-financial reporting, can be reduced. I think that is a recognition that this is an issue that governments think worthy of looking at further.
Has the government indicated to you that it would be willing to delay implementation of scope 3 reporting or, indeed, drop it altogether?
No, they've sent us the terms of reference, which ask us to look at different options for reducing the burden.
Looking at ways to make a bad idea more palatable!
When we look at that, we will look at the full suite of different options that might be available for the scope 3.

I'm going to follow up with just two questions about some inquiries that you've got on the go at the moment and when they might be reporting. One is the business reporting requirements inquiry. Is that the same inquiry that you're referring to now?
That's right.
The interim report, you said, is due next month, and the final report—when did you say that's due?
On 24 February.
You said that the interim report will be made public very quickly, but the final report goes to government and then it's their decision on what to do with it.
They need to table it within 25 sitting days.
The other report is on reducing barriers to business dynamism.
The interim report is also to be released in November, so that's coming up soon. The final report is to be provided to government in May next year.
Do you have a specific date in mid-November that's scheduled for both of those reports?
I don't have that here right now, but I think we are working towards a specific date. I think we're probably close enough now that we could provide a date that we're intending.
Terrific. Thank you, Chair.
That concludes our questions, doesn't it?
Sorry—I really rushed through those. I'll put lots on notice.
I like the productivity!
Thanks to everyone for their brevity. That concludes our questions with you, representatives from the Productivity Commission.
The committee now welcomes representatives from the Australian Office of Financial Management. Do you wish to make an opening statement?

I would like to make a very short opening statement, thank you. Since last Senate estimates, the Australian Office of Financial Management has continued to focus on its core purposes, issuing debt securities on behalf of the Australian Government, managing cash and debt portfolios, and implementing initiatives in the Australian securitisation market. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continue to contribute to energy price volatility and inflation uncertainty. Sovereign bond markets remain functional, with yields elevated and occasionally volatile. Central bank policy expectations remain a key market driver of global sovereign bond yields amid persistent inflation risks. Despite the prevailing volatility, the Australian Commonwealth government bond market has remained functional, deep and liquid. The depth and liquidity of the ACGB market, together with Australia's modest debt levels and smaller deficits relative to global peers, remains appealing to investors. Tenders across all three AOFM funding instruments, Treasury bonds, Treasury index bonds and Treasury notes have proceeded smoothly, supported by consistently solid demand from market participants. Coverage ratios and tender spreads to mid-market levels have remained strong. I'd like to provide the committee with an update on the progress of our issuance plans for 2026-27 financial year. For 2026-27, based on budget estimates—
Is this a short statement?
Very short.
Okay, could we go as quickly as we can, because we are running quite short on time.
Okay. Can I do maybe the last two paragraphs?
Sure.

Okay, let me talk about issuance. In regard to the independent review, which was released on 26 April 2026, it confirmed that the AOFM is continuing to perform its core functions and that the sovereign debt management program is highly regarded by market participants. The Treasury and the AOFM agreed to six recommendations identified by the review and, as at October 2026, the AOFM and Treasury have fully implemented four of the six recommendations, as well as progressing on the remaining two. In regard to the organisation, I'm pleased to share that 100 per cent of AOFM participated in our APS employment survey. We saw improvement in results across all indices and they exceeded APS average on every measure. Results improved from 20 to 25 in 96 per cent of questions, demonstrating that focused efforts have translated into positive improvements in leadership, communication and overall organisational structure. Alongside these results, our workforce remains stable, with staff turnover for 2025-26 being 16 per cent, below the five-year average of 22 per cent. Thank you for the opportunity to do a truncated version of the opening statement, and I welcome your questions.
Thank you very much. I didn't realise that it was tabled and in front of us. Anyway, we all have the full statement here.
Thanks and good evening. Can you tell me the total Australian government securities on issue at the moment?
It's $995.9 billion.
What was the last issue of 10-year Treasury bonds? What was the weighted average yield for that last 10-year Treasury bond you took to market?
I'll pass to the Deputy CEO to answer that question.
We last issued a 10-year tender of a billion dollars of the October 2037 maturity on 27th October. The weighted average yield there was 5.2 per cent. Coverage ratio was 3.1 times covered.
What are 10-year Treasury bond yields trading at on the secondary market at the moment?
Around 5.2 per cent.

I noticed in your opening statement you talk about the issuance of Treasury bonds over 2026-27 being expected to be around $125 billion. Is that new debt or does that include the rollover in existing debt?
That includes refinancing as well.
Okay. How much debt do you expect to have to refinance by the end of this calendar year? Have you got the breakdown of those?
We do.
It's about $79 billion of refinancing. Half of that has already matured, in September 2026, and the other half roughly will mature in April 2027.

Okay, so it's $79 billion by the end of this financial year. In the budget papers, they assume a weighted average cost of borrowing for issuance of Treasury bonds at 4.8 per cent, which is up from what it was, 4.4 per cent at MYEFO.
That's correct.
Is your advice to Treasury that they will need to increase that assumption in the upcoming MYEFO?
We're in the process of doing the mid-year economic update and the latest yields will be updated in the next budget release.
Okay, but it's going to be higher than 4.8 per cent, isn't it?
That's correct.
Have you done a calculation of how much that will add to interest repayments?
That's a better question for the Treasury, but I would note that the budget papers do have some sensitivity analysis that you could refer to if you were looking for a quick answer.
But the general view, without having to quantify it, is that budget estimate will need to be revised up later.
It will. That is correct.

Just looking at Australia's 10-year Treasury bond yields, they are higher than Portugal, higher than Italy, higher than Greece, higher than Spain, higher than France, higher than the United States, higher than Canada, higher than Japan, higher than New Zealand. They're some of the highest amongst advanced economies in the world. Why is that?

I guess to start with, the year levels reflect each economy's policy rate outlook, inflation, growth and term premium. With the RBA actually having a target rate of inflation between 2 and 3 per cent and 2.5 per cent as the mid-percent, that is actually 50 basis points higher than a lot of the advanced economies. Certainly since the GFC, we have continued to have higher rates than most advanced economies, and this actually is reflective of our stronger economic performance. In regard to European yields—you talked about Portugal—it reflects structurally lower growth and a history of heavy central bank buying of bonds, which actually influences some of the pricing. The other sort of factor that we look at is that Australia has historically run current account deficits, so we have historically relied more on foreign capital, which means that investors sometimes require a higher yield than in economies with more domestic savings.
What about the inflation outlook and the inflation expectations?
That is definitely a component of it.

What does that do? Which way does that tend to push Australian bond yields? If inflation and the inflation outlook is higher in Australia than in some of those other economies, what does that do to 10-year Treasury bond yields?

Inflation is reflective of both domestic factors and international factors. Certainly what we've seen since the Middle East conflict is that those global factors are playing more into yields, and certainly what we've seen is that our increases since February have been smaller than those in some of those other advanced economies.
Our increases in Treasury bond yields?
Yes.
But the buyers of government debt, Treasury bond yields, also look at which way monetary policy is going, right?
They do.
Are you seeing on the bond market an expectation that the Reserve Bank will need to further tighten monetary policy this year? I see you nodding, Mr Wheadon.

Certainly the market does, indeed, have another rate hike priced in for this calendar year. In fact, there's about one to and a quarter hikes now priced in for the rest of the year. That would take our cash rate—
About 30 basis points?
About 30-ish.
Does that feed directly into the Treasury bond?

Yeah, the front end of the yield curve is anchored by the RBA. With the longer-term bond rates, the biggest component of a 10-year bond rate would be expectations for the future path of the cash rate over time. Right now, the differential is 4.6 per cent on the cash rate, expected to go up to 4.9, call it circa 5. The 10-year bond yield is around 5.2 per cent, so it's relatively flat in terms of that at this point in time.
Have you got a figure of what you expect Australian government bonds on issue to be at the end of this financial year? Do you model that or is that only Treasury?
There's no update to the budget number, and I think the budget number was just over a trillion dollars by the end of the year.

Okay, no changes to that. I do have some further questions on the Debelle review recommendations, but I'm happy to put those on notice in the interests of time. Thank you for addressing some of those in your opening statement. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much, Senator Sharma. That concludes our questions with the AOFM. Thank you so much for coming this evening.

I now welcome representatives from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. We do have your opening statement here and would very much appreciate it if you are happy for us to table that, and we can go straight to questions.
I'm very happy to do so, thank you, Chair, and good evening to senators.
Thank you. First off, we have Senator McDonald.

Thank you. Good evening. It's lovely to see you. Can I just clarify your responsibilities now with gas market reporting and gas prices reporting? That will all be handled by the AER by what point? Can you just give me that timeframe, please?

We are currently working together with Treasury, DCCEEW and the AER in respect of timing that the government is to make a final decision on. We are continuing to review gas pricing and the ADGSM advising at this current time. I believe that the decision should be made and announced fairly soon, but I'm not sure of the exact timing.

Could you advise what information you have on average cost of production for gas in Australia? Could you divide it up roughly into markets? What markets would you divide it up into? Could we do Victoria and Queensland? We haven't talked about the regions before. I think we've just talked about the east coast.

Yes, though we have looked at the southern states. We had both cost of production from earlier periods, so looking at $9 through to $12. I will check with our head of this team, Angela Woo, who is right here, as to more recent data that we have.

The ACCC itself has not produced gas production estimates, but we did commission Rystad Energy to produce some estimates for us. They were published in conjunction with our December report last year. That report provided some gas production costs based on what they called supply regions, and so they identified 21 supply regions. We can provide you the link to the publication. It estimated production costs based on what they called a full life cycle production cost basis, which looked at past costs as well as future costs, and then a forward-looking basis. The forward-looking basis costs were based on basins that are fairly mature and that have recovered their sunk costs. So they've got quite a bit of detail on how they calculated the average production cost for those basins.
Terrific. So you'll give me that link on notice?
Yes.

Ideally, could you give it to me tomorrow, because we'll have the second of our gas reservation inquiry hearings on Friday, so it would be the most helpful. Could I turn now to something quite different, which is airline pricing? Can you tell me what airline fares monitoring the ACCC is doing?
We currently have underway an airline pricing review. The review looks at the major metropolitan routes and a selection of regional routes.
Is Mount Isa on the regional route, from both Townsville and Brisbane?
It is not consistently. However, we are able to access that information.

Specifically, how is it possible that airlines—a big red kangaroo airline—are able to advertise a price that would involve two legs so that, when you search the two legs, it is 25 per cent higher than going in and searching the legs individually? Is that a reasonable thing for an airline to do?

It is important to understand the particular features, structurally, that are occurring in relation to remote routes. I'll start broadly and then come specifically. I expect you're travelling on a number of these routes, so you would know that there's much less competition that travellers are facing. Mount Isa is a remote route, even for regional but also major city routes. Our latest report showed that 72 per cent of remote routes were serviced by only one airline in July 2026 compared to only 13 per cent of major city routes that were serviced by only one airline, and also that real average revenue per passenger on remote routes had increased by 3.6 per cent in the year to July 2026, while it declined on major city routes, down 4 per cent, and regional routes also, down 1.5 per cent.

Moving specifically to the question of Melbourne to Brisbane and Brisbane to Mount Isa, looked at separately, Melbourne to Brisbane is served by two groups—because it's Qantas and Jetstar in the Qantas group and Virgin, so you have three airlines, though from two groups—with frequent services and substantial passenger volumes, and that supports a wider range of fares. Brisbane to Mount Isa has only two, Qantas and Virgin. Virgin is also only doing three return services per week. Unfortunately, Bonza flight between Mount Isa and Gold Coast no longer continues. We also see that business travel is a substantial proportion of travel to and from Mount Isa and you can see some differentiation in charging by airlines when they know that many passengers are FIFO passengers, so there are some features of the nature of the passengers in terms of the way in which pricing is being undertaken.

It would not surprise us, because there's more competition from Melbourne to Brisbane than Brisbane to Mount Isa, that you would see a differential, and given the higher rates that there are for remote routes. It would be of interest or concern to us if actually there was confusion through misleading price disclosures, depending upon whether you searched for the legs separately, as compared to one trip which involved the two legs. That would be of concern.

I will provide you with some specifics on that one. I don't want to hold up the committee, because this is a very specific issue, but it is regularly $1,200 economy to fly from Brisbane to Mount Isa on a jet, and it's very hard to get the local pricing stuff that's advertised because there are very strict rules about booking from that place away and back, and that's not usually how life works—but I think it is outrageous and the dynamic pricing, which drives up the price fast, again, is unconscionable. I know that we have examined airfare flights many times, but for people who want to live in parts of the country where they do important work to be, frankly, gouged because there's a large FIFO or company clientele, I think is extraordinary. I support everything we can do to shine a light on the appalling behaviour, particularly of Qantas. I see people driving that distance—24 hours to drive from Brisbane to Mount Isa, and about 12 hours to drive from Brisbane to Townsville—because they cannot afford to get on one of these outrageous flights. Also, it's dangerous. The roads are dangerous. I know that won't be the only route. We've talked about this several times. I don't know what we can do, as a parliament, to discourage this outrageous dynamic pricing and price gouging, and I don't know what more to do on that.

Finally, because we have to move on, I just want to ask whether you're doing anything further with insurance price monitoring, particularly for the northern cyclone reinsurance pool.

That particular inquiry has concluded, and we produced the final report, which did show some impact of the cyclone reinsurance pool, particularly in the higher risk areas. There were some material reductions, and some extension of availability, though those benefits were much less in the medium areas and there was somewhat higher pricing in the lower risk areas.
We will, no doubt, be calling you from that committee to get some expert analysis a little bit later. Thank you.

Thanks very much for your attendance this evening and your ongoing cooperation with various matters for me. There are two that I would like to raise this evening. The first is an update on the Craveable Brands matter. When we met at the last estimates, I got the strong indication that we were close to a decision or announcement. There hasn't been one thus far, and I was hoping you might be able to update me on the progress of that investigation and when my constituents might get an update from the ACCC.

Thank you, Senator. We are very actively engaged in that investigation. We consider that there are serious matters that we need to conclude the investigation in relation to. I know that team is very focused on it. I will pass to the head of our Consumer and Fair Trading Enforcement and Compliance Team, Lauren.

I do apologise, Senator, that I don't have more of a specific update for you, other than to say that we are progressing as quickly as we can. We are hoping to take the matter to our commissioners for a decision in the new year, and that is how we're progressing at this stage. We've met with you separately and provided some information about the various complications of this matter. My prediction of that timing is an estimate, but it is certainly our goal to move as quickly as we can. We are engaging with all parties involved in the matter and are very happy to speak further to franchisees.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: The extension of the time before a decision goes to commissioners is a demonstration of the increasing complexity and seriousness of the matter?

Correct. It is very serious and complex, and it's very important that we get it right and ensure that any outcome we seek to achieve is long-lasting and impactful. It's important that we do that properly.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: Many of the senior directors and employees of Craveable Brands have now left those positions. How does the ACCC investigate and prosecute when those individuals are no longer in those positions?
It doesn't impact our ability to investigate fully and also examine those individuals to the extent that they can provide information to support the investigation.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: Have Craveable Brands cooperated with the investigation?
Yes.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: And they are continuing to cooperate?
Yes.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: Is the matter that will be put before commissioners for decision early in the new year likely to slip further? Have you got a higher level of confidence that the matter will get to a decision early next year? Is it a greater level of confidence than we had at the last estimates because that has slipped?
I have a high level of confidence this time.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: Could I turn to a second matter. I wrote to the ACCC about this. This is the matter involving Woolworths employees—not one, not undercover, not subtle—going on what I think Woolworths called a marketing exercise to an IGA store in Taylor Road dressed in Woolworths attire. For full transparency, I wrote to the CEO of Woolworths and got a very unsatisfactory response not from her but from others in the organisation. I followed up with the Woolworths CEO again asking questions in response to the letter that I got from one of her leadership group. I've not yet had a response to that. Chair, could you give me an update on what, if any, inquiries the ACCC has made in regard to this matter?

We are continuing to monitor and consider concerns and have made some inquiries in relation to the behaviour, which we are treating as alleged anticompetitive behaviour, including assessing the issue that has been raised by the Taylor Road IGA store owners about the Woolworths employees surveying their IGA store.
When you say 'alleged anticompetitive', is that a position that you have come to or is that an allegation that others have made that you're inquiring into?
That's an allegation that has been made by the IGA store owners.
You said you were monitoring and responding to inquiries. Is that the same as investigating?
Yes, and considering concerns.
What is the timetable or the process that is involved in that consideration of concerns?
I think it's too early to say, because we need to scope it further.
Have you spoken with Woolworths, and have you asked Woolworths for an explanation or an account of the matter from their perspective?
I do not know the answer to that looking at the material that I have, and I expect that we should take that on notice.
It would be very strange not to have spoken to Woolworths, given that this matter arose some six weeks ago. It would be, wouldn't it?
My understanding is that initial inquiries are being made with the IGA store owners and sometimes we. It's best to get that factual information first before taking the inquiries to that next step.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: It doesn't take four to six weeks to establish the facts from the IGA Taylor Road. I visited them myself and was quickly able to ascertain the facts. They wrote to me with the facts.
