I think they've written to you with the facts. It seems very strange not to have called Woolworths in for an explanation.

I think the next step that Gina spoke to though is looking at the facts and determining whether there is any potential allegation and what more we would need to support any such allegation. It takes time to thoroughly consider these things.
witness_position: Executive General Manager, Consumer and Fair Trading

text: Woolworths characterises this as local market familiarisation. Woolworths conducted an internal review. They've not yet made it available to me, but I've asked for it. They have acknowledged that this event fell well short of their own standards. Perhaps I should share my correspondence—and their correspondence with me—with you. I don't know how the owners of the IGA store in Taylor Road are going to respond when they hear the evidence tonight that Woolworths has not even been approached. It's not as if they're short staffed. Is this common behaviour from big supermarkets?

I would ask that we have the opportunity to provide the information to you so that we know we're all coming to the same-facts situation. We need to be able to confirm that we've not spoken to them, and we're not in a position to do that at the moment.
Okay, but if you had spoken to them you would know that.

It can sit within a team without coming to our attention. However, I think, Senator Smith, you were about if we were aware of this conduct occurring on other occasions? The answer to that is, to my knowledge, no. We do know there is very extensive gathering of information about competitor pricing, but not that it would involve such a manner.
It was brazen and at a time when there's a tremendous amount of scrutiny of Woolworths and its competitors from consumers and indeed from the—
From the ACCC.

Itself. Wow! They seem a bit immune to public sentiment and public concern. I'll leave it at that. Thank you very much, and I look forward to hearing about whether or not Woolworths has been engaged at this point. If it hasn't, I look forward to being reassured that it will be. They have done an internal review. I would have thought that that was a very important first step.
That concludes our questions for the ACCC. We thank you very much for coming tonight.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: While everyone is settling into their chairs, I would like to welcome, on behalf of the committee, representatives of Housing Australia and officers from the Department of the Treasury's Housing Group. In the interests of time, if you have an opening statement, is it available to table so that we can go straight to questions?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Thank you, Chair. Housing Australia doesn't have an opening statement for today.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We will go straight to questions, then.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Chair, if I may, we do have an opening statement, which really arises out of the matters considered by the references committee last week. I'm happy to table that, given the time, just, in particular, to help the committee understand the roles and responsibilities between Housing Australia and Treasury.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That is fantastic. Thank you very much, Mr Rimmer. We will make sure we get copies of that to everybody as we get going. Senator Bragg.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Thank you for being here this evening. I have some initial questions for the new chair. Congratulations on your appointment.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'd just like to ask about how your appointment came about. Did you apply for this role, or were you approached?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I was approached.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: By?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm trying to remember—by a number of people, actually, one of whom was Mr Rimmer here.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You were approached by Mr Rimmer. Did you bump into him at the airport or—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No, he called me.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: He called you by phone?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: He called me to ask me if I would be interested in being considered.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: He suggested that you should consider applying if you were interested?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And you submitted an application to someone at the Treasury?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I submitted a CV, yes.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: To the Treasury?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, indeed.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Did you meet with other government officials before your appointment was announced, such as the minister or other people?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I spoke to the minister; I did not meet with her. I also spoke with the Secretary of Prime Minister and Cabinet.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Were you asked to submit any disclosures about real or perceived conflicts of interest?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I spoke of real or perceived conflicts of interest because I do have a number of roles other than this one, so we did discuss the fact that I'm still a member of a major bank board, and there could be a perceived conflict of interest, given banks are involved in funding some of the affordability schemes. I also discussed my role as Chair of the Super Members Council and whether there could be perceived, as opposed to real, conflicts there. But, yes, all of those matters were discussed.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Who decided, ultimately, that the Super Members Council real or perceived conflict was manageable and didn't need to be eliminated?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator, I can—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Perhaps the Treasury could answer that. I can tell you what the process is for managing it, which is not that uncommon, but yes.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This was a closed, competitive process run in accordance with the Australian Government Appointments Framework. As part of the Australian government appointments process, it's normal to submit a personal interest declaration form. Ms Sherry did that. That matter was then considered by cabinet in the normal process for significant appointments, and Ms Sherry was appointed following that process. In relation to conflicts, there's the initial consideration by cabinet. There's also a requirement under the PGPA Act rules to disclose any material personal interests. In addition, Housing Australia has its own internal policies about the management of conflict of interest and processes to ensure that individual board members or, for that matter, members of the executive who have conflicts manage those conflicts in a way that's appropriate and consistent with good governance.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In this case, it was decided that this was not a conflict that needed to be eliminated.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, that's right. Implicitly, it was decided that it was a conflict that could be managed.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that. I'm asking questions so that we have a proper public record of these matters, because these are matters of public interest. I think it's good that people of great experience in public companies are prepared to help serve their country in different ways, but it's also appropriate that the Senate considers whether or not there are conflicts which need to be discussed in these forums. In relation to this particular perception, which some may have, around the Super Members Council being a lobby shop, effectively, for the super funds, which have been successful so far in being able to pick up money from the housing future fund, I think the ordinary-person test here—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: If I may say, though, it's not the Super Members Council that has done that—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: it's the individual funds who have been able to do that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that. In the case of the assembled transactions, which I think are $2.5 billion over the course of the contract period of 25 years—a significant amount of funds—both of the organisations which are major investors in Assemble, Hester and AustralianSuper, are on the board of the Super Members Council. What happens when these contracts, which are material to the operation of the HAFF, come up in the course of business of the housing future fund?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: If there was any perception of conflict, I would step aside—firstly, if they came to the board, because most of them actually sit within the delegation of the management as opposed to coming directly to the board. If any of those funds came to the board and it was felt there was a perception, I would step aside. That's the way we also manage it for other members of the board. We have a member of the board who's involved in community housing and a member of the board who's involved in building in the development sector. Anybody, where there's a perceived perception or actual perception, steps aside from a decision where that may impact.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: But, if such a material amount of funds is being allocated to Assemble, I would have thought that every board meeting would be considering how those contracts are going, given so much of the taxpayer funds have been allocated to these particular entities.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I've been chair for two meetings. It has not come to either of those meetings, but largely the management of the contracts actually sits within the delegation of the CEO and the team inside Housing Australia. It was decided prior to me becoming chair and it is now within the delegation of the CEO and the management. If there was a reason it had to come to the board and there was any sense of perception of conflict of interest, I would step out of that conversation.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Your policy is that the chair will recuse themselves if these issues come up; otherwise it's business as usual.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And it's fairly normal practice in organisations that, if there is actual or perceived conflict of interest, you would step aside for that discussion.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The government have an agenda to try and help institutions get access to this fund. I would have thought that, in a day-to-day sense, a lot of these issues would come up at the board meetings.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I can help. I've been an observer at a number of board meetings, perhaps more meetings cumulatively than other people at the table. Housing Australia doesn't preference any particular form of institutional capital. You're right: the government's policy is to try and attract capital into the Housing Australia Future Fund to reduce the cost to the taxpayer and ensure that the fund operates as effectively as possible. It's simply not the case that the interests of individual superannuation funds are considered often or frequently, or even at all. And, in any case, the Super Members Council is not an investor. It is a peak body that represents the interests of profit-for-member superannuation funds. It is a very remote perception of conflict that, in the interests of complete belt and braces, the chair has indicated that she would recuse herself from certain discussions. But it's really a very remote conflict in the first place.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, if you're giving 20 per cent of the taxpayer funds to one entity which is a related entity, in some way, to this organisation, I think it's a reasonable line of inquiry for us to make.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: A related entity has quite a precise meaning, and that is 100 per cent not accurate.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, there are a thousand different definitions of that, I can assure you, as someone who looked at this as a day job for quite a long time. How's the fund going at the moment? It's done—is it 1,600 homes so far?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No, it's a bit more than that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think these questions are for the agency, not for you.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: At the moment, since launching the Housing Australia Future Fund, as at 30 September 2026 22,631 social and affordable homes have been approved across funding rounds 1, 2 and 3. As at 30 September, almost 50 per cent or more than 10,700 of these approved social and affordable homes have either been completed or are currently under construction. So, to be specific, the completed home number is now sitting at 2,062, in construction is 8,683, and there are more homes progressing through planning and predevelopment.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In terms of the targets that you were supposed to meet that we had an earlier interaction about, am I right in saying that you should have hit 6,000 by this stage?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think this was a conversation we had last week at the social housing—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, I just wanted to tie it up.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Very happy to close it out. I believe the number you're referring to is from our 2025-26 corporate plan. For 2025-26 there was sort of a corporate target that's in there about what we would contract. It was a contracting target for that financial year, and that contracting target was 6,000.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You didn't have an actual completions target.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's right. And I think what's important to point out in this regard is that, when we think about the program, the targets were structured taking into consideration where the program was up to. In the early years of the fund we always intended that a part of that was about contracting the program. That's because with any of these deals of these scales, particularly some of the ones of significant size where there's over quite a number of dwellings, these partnerships can take time to form. And, like anyone who's trying to build a home, there are a range of steps required. We need to secure land, secure finance and contract with builders, and we know what sits at the heart of enabling that to happen is contracting. So that really informed our targets.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Will you do targets for completions for the remaining years of the fund?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We talked a lot about targets last week, as well.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's right.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The Australian government has committed to deliver 40,000 social and affordable homes—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that. Everyone knows that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: By 30 June 2029. We as a corporate entity have developed some targets to guide our delivery program, and they're set out in our 2026-27 corporate plan.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Are these contracting targets, or are these completions?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It includes two types of targets. One is a funded target, and one is a completed target.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Do you mean a completed home or not?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That means a completed home.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We just want some simple answers here. These are simple questions. How many are you supposed to have done by the end of this financial year?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The target for the end of this financial year is 3,900.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And next year?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Next year, as set out in our corporate plan at the moment—I'm just doing the maths on the spot—it is 11,600.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And today we're at 1,600.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Sorry, I should say they are cumulative targets. So that 3,900 will be included in the following year. Then, by 2028-29, the remaining—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Sorry, Senator. You just said something that is not correct. It's not 1,600 today.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's 2,000. As at 30 September, 2,062 social and affordable homes have been delivered.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Under the HAFF?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That is under the HAFF.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's 2,000 now.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Did you have targets for completions for prior financial years, or did you only have targets for contracts?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: For our corporate plans, we set out targets for contracts, and that was guided by the stage of what we expected the program to be up to.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: When did you start having targets for completions?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The targets that are set out in our corporate plan for 2026-27 are completion targets.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is the first time.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is right.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is Senate estimates, so we ask a lot about targets and about what you're doing with taxpayer funds. This is the first time. This is 2026-27, and your target is 3,900 completions.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It is 3,900.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's good. That should, I imagine, working backwards from the 40,000 or 30,000—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The target under the HAFF was 30,000, which is 20,000 social homes plus 10,000 affordable homes. There's also the National Housing Accord, and that has an additional 10,000 affordable homes. We call the HAFF a combination. It's shorthand for both arrangements, which brings us to the target of 40,000 homes.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And the 40,000 is due by 2029-30?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: They're due by 30 June 2029.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So by the end of this financial year you'll be 10 per cent of the way there.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In delivery.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that. The view is that you'd build it up rapidly in the last couple of years of it. That's the plan.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: If I may jump in—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think it's all good. I think we're making progress here. We're getting simple answers and simple questions, so that's fine.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The contracted numbers should give more confidence of the pace of delivery over time.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's helpful. How many people are working in Housing Australia at the moment?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: As at 31 August, there are currently 257 staff employed at Housing Australia.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: How many are in corporate and government affairs?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We have a function that's called public affairs and government relations. Is that the function you're asking about?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes. I've been asking these questions for years to all sorts of different government agencies because it bedevils me that the government would have a government affairs department. I'm not picking on Housing Australia. I think it's a very strange and unusual decision to spend taxpayer funds this way. How many people work there, and how much does the function cost?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The key things I'd like to call out are that that team has a range of functions and responsibilities. They manage the flow of government business. That is things like ministerial and departmental requests, questions on notice and Senate orders. They manage our corporate and regulatory reporting requirements. They look after media and communications. They look after stakeholder and industry engagement. They look after events and speaking engagements, corporate planning, and performance reporting data and program insights to support our continuous improvement across the organisation. This is a team that undertakes a range of functions. I think the title is probably less relevant to the functions that they actually undertake. That team comprises 10 staff. That's about four per cent of Housing Australia's current workforce.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: And the budget?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I don't believe I have that specific detail with me. I can look to find out.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Now might be a good time. I'm going to rotate the call. Senator McGrath?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'd like to ask some questions about urban policy.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Unsurprisingly, Senator!

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm sorry.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We like talking about urban policy.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I don't want to disappoint people. Minister, you can leave the room!

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I was just wondering whether I might. I'm more periurban policy, Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm everywhere. How many times has the Urban Policy Forum met since the 2025 election?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I can start with that, and my colleagues may wish to add to it. The Urban Policy Forum has not met since the 2025 election. When it was initially established, it was for an initial period of two years with a particular membership. That period of two years has now expired, and the government in due course is giving consideration to what happens next about the Urban Policy Forum.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: My understanding is that the Prime Minister made an election commitment prior to the 2022 election to establish an urban policy forum to advise the government on urban policy issues, which they did. According to the National urban policy, the Urban Policy Forum is to play an ongoing role in the implementation of the policy. You confirm that the policy forum hasn't met since the 2025 election. Has the minister met with the Urban Policy Forum?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The Urban Policy Forum no longer exists in the current membership. The membership has expired.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: When you say 'expired', did the minister write to the members thanking them for their service? How did it expire?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Mr Coates might be able to—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Certainly. The Urban Policy Forum expired after the term of two years in May 2025, and no subsequent appointments have been made.
witness_position: Assistant Secretary, Housing Industry Capacity, Productivity and Planning Branch

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: But did the minister write to the members to say: 'You're expired,' but probably using nicer language?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'd have to take that on notice. I'm not sure that we know that at the table right now.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Okay. Now that we don't have an urban policy forum, what is the government using to replace the Urban Policy Forum?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Perhaps I've not been clear. There's no decision from government to not have an urban policy forum. It's merely the fact that the membership of the Urban Policy Forum has expired and it hasn't yet been replaced.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Hang on; I get you. So there is still an urban policy forum, but there are no members of the Urban Policy Forum.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I appreciate the semantics are perhaps a little bit tiresome—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm just trying to understand them.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: but I just want to be clear that no-one has made an active decision that the Urban Policy Forum no longer exists.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I believe that it was convened for two years. The two years concluded in March 2025—as you say, prior to the last election. It's a matter—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So the government made a decision not to continue the Urban Policy Forum.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It was convened for two years. It did those two years, and that was—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Minister, this is turning into a 'dead parrot' sketch in terms of—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It had a two-year life, and—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So it's a dead urban policy forum.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, I wouldn't use that language to describe it.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm thinking about it; it's becoming a Monty Python conversation here, in that urban policy is very important—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's a one-sided Monty Python discussion.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's your side. I'm trying to ascertain, because I have a very strong interest in urban policy. Two-thirds of Australians live in what are classified as urban areas. The government made a promise about having an urban policy forum. We seem to have an urban policy forum but have no members on it. So does it still exist?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's a matter that's under consideration by government. But can I just reassure you, because I, like you, share a very strong interest in urban policy and making sure that the Commonwealth fully engages with the productivity and other interests that are involved in cities policy. The Commonwealth has a minister for cities. This is a part of the minister's role that she takes seriously. It's a part of the Department of the Treasury's role that we take seriously. It's something that's incredibly important to the country's future, and it's something that is important to us as officials. So the fact that the Urban Policy Forum has not met for a period of time should not in any way be taken as an indication of lack of interest or focus in this area. I don't mean to be ridiculous, but the truth is there is a lot on in relation to housing, homelessness and cities policy. There is a significant set of policy challenges—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I know; I appreciate all that. I'm just trying to work out what happened to this—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, I can tell you that—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Sorry, Minister—I made a freedom-of-information request back in September, asking for copies of any correspondence between the minister and her office and any members of the Urban Policy Forum since responsibility for the Urban Policy Forum was transferred to Treasury in 2025. From memory, I think there was a nil return on that. When did the minister write to the former members of the Urban Policy Forum saying their services were no longer required? Was that July? Did I hear that correctly?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We've taken that on notice.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It was in October 2025.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So that's when the minister wrote, in October.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Indeed.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Are you sure about that, Minister?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's how I'm advised. If I'm wrong, we'll correct that in due course.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No worries.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'll do my best on this matter.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Are you sure it was October 2025? It wasn't July of this year? I'm just trying to help you and your team at the moment.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's what I'm advised. I'm sure there's a team, as you say, watching all of this, and, if they want me to correct, I will happily correct. But that's what I'm advised, and it's a matter for the minister how she proceeds from here.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text:
The urban policy implementation plan says:

The Urban Policy Forum of government-appointed urban policy advisors, including academic, local government and industry representatives, will be retained to provide advice on the implementation of the urban policy agenda.

So it was very important a couple of years ago, I'm trying to understand why it isn't important now.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator, you're at eight minutes. I'll have to rotate the call shortly.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator, from Treasury's perspective, I don't think it's safe for you to draw that conclusion from the material that's been offered in evidence to that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think the Urban Policy Forum was a good thing; I think it was good to have all the stakeholders involved. The Urban Policy Forum exists, but it hasn't had members—depending on whether the minister's right or I'm right—since October last year or July of this year. I suppose my question is: when will new members be appointed to it, or has the government decided not to appoint any members to it?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: As Mr Rimmer said, it's being considered.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Do we have a timeline on when it will be considered?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Not to my knowledge.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Can I just add one more thing, which is that we meet with a wide range of urban policy and cities policy stakeholders, including some former members of the Urban Policy Forum and, potentially, some future members. We meet with relevant stakeholders.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: To that, I've had meetings. There was a very good breakfast this morning and a roundtable yesterday because city day's coming up; it's urban cities week. The stakeholders are saying that they're disappointed about the government's failure to make appropriate appointments to this particular body. So when we say that we don't know what the timeline is—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's a matter for the minister.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator McGrath, I'm at 10 minutes. I'm going to have to rotate the call. Senator Bragg.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In terms of the financing of this particular fund, the Final Budget Outcome of 2024-25 suggests Housing Australia underspent a bit over a bill. It did the same in 2025-26. Is that right?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There is definitely a positive figure in the final budget outcome. From memory, it's $1.1 billion.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's right.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: About $400 million of that is a technical issue about the way ABA is financed and a liquidity fund, basically, as money flows to and from central government and Housing Australia. So that $400 million is really a technical issue.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So it's not an underspend then?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No, the—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It is technical, is it? Okay.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There is a matter that is more appropriately thought of as closer to an underspend, which is the initial predictions for Help to Buy expenditure were out by about 15 per cent in the first year just because it was a part-year effect, so there was $187 million there. The largest number was draw down of HAFF concessional loans, which was just a little bit behind schedule and was showing a variance of $506 million, and that really just reflects different decisions made by proponents about when they were ready to draw down those loans that they'd been granted.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So it doesn't reflect any inability to get the money out the door?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No. We would probably all prefer that the concessional loans and other financing were flowing as fast as is possible, because I think we all understand how important every social and affordable home is to get as soon as possible.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's not behind schedule. Okay, that's good to know. Has the board considered this ANAO report?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The ANAO report?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The Auditor-General's report.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm about to frustrate you, but this has been mischaracterised in Senate considerations.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I appreciate you being here as Treasury official, but I'm here to ask questions of Housing Australia.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The ANAO report is a report into Treasury's management of this program. It's not a report into the HAFF. It's not a report into Housing Australia.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I understand that. I'll come to you in a minute, thanks, Mr Rimmer. Has the board considered it?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Not at this stage, no.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Hasn't considered it, okay. You can answer now. What have you done with it?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The ANAO made, from memory, five recommendations. Ms Hunter can talk to the detail of those.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'll just ask you a question before you do your set piece. The ANAO said 1,400 houses of the 40,000 had been built. Of those, 700-odd were new homes and 670 were purchased. We've discussed this before. I mean, you know, Minister Ayres has said it's not buying houses. You say it's not buying houses.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, but none of them have been lived in.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The ANAO says—well, you're buying them from developers.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You're in a desperate, sad rush—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Here we go.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: to mischaracterise this effort. They are all built for the HAFF and delivered, and payment is delivered at the time at which they put the key in the lock, and that is the way that that is contracted to happen. You have been desperate to try and mischaracterise that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That is what the Auditor-General said.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Oh, no—no, no, no, no.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Have you read the report?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No, but I've watched your approach to these issues over many years now, trying to stop the HAFF in the Senate then complaining about it being delayed—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You haven't read it.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: and then mischaracterising the good work that has happened here.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So is the Auditor-General wrong?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The problem with the approach that you take—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Everyone's wrong, except for you.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: at a level political level is that every day more homes are built—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, some you are buying.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: and your arguments look weaker and weaker, which I think is why you're less committed to it,

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You bought 670.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: which is clear from your conduct tonight—less and less committed to this argument because the program is becoming more and more successful.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, you haven't read the report. That's what this reveals.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, I know exactly how the HAFF conducts—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It said it bought 670.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, built for the HAFF and delivered for the HAFF and paid for by HAFF.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Bought by the HAFF.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: They would not otherwise have been constructed. Nobody's ever lived in them before.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is probably not going to get us to where—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Let me come back to the department. What did the department advise in relation to this SmSf ban?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The management of the SMSF ban was in a different part of Treasury. It was in the Revenue Group. The Housing Group was peripherally involved in that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's fine. How many guarantees have been issued in the last year? Is it about 100,000?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We can get that.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think it's a Housing Australia question. While you are looking for that, I'll just give you some context. The Reserve Bank today suggested there'd be about 5,000 Australians in negative equity, likely in this scheme. How does that accord with your figures? How many people do you think are in negative equity in this scheme?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm not sure I would characterise the Reserve Bank as having given the evidence that you've just described. I have the transcript in front of me.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You'll have to check the Hansard then.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You did discuss the number of 5,000 with them, but I'm not sure that they said that the number was 5,000.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In fact, they said that the figure comes from a simulation, not from a real sample, of five per cent deposit scheme participants.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: They said it was quite a reasonable assessment.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: They said that it was from a simulation. It's an incredibly robust program.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So how many are in negative equity?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There will be a number of five per cent deposit scheme guarantees that have loan-to-valuation ratios greater than 100 per cent. I think the Reserve Bank said in the Financial stability review that, in the market as a whole, the figure is about one per cent. Clearly, if you start at 95 per cent, you are at higher risk of being in that situation.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So how many? Do you know?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think it is important just to go back a step. A large number of five per cent deposit scheme guarantees actually start at lower than 90 per cent loan-to-valuation ratios, so they're in a better position. It's also the case that five per cent deposit scheme mortgages reduce in their LVR quite quickly. So, when you take all of those things into account and you look at the 99.7 per cent in front of expected loan performance outcome, the scheme is performing very well.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: How many—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator Bragg, I'll answer the question for you.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Thank you for that very lengthy speech, but I want to know how many.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You know that you're asking a question that by definition cannot be answered.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Why?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's because you would have to value every single person's—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You are running an insurance company here, and you've got no idea what you're doing.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I know you don't want to hear this. You'd have to value correctly every single person's home, which you can only do by selling it. It's utter garbage, the proposition that you are trying to advance.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Have a look at the Cotality data.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In all, 0.01 per cent of these claims have ever been paid out. I know that you disrespect young Australians who take five per cent and get the support of the government to buy a home.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We introduced the scheme, actually.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You'd much rather that people were forced to do it with the old bank of mum and dad, which most people don't have access to.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's not right. These kinds of speeches are very unhelpful.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You don't like it. It's the kind of snobbery that characterises your position.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We introduced the scheme. You know that, and you're misleading the Senate.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's the kind of snobbery that characterises your position.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The minister's political speeches don't help us.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It is an argument that cannot be made out. All of the evidence shows—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Chair, we've got a lot of questions to ask tonight.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: that people who take the five per cent deposit approach it with real seriousness, and there is very strong evidence to show this a robust scheme.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Who started this scheme then?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This scheme has been expanded by this government.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Who started it?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Well, like many things, there's a residue of the scheme that's come through from the previous government.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I think it's called the Liberal Party.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We expanded it and made it much bigger.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We've got very limited time.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: What a waste of time.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Could we narrow our questions to the ones we really need. I'm going to need to go back to Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm just going to finish my line. I don't think they know the answer.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You got the answer; you just don't like it.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Do you have a number?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We've given the evidence we've given. There have been only 15 guarantees called in in the operation of the scheme, so the scheme is performing very well.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: How many of these guarantees have gone to noncitizens in the last year?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Are we able to provide you with different timeframes in the last year? I can provide you with a share of guarantees issued by residency status as of 31 August 2026. Since permanent residents became eligible in the scheme, that might be a more relevant measure. That was on 1 July 2023. Seventy-three per cent of guarantees—that's 108,832—have been issued to Australian citizens; seven per cent, which is 9,712, of guarantees have been issued to an Australian citizen purchasing jointly with a permanent resident; and 20 per cent, which is 30,517, of guarantees have been issued to permanent residents.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That's since 2023?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Since 1 July 2023.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Do you have any data on the scheme post 1 October 2025, when the government abolished the means testing? Last time you gave evidence, I think you said that it was 50,000 permanent residents who had accessed the scheme. Are you saying it's now 30,000? Has that been revised down?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I was talking about the number of guarantees since 1 July 2023.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: How many people?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I have guarantee data.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So it was 51,000 people last time. You don't have the people data this time; is that what you're saying?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I have the guarantees. Our view is that it is the most accurate representation of the scheme. People apply for a guarantee. They can do it singly or jointly at the household level. We do refer mostly to the number of guarantees that are issued.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: On your own website, you talk about people. In the interest of time, you're saying there are 30,000 guarantees since 2023, yes?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm saying that 20 per cent of all guarantees since 1 July 2023, which is the date when permanent residents became eligible, have been issued to permanent residents. There was a further seven per cent, which was 9,712 guarantees, that had been issued to an Australian citizen who had purchased jointly with a permanent resident.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Do you have any information since 1 October 2025, after the means testing was abolished?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Is there a particular dataset that you're—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: What about people earning more than $200,000. Or maybe I should ask it in your way: how many guarantees have been issued to people or couples earning more than 200 grand?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I can take you through some of that data. The total number of guarantees since 1 October 2025, when the scheme expanded, is 59,953. That's the total. The majority of those guarantees are issued to people with an income of less than $200,000, and this includes single households and joint borrowers. Around two per cent of single borrowers have had an income above $250,000—and I note that this is income that is servicing debt solely, that is, without a secondary income. There are 36,238 guarantees for joint borrowers since expansion. The majority of guarantees are joint borrowers. Of these, 3,492 have a household income above $250,000. I do note that for these households there are two incomes that are contributing to that income level.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Have any gone to more than $400,000 a year?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I don't have that data with me. I just have $250,000 and over.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You break down just above and below 200,000, do you?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: My highest income band is above $250,000.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: So you don't know anything above that?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That data would be held by Housing Australia. We could take that question on notice.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Can you provide that, on notice, to us in bands of $200,000 up to a million dollars, I suppose.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We can take that on notice.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm going to have to rotate the call after this question, Senator Bragg, because your colleague has just five minutes worth to finish off.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Who has questions?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Senator McGrath.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Okay, go on then.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Oh, thank you! Minister, in 2021 the Prime Minister said Labor were going to sign city deals and would look to sign new city partnerships that met the needs of local communities based on local understanding and transparent criteria. What work is underway to sign new city partnerships?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'll seek some advice about that and maybe come back to you. It's not something I'm in a position to talk to you about this evening. You refer to comments in 2021; is that right?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes. I'll put it to the department then.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, they may be in a position to provide you with some more information.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: What work is underway to sign new city partnerships?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There is a large volume of work currently underway to work with local government and state governments in particular about expanding housing supply through partnership models. In fact, I think there's $8.5 billion worth of enabling infrastructure funding out there on the table at the moment.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Okay, but how many—whatever you want to call them; the Prime Minister called them 'city partnerships'—are in existence?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: The concept of city partnership—capital-c, capital-p—is not something that's part of the government's current agenda, but there are a range of other programs that perform pretty similar functions. When you look at the city deals and what they were, a lot of them were about enabling infrastructure and community infrastructure.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There's no such thing as a city partnership?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Not at the present time.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Would this be another broken election commitment, Minister?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: No, we're—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Seems like it.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: As the Secretary or as the Director-General of the Housing Group, I should say—I've elevated him, briefly, for a few minutes—has indicated, substantial investments in infrastructure that go to—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You promised city partnerships. None have happened. That was four years ago.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: There is a substantial investment from the Commonwealth in the infrastructure that is really the meat of the old city partnerships. We're in 2026.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes, it's five years since. It's a broken promise.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We are, as you say, five years down the track, and we're in a very expansive program.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Can I ask a very earnest question, though.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Yes.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: In QON 180 you say that Minister O'Neil was first provided with a copy of the draft State of Australian cities report on 5 September—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm sorry, the draft what?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is to the department—on 5 September 2025. Why was this draft report, which was a key election commitment in the minister's portfolio, not included in her incoming ministerial briefing when she became Minister for Cities?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I don't think anyone at the table was present—this part of Treasury didn't exist—at that time, so I'm not sure we can help you with an answer to that question.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It is, though, a very earnest question, and we'll—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm going to give you an even more earnest question—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We'll very earnestly take it on notice.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: in relation to dashboards, which I get particularly excited about. In QON 169—this is relating to dashboards of planning, land use and housing supply data—you advise that jurisdictions are expected to deliver this by the end of 2026. Is that timetable still on track, and on what date will the dashboards become operational?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: It's good to be able to answer a question for you, Senator.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Housing Supply, Productivity and Engagement Division

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: You're going to end on a positive note, aren't you?

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I am. I'm going to tell you that those dashboards are to be delivered to CFFR at the end of the year. We are working very closely with states and territories. We've had a number of engagements with them about the production of the dashboards. They are working on the data that is needed to populate those, and we expect those to be delivered to CFFR at the end of the year.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Housing Supply, Productivity and Engagement Division

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I was going to tell you needed to get out more! She's actually given you an answer. That's a very good development.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: This is what it's all about. It's an exchange of information. This is to be the model of what estimates are about—questions being answered. Minister, you should take note.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I'm all ears.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: Sadly, that's all. I've got more questions, but, looking at the time, I'm not going to push my luck.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: We can place the rest of them on notice. That concludes today's hearings.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I haven't finished. Can we run through another process? Only having one hour for this whole housing thing is just ridiculous.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: That will have to be taken offline because the program has been agreed to by the committee—

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: I get that, but we've barely scratched the surface.

agency: Department of the Treasury Housing Australia
text: and we've hit the 11 o'clock mark tonight. That's something we can discuss offline. Thank you to everybody who attended today. I note that all items tabled throughout the day will be accepted. I thank Minister Ayres, Minister Gallagher, officers from the Department of the Treasury and the Treasury portfolio and everyone who gave evidence to the committee today. I also thank Hansard and Broadcasting, my deputy chair and fellow committee members.
